Notably, emerging market economies face heightened risks amid a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar, and possible trade protectionism measures by the US. Nevertheless, liquidity positions remained sound, and aggregate amount of RMB loans increased further in the second half of 2016. Following the introduction of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment, but has rebounded somewhat recently. Looking ahead, banks should prudently assess the possibility that the pace of US interest rate hikes may be faster than expected, as well as the impact of broader policy uncertainty in the US, particularly the risk of significant fund outflows and the potential impact on local interest rates. Following the election of Trump as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainties. Not only was the election outcome unexpected by the market, but the associated market reactions were also surprising. In particular, expectations that measures introduced by Trump, such as tax reform, increased infrastructure investment and deregulation, would boost US economic growth drove global equity markets higher. After the new US administration takes office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. However, the anticipated tax cuts by Trump may fail to provide the expected stimulus to US economic growth. In particular, as US economic activities are already close to their potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, but would exacerbate upside risks to US inflation. While it remains uncertain whether the Fed will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary tightening as a result, long-term bond yields have risen visibly, partly reflecting market expectation that inflation risks are increasing. Meanwhile, rising trade protectionism would result in a "lose-lose" situation for both the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions, undermine overall welfare, hinder global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to global economic outlooks. At the same time, political instability remains a major risk and headwind, particularly for the European economy where recovery remains weak. As for emerging market economies, the risk of fund outflows due to a faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar has increased. This could weigh on economic growth and exacerbate the risk of rapid fund outflows. Indeed, amid expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration and concerns over surging energy prices, the market has repriced inflation risks, leading to broad-based and notable increases in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. The findings suggest that since the "taper tantrum" in 2013, the influence of the US Treasury bond market on sovereign bond markets has deepened, and that US interest rate hikes and tightened financial conditions would have significant impacts on both advanced economies and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016 as exports recovered, but market volatility, including regional currency depreciation and rising sovereign yields caused by earlier concerns over possible policy changes by the new US administration, only gradually stabilised earlier this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but it faces rising risks and uncertainties. US interest rate hikes, regional currency depreciation, and heightened financial market volatility could lead to tightened financial conditions. Meanwhile, the US may adopt protectionist policies, which could affect economies in the region, although the actual impact remains unclear at present. In Mainland China, overall economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016, supported by robust infrastructure investment growth and improved private sector business spending. Although the economy continued to show signs of stabilising, uncertainties remain regarding the Mainland's growth outlook. In particular, given the government's determination to curb rising property prices, if the real estate market continues to cool, the contribution of the real estate sector to growth may diminish this year. Meanwhile, the continued推进 of economic structural adjustments and changes in China-US trade relations may add to uncertainties in the near-term economic outlook. Externally, although the RMB exchange rate remained stable against the CFETS basket during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, before seemingly easing slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilisation in private sector economic activities, there remain some concerns in the market about the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly given the divergence between accelerating M1 growth and slowing M2 growth. Box 2 (see page 24) examines whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Box 3 (see page 27) explores factors that may have contributed to the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings indicate no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, and that the main reason for M1 growth being significantly faster than M2 is that monetary easing in recent years has reduced the opportunity cost of holding liquid money, while rising economic uncertainties may have increased precautionary demand for money. Hong Kong's economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth rose to 1.2% in the fourth quarter from 0.8% in the third quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while buoyant infrastructure activities in the fourth quarter boosted investment growth. Externally, growth in goods exports rose alongside improved regional trade flows, while exports of services recorded steady growth amid a recovery in trade-related and transport services. Due to faster growth in imports of goods and services, net trade continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half. Amid rising economic growth, the headline unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain mild. The Government and market consensus forecast real GDP growth for 2017 at 2-3% and 2.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook still faces significant external headwinds. Protectionist rhetoric from the new US administration has increased downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong's external demand. Amid upward pressure on the US dollar and expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, global financial conditions are expected to become less supportive of the real economy, and tail risks could potentially lead to tightened local financial conditions. Box 4 (see page 41) discusses the compilation of a Financial Conditions Index for Hong Kong to facilitate monitoring of local financial conditions. Since the second half of 2016, local inflationary pressures have remained mild, while quarterly inflation momentum picked up slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to food price volatility and rising housing rentals. With import prices remaining stable and domestic cost pressures mild, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, though it weakened occasionally following the US rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered. Alongside US dollar appreciation, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate rose further. Due to the large Monetary Base, HIBOR remained low, but has risen since October due to year-end funding demand and catch-up with US rate hikes. Consequently, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in housing loan business, the average mortgage rates edged up to 2.07% in January 2017. Aggregate amount of RMB loans accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with 2.2% in the first half. Growth was supported by strengthening local economic activities and increased financing needs of multinational corporations towards the end of the year. Domestic loans growth picked up slightly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a slight decline in the first half. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loan recorded growth of 3.2% as borrowers in the Mainland gradually reduced repayment of foreign currency loans. Banks' funding position remained largely sound. The Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio edged down to 77.1% at end-2016, reflecting that deposit growth outpaced loan growth. The overall foreign currency LTD ratio fell to 59.9% at year-end, while the US dollar LTD ratio declined notably to 63.8% due to strong growth in US dollar deposits. Due to US dollar strength, both onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this background, the offshore renminbi (CNH) liquidity pool in Hong Kong (comprising Customer deposits and certificates of deposit) consolidated further alongside other offshore renminbi markets, and volatility in CNH HIBOR increased notably. Nevertheless, banks' management of renminbi liquidity remained robust, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Offshore renminbi business in Hong Kong is likely to continue facing headwinds arising from uncertainties over the RMB exchange rate trend. Amid improving global market conditions, the Hong Kong equity market closed significantly higher during the reporting period. Although the US presidential election yielded an unexpected result, the market experienced only a brief shock. This was mainly because investors' optimism about fiscal stimulus measures by the Trump administration drove global equity markets higher. While benefiting from this, the local market remained cautious despite optimism, possibly due to concerns over a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, challenges facing the Mainland economic outlook, uncertainties over renminbi policy, and controls on fund flows. Looking ahead, while the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuations could provide support. Although Hong Kong dollar bond yields rose sharply towards the end of last year and spreads against US Treasuries widened rapidly, the Hong Kong dollar bond market continued to expand steadily during the reporting period. Meanwhile, the CNH debt market in Hong Kong recovered in the second half after contracting in the first half of 2016, but new bonds issued for the full year still declined compared with the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their earlier yield-seeking investment strategies, both the Hong Kong dollar and CNH debt markets would come under pressure. As US trade policy remains unclear and the RMB exchange rate may continue to fluctuate, the outlook for these two bond markets in the coming six months will remain subject to significant uncertainties. Following the introduction of new stamp duty measures by the Government, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment, but has rebounded somewhat recently. In view of renewed market exuberance, the Government raised stamp duty uniformly to 15% in November. Transaction volume in both primary and secondary markets declined in the subsequent two months. However, transaction volume has risen recently, partly reflecting developers increasing launches of new residential property projects. Meanwhile, property prices continued to rise to new highs, albeit at a slower pace.

Following the unexpected election of Trump as US President, uncertainties surrounding US policy have increased. While market focus has been on the potential short-term benefits of large-scale fiscal policy and business-friendly measures, US economic activities are now close to their potential. Fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a modest cyclical boost to US economic growth, but could further heighten upside risks to inflation. More importantly, emerging market economies face increasing risks from fund outflow pressures stemming from an accelerated rate hike path by the Fed and a strengthening US dollar, while potential trade protectionism measures by the US also pose threats to global trade. In East Asia, real economy activities improved slightly in the second half of 2016, and export volumes have recently seen increases. However, Against this background of US interest rate hikes, US dollar appreciation, and potential US protectionist measures, financial market volatility is expected to persist, and downside risk to US economic growth has risen. In Mainland China, supported by robust infrastructure investment growth and improved private sector business spending, overall economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. The Mainland economy continues its rebalancing process with steady expansion in the tertiary sector, but ongoing structural adjustments and changes in China-US trade relations may increase uncertainties regarding the near-term economic outlook. Given the government's determination to curb rising property prices, if the property market continues to cool, the contribution of the real estate sector to economic growth may diminish this year. Externally, although the renminbi remained largely stable against the CFETS basket during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Following the unexpected election of Trump as US President, global financial markets reacted strongly. In particular, market expectations that Trump’s policies—such as tax reform, massive increases in infrastructure spending, and deregulation—would boost US economic growth and inflation spurred major equity markets higher (Chart 2.1). Consequently, heightened market expectations for US inflation and US interest rate hikes led to a sharp rise in US Treasury yields and a stronger US dollar. Chart 2.1 Equity market indices of selected advanced economies However, the anticipated Trump tax cuts may fail to deliver the positive impact on US economic growth that markets expect. While shifting economic policy reliance toward fiscal easing would help alleviate the heavy burden on monetary easing, given the current stage of the US business cycle, whether now is the appropriate time for fiscal easing is debatable. Although US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap is gradually narrowing, and the unemployment rate in February was consistent with the Fed’s estimate of the natural unemployment rate at 4.7%, reflecting that US economic activities are already close to their potential. With the US economy currently in an expansionary phase, the fiscal multiplier would be lower than during periods of economic downturn (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. Indeed, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labour or capital could lead to reduced tax revenues (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. Regardless, with diminishing spare capacity, any further measures to boost economic growth, even if their real impact on economic growth is limited, could push up inflation. Meanwhile, other factors such as rising energy prices and commodity prices, as well as potential trade protectionism measures including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, could also heighten upside risks to US inflation. Despite increased risks of rising US inflation, the Fed has remained cautious about tightening US monetary policy and tends to maintain an ultra-loose policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partly reflecting increased US inflation risks. Since the US election, although market forecasts for future federal funds rates have been raised to approach the median of the Fed’s projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the Fed’s longer-run projections (Chart 2.2). Therefore, an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes could trigger risks of significant market volatility. While financial market focus has been on the potential short-term benefits of expansionary fiscal policy and business-friendly measures driving stronger US economic growth, long-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policy and further increases in US debt. Indeed, the Trump administration may fulfill campaign pledges to adopt trade protectionism measures. Increased trade barriers would cause market distortions that harm overall welfare, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to global economic outlooks. Chart 2.2 Projections of future federal funds rates: Fed vs. Market In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and headwind to European economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the Euro area has gradually improved, with real gross domestic product (GDP) growing moderately by 1.7% year-on-year in the fourth quarter, only slightly below the 1.8% increase in the third quarter, compared to the relatively strong recovery of the US economy, economic activities in the Euro area remain only marginally above pre-global financial crisis levels (Chart 2.3). Since the Brexit decision last summer, markets have worried about the eventual disintegration of the Euro area. Although Italy’s economic and political situation appears to have stabilized following the formation of a new government and the implementation of banking sector rescue measures, upcoming elections in Germany and France (and possibly Italy) could become political flashpoints Against this background of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment. Partly due to increased political uncertainties, sovereign yields in Europe have continued to climb, and corporate bond spreads have widened, particularly in peripheral countries. This could create a vicious cycle affecting the real economy and potentially put pressure on commercial real investment in the Euro area. Chart 2.3 Real gross domestic product (GDP) of major advanced economies In Japan, real gross domestic product (GDP) was revised upward in recent quarters, with the annualized growth rate in the fourth quarter of 2016 rising to 1.6% year-on-year, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, indicating a stronger-than-expected recovery. However, partly due to structural issues in labour markets, wage growth has been sluggish, leading to weak consumption growth. Meanwhile, the recent rapid depreciation of the yen implies that the downward pressure on "new core" goods inflation from earlier yen appreciation is set to fade. Coupled with a stronger-than-expected recovery, this suggests an improved near-term inflation outlook; while "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) fell to 0.1% in December, it is poised for bottoming out. Nevertheless, facing long-term and structural headwinds, growth may remain slow, and inflation expectations remain anchored at around 0.5%–0.6%, below levels seen when Abenomics was launched in early 2014. Thus, the risk of the inflation rate failing to reach the Bank of Japan’s 2% medium-term target persists. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, given reduced US imports post-global financial crisis and the possibility of US protectionist policies, the benefits of faster US economic growth transmitted through trade channels may be limited. At the same time, an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation will lead to tightened financial conditions, exacerbating downside risks to growth. This could weigh on economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration, coupled with concerns over surging energy prices, have led to a repricing of inflation risks, resulting in broad-based and significant increases in long-term bond yields across both advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia3, real economy activities have recently regained momentum, with regional gross domestic product (GDP) seeing modest growth and inflation rising. Real GDP growth — In the second half of 2016, as Private consumption remained stable in many regional economies, economic growth generally remained largely stable. Meanwhile, exports generally saw modest increases from the low base in 2015. This benefited not only from the stabilisation of growth in China but also from improved performance in advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters (e.g., Malaysia and IDR), the rebound in commodity prices provided additional support. Other major exporters (e.g., South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore) also resumed their uptrend driven by export growth in electronics and semiconductor sectors. Inflation — With the rebound in commodity (especially oil) prices, producer price inflation generally mirrored an upward trend. While this will push up industrial costs or even consumer spending, consumption and investment growth may benefit from diminished risks of prolonged deflation. Accelerating producer price inflation may exert upward pressure on Consumer price inflation; the actual impact depends on the extent to which producer price increases are passed through to consumer prices, which varies across economies. Consensus forecasts for the consumer price index (CPI) indicate that while inflation in many regional economies will remain slightly below central banks' 2017 targets, it will rise closer to target levels (Chart 2.4). Except for IDR, central banks in the East Asian region generally maintained their moderately loose monetary policy unchanged, while IDR cut rates twice in September and October last year to boost growth. Chart 2.4 Headline consumer price index inflation, forecasts, and central bank targets in East Asia Despite improvements in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 caused short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign exchange markets — Following the US presidential election, investors anticipated rising US inflation, leading to foreign exchange (FX) depreciation against the US dollar for most regional currencies. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies experienced smaller depreciations or even slight appreciation since the US election (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Changes in spot FX depreciation against the US dollar and nominal effective exchange rate post-US election Bond and equity markets — Asset prices dipped briefly after the US presidential election but quickly achieved stabilisation. Spreads between sovereign bonds of East Asian economies and US Treasury bonds widened. However, as markets stabilized, yields in some regional economies declined somewhat but have not returned to pre-election levels (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, spreads have narrowed compared to pre-election levels. Chart 2.6 Spreads between 10-year sovereign bonds and US Treasury bonds Portfolio investment flows — Portfolio investment fund outflows occurred in East Asia in the fourth quarter of 2016, albeit at a slower pace than during the "Taper Tantrum" in mid-2013. Net inflows resumed in the first few weeks of 2017, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, regional growth is expected to remain stable but at a pace still below historical averages. Due to heightened uncertainties regarding both the new US administration's policies and the Fed's potential policy responses, financial markets are likely to remain volatile. Significant increases in the US dollar and yields may attract flows from the region to the US, prompting investors to reduce holdings of regional assets, a concern particularly acute for assets with already elevated valuations. Tightened financial conditions under these circumstances would also impose repayment pressures on corporates with significant US dollar-denominated debt. From a macro perspective, widespread global rate hikes could also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, weighing on aggregate demand in the short term and potentially affecting potential growth in the long run. Finally, regional exporters face the potential threat of trade protectionism policies pursued by the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has continued to widen in recent years (Chart 2.7), particularly in major regional export industries such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, apparel, and textiles. Over the past two decades, increased US imports in these industries have resulted in substantial job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalizing US manufacturing could pose significant risks to regional exporters.

Accelerated growth in private consumption and buoyant public sector building and construction activities drove a slight pickup in Hong Kong's economy growth in the second half of 2016. Given the increasing uncertainties in the external environment, economic growth is expected to remain mild in 2017. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate domestic growth drivers, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained. Hong Kong's economy growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer confidence and steady labour market conditions, private consumption growth accelerated, becoming a major driver of gross domestic product (GDP) growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the Third Runway at the Hong Kong International Airport, building and construction activities also became buoyant. However, weak corporate capital spending narrowed the contribution of aggregate investment to gross domestic product (GDP) growth. Externally, both export and import of goods accelerated alongside rising regional trade flows (Chart 3.2). Trade-related and transport services drove further growth in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded partly due to strong outbound tourism demand by local residents. Net trade continued to drag on gross domestic product (GDP) growth. Chart 3.1 Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports The labour markets remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% in the first three quarters before some moderation to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, the unemployment rate in several major industries declined in the second half, including retail, accommodation and food services, partly reflecting stabilisation in the retail sector slowdown. Total employment reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained stable at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment Real economic growth is expected to remain mild in 2017. On the external front, global economic and trade growth may continue to be mild amid uncertainties in the global macroeconomic and financial conditions. Coupled with the appreciation of the real effective exchange rate of the HKD caused by a strong US dollar, Hong Kong's export performance will be dampened. Domestically, while stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to increase modestly, dragged down by rising interest rates. With increased housing supply and planned commencement of various infrastructure projects, building and construction activities should see steady growth, but sluggish business sentiment and rising interest rates will weigh on corporate capital spending. The Government currently forecasts real gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 2017 to range between 2% and 3%, while private sector analysts' estimates average 2.0%. The growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly those stemming from the external environment. Policy uncertainty under the new US administration will cloud global economic outlooks, and potential trade protectionism policies could create headwinds for global trade flows. The Brexit process and elections in several major European countries may also lead to asset market volatility and affect HKD fund flows. Furthermore, US interest rate normalization will tighten local monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, local inflation has generally remained mild, despite an uptick in quarterly momentum in recent months. Year on year, the underlying composite consumer price index (CCPI) remained stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects Inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before declining slightly to 2.4% in January. The rise in Inflation momentum was mainly due to elevated prices of tradables and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). Specifically, price inflation for tradables rose from negative territory in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, mainly driven by basic food and clothing prices. Meanwhile, since the third quarter, as the decline in fresh-letting residential rentals narrowed and following the upward adjustment of public housing rental in September 2016, the housing rental component of the CCPI increased, but subsequently moderated slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation classified by major component Chart 3.6 CCPI rental component and market rental In the near term, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained due to weak import prices and moderate Domestic cost pressures. Imported inflation will remain low as the strong HKD partially offsets the impact of bottoming out global commodity prices (Chart 3.7). Domestically, the output gap was estimated to remain close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressures and thereby contain inflation in the services component. Despite tight labour markets, wage increases have been modest in recent quarters; real earnings per person increased by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 before declining by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Against this background of persistent external uncertainties leading to prudent business sentiment, increases in labour costs should be restrained. Moreover, given the lacklustre retail sales performance in recent months, increases in retail property rentals are expected to be mild. Furthermore, the impact of softened fresh-letting residential rentals earlier will gradually feed through, helping to ease inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate is expected to decline throughout the entire year of 2017. The Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate for the year at 2.0%, lower than the 2.3% recorded in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour cost and real earnings per person The inflation outlook faces both upside risks and downside risks. On the downside, if inflation accelerates under the Trump administration, it may lead to a faster-than-expected rate hike path for US interest rates, potentially pushing up local mortgage rates and increasing downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. At the same time, appreciation of the HKD may keep import prices weak and simultaneously weaken Hong Kong's attractiveness to visitor arrivals. On the upside, if the global economic expansion is faster than expected, it may accelerate Hong Kong's economic growth and push up demand-led international commodity prices, thereby bringing upward pressure to local inflation. Additionally, the raised statutory minimum wage will take effect on May 1, 2017, which may cause further increases in inflation, though the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed through to consumer price index.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose alongside US dollar counterparts. Partly due to an improved local economic environment, aggregate amount of RMB loans continued to increase modestly. Looking ahead, amid a faster pace of US interest rate normalization, uncertainties regarding the policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe, volatility in HKD fund flows may increase. Despite financial market volatility, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November caused Asian currencies to generally decline, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar remained steady. However, the interest rate projections announced by the Federal Open Markets Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on December 13–14, 2016, fueled market expectations of faster US interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened alongside other Asian currencies, but began to show signs of weakening from mid-February as market expectations for a US rate hike in March increased. During the reporting period, the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund flow indicators Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators Amidst US dollar strength, the nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) of the Hong Kong dollar rose by 4.9% between August and December, before stabilizing recently (Chart 4.3). As the impact of narrowing inflation differentials between Hong Kong and its trading partners was minor, the real effective exchange rate index (REER) closely tracked the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER). Chart 4.3 Nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) and real effective exchange rate index (REER) Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest Balance of Payments statistics showed that non-residents’ equity investments and debt securities recorded net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and substantial initial public offering (IPO) activities (Table 4.A). However, partly driven by increased holdings of US bonds by Hong Kong banks, residents’ debt investments recorded sizeable outflows, which more than offset the inflows from non-residents. Consequently, cross-border portfolio investment recorded net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds indicated portfolio investment outflows in the last quarter of 2016, mainly because the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election, coupled with expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, put the local financial market and other Asian markets under stress (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data showed that Hong Kong’s portfolio investment faced net inflows in the first quarter of 2017, partly due to improved performance in global financial markets as investors were optimistic about the adoption of expansionary fiscal policy in the US. Chart 4.4 Market survey on equity and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, volatility in HKD fund flows may increase. A faster pace of US interest rate normalization would increase the risk of a reversal in HKD fund flows. Meanwhile, amid uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process, and elections in EU member states, fund flows may become more volatile. In addition, increasing demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may exert net inflows pressure on the Hong Kong dollar. Although northbound trading initially exceeded southbound Stock Connect following the launch of Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment fund flows between Mainland China and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising US dollar counterparts and financial market volatility, Hong Kong’s monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The HKD Monetary Base remained sizeable and further increased by 1.7% in the second half, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered, the Aggregate Balance and the total amount of outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) generally remained at a high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Among these, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) correspondingly increased, as EFBNs worth HK$49 billion were issued to meet banks' substantial needs to manage their liquidity. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base As the local economy became increasingly robust, the growth pace of Hong Kong dollar money supply accelerated. Growth in broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half to 6.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded faster growth of 6.6% in the second half (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by increased transaction demand arising from stronger local economic activities and a rebound in initial public offering (IPO) activities. Analyzed by counterpart assets, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflected increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks’ net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which respectively reflected money derived from credit expansion and net inflows of HKD funds into the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterpart assets On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits remained mixed. After growing by 10.2% in the first half, US dollar deposits recorded a higher increase of 12.8% in the second half amidst US dollar strength (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits further contracted by 10.3%, mainly due to a decrease in RMB customer deposits. Overall, total deposits with AIs increased by 6.2% in the second half of 2016, with growth for the entire year reaching 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth Amid expectations of US interest rate normalization, banks’ wholesale funding costs increased in the fourth quarter of 2016. Although Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained low, it rose partly driven by year-end financing needs and catch-up with the increases in US dollar Interbank Offered Rates. The overnight and the three-month CNH HIBOR rose by 54 and 46 basis points respectively in the second half to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards alongside the US dollar yield curve, with yields on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rising by about 90 basis points to close at 1.93% at end-December. Entering early 2017, due to reduced financing needs, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) generally declined, while yields on long-term Hong Kong Government Bonds also dipped slightly alongside US Government Bond yields. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) and 10-year Government Bond yields Due to the banking system's large deposit base, interest rate increases on the retail front were relatively small. Banks’ average funding costs (as measured by the composite interest rate) remained at a low level, rising only marginally by 6 basis points to 0.32% in January 2017 compared to seven months earlier (Chart 4.9). Due to relatively stable funding costs and intensified competition in the housing loans business, the average lending rate for new mortgages fell to a recent low of 1.71% in October 2016, before rebounding to 2.07% in January 2017 as Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rose. Chart 4.9 Composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Looking ahead, the pace of local interest rate increases will hinge on the speed of US interest rate normalization, the scale of fund outflows, and global macro-financial developments. Upward pressure on local interest rates, coupled with the rise in the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar alongside the US dollar exchange rate, may reduce the support of local financial conditions for the real economy. Box 4 discusses the compilation of a Financial Conditions Index for Hong Kong to monitor local financial conditions. Driven by stronger local economic activities and rising demand for cross-border financing, aggregate amount of RMB loans further increased by 4.2% in the second half, following a 2.2% increase in the first half (Chart 4.10). As economic growth drivers strengthened, domestic loans growth accelerated slightly from 3.2% in the first half to 4.0% in the second half. Loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half after a slight decline in the first half, partly reflecting increased year-end financing needs of multinational corporates. Analyzed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loan also recorded moderate growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced repayment of foreign currency borrowings. For the entire year of 2016, aggregate amount of RMB loans increased modestly by 6.5%, compared to 3.5% in 2015. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Analyzed by economic sector, domestic loans performed differently in the second half (Chart 4.11). Loans to financial and finance-related firms and the information technology sector recorded double-digit growth in the second half, partly reflecting strong financing needs driven by better growth outlook in these sectors. Loans to construction and property development also accelerated alongside increased private construction activities. On the other hand, despite signs of improvement in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade financing and to manufacturing, wholesale and retail sectors declined. Chart 4.11 Domestic loan growth by selected sector Household debt growth accelerated to 4.3% in the second half, compared to 0.5% in the first half. Within household debt, partly reflecting an improved economic environment, Personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal loans) rose by 7.2% (Chart 4.11), and residential mortgage loan growth accelerated to 3.1%, mainly reflecting buoyant housing transactions between July and October. Consequently, the household debt-to-GDP ratio also rose from 65.8% in the second quarter of 2016 to 67.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Household debt-to-GDP ratio and its components Banks’ funding positions remained broadly stable. Reflecting that deposit growth outpaced loan growth, the Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio dipped slightly from 78.2% at end-June 2016 to 77.1% at year-end (Chart 4.13); meanwhile, the overall foreign currency LTD ratio fell from 61.4% to 59.9% at year-end, among which the US dollar LTD ratio dropped significantly to 63.8% due to strong growth in US dollar deposits. The HKMA’s Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook indicated that loan demand would remain soft in the near term. Due to US dollar appreciation, both offshore renminbi and onshore exchange rates weakened (Chart 4.14). The offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a discount to the onshore rate for most of late 2016, closing at a yearly low of 6.98 against the US dollar at end-2016. The CNH interbank market faced renewed liquidity tightness in December, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks’ precautionary financing needs ahead of year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks increased liquidity buffers amid worsening market sentiment, the overnight CNH HIBOR surged to 61.3% on January 6, 2017. Rising funding costs subsequently led to short covering, driving a rebound in the offshore renminbi exchange rate in early January 2017, and the spread between offshore and onshore turned into a premium. Since mid-January, both offshore and onshore exchange rates have stabilized somewhat, liquidity positions have gradually improved, and The overnight and the three-month CNH HIBOR fell to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively by end-February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, Retail banks’ profitability improved compared to the same period in 2015, driven by growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a decrease in loan impairment charges. Banks’ capital positions and asset quality also remained robust. Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) saw visible increases following the US rate hike in December, closely tracking US interest rates, the liquidity positions of the banking sector remained sound. Supported by a large retail deposit base, funding costs for Retail banks remained largely stable and at low levels. However, banks should prudently assess the impact of a potentially faster-than-expected rate hike path in the US, particularly the risk of significant fund outflows and the subsequent potential impact on local interest rates. Furthermore, given the continued rise in leverage among non-local corporates, a substantial increase in interest rates could lead to a deterioration in banks’ asset quality. To enhance the resilience of Hong Kong banks against system-wide risks, the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio requirement will be raised to 1.875% effective from 1 January 2018. Retail banks’ profit improved, with the return on assets rising from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 (red line in Chart 5.1). The improvement in profitability was attributable to increases in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment charges. For the entire year of 2016, Retail banks’ overall pre-tax operating profit grew by 8.7%, while the return on assets rose from 1.05% for the full year of 2015 to 1.10%. Chart 5.2 Retail banks’ net interest margins (NIMs) Wholesale funding costs in Hong Kong saw visible increases following the resumption of US interest rate hikes in December 2016. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose significantly by 33 basis points in December 2016, although it remained at a low level by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates However, the overall impact of US rate hikes on Retail banks’ HKD funding cost remained mild. This is because retail deposits are the primary source of funding for Retail banks, and retail deposit rates remained stable and at low levels despite rate hikes. Under these circumstances, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for Retail banks, edged up by only 5 basis points to 0.31% in December 2016, after remaining at a low level of around 0.26% for more than a year. On a broader level, a similar trend was observed in the total HKD and USD funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong. While the average HKD and USD funding cost in the non-deposit market increased by 28 basis points in the second half of 2016, the increase in average deposit funding costs in the retail market was smaller, rising by only 11 basis points. Overall, the average total HKD and USD funding cost of licensed banks increased by 17 basis points (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and USD funding costs and tenors of licensed banks The magnitude and pace of increases in HIBOR exceeded those of banks’ funding costs, which could be beneficial to some Retail banks. This is because they have actively promoted HIBOR-linked housing loans over the past few years, and rising rates on such loans may help widen their overall NIMs. However, the improvement in NIMs may be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In fact, there are signs that some banks have lowered their mortgage rate spreads over benchmarks and/or offered more attractive mortgage terms to attract customers. Over the longer term, as further rate hikes are expected in the US, banks may soon face upward pressure on retail deposit rates, thereby affecting their funding costs and having a more significant impact on NIMs. Banks’ capitalisation remained strong and much higher than international minimum requirements. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) remained at a high level of 19.2% at end-December 2016 (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio stood at 16.4%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Locally incorporated AIs are required to comply with the revised capital adequacy framework Basel III, which came into effect on 1 January 2013. Therefore, capital adequacy ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity positions of the banking sector remained sound during the reporting period. Although the average LCR of category 1 institutions dipped slightly from 158.0% in the second quarter of 2016 to 156.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016, it remained at a high level (Chart 5.6). The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions also remained stable at 51.0%. Both ratios remained much higher than their respective minimum supervisory requirements, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector is resilient to liquidity shocks arising from potential fund outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.6 Liquidity Coverage Ratio Customer deposits remained the major source of funding for Retail banks. The share of customer deposits in banks’ total liabilities increased from 71.7% at end-June 2016 to 73.1% at end-December 2016 (Chart 5.7). Over the same period, the LTD ratios in HKD and foreign currency also remained largely unchanged. Estimates indicate that, assuming a parallel interest rate shock of 200 basis points across all maturities, the decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would be equivalent to 3.92% of their total capital base as at December 2016 (Chart 5.9). During the reporting period, the asset quality of Retail banks’ loan portfolios remained robust, with the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans remaining at low levels of 0.72% and 0.53% respectively at end-December 2016. Both ratios remained low by historical standards (Chart 5.10). Chart 5.10 Asset quality of Retail banks Despite current asset quality remaining robust by historical standards, banks in Hong Kong should continue to monitor the external environment; as the assessment in Topic 5 indicates, loans for use outside Hong Kong recorded rapid growth since the global financial crisis, suggesting that banks’ asset quality has become more susceptible to the external environment. Banks’ expectations for near-term credit growth varied. The HKMA’s Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook conducted in December 2016 showed that while a significant share of surveyed AIs expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, the proportion expecting an increase in loan demand edged up to 14% (Table 5.A). In the second half of 2016, the credit risk associated with unsecured personal loans remained contained, with the annualised credit card charge-off ratio and delinquency ratio declining to 1.92% and 0.24% respectively at end-December (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Charge-off and delinquency ratios of credit card advances and bankruptcy petitions Banks’ housing loan portfolios remained robust, with the delinquency ratio staying at 0.03% at end-December. The average loan-to-value (LTV) ratio of newly approved mortgage loans was 51.3% in the fourth quarter of 2016 (Chart 5.12). This LTV ratio is much lower than the 64% recorded in September 2009, before the HKMA began implementing seven rounds of countercyclical macro-prudential measures. However, the debt servicing burden index for new mortgages rose from 44.0 in the second quarter of 2016 to 48.8 in the fourth quarter (red line in Chart 5.12), mainly reflecting an increase in the average size of new mortgages (Chart 5.13). Continued US interest rate normalisation may further increase personal debt servicing burdens. A sensitivity test indicates that if interest rates were to rise by 300 basis points with other conditions held constant, this index could rise significantly to 67.3 within four quarters. Banks should remain vigilant against the risks associated with a continued rise in personal debt servicing burdens. However, the actual impact on individual banks’ asset quality depends on the characteristics of their corporate loan portfolios. As markets reassessed inflation risks in the US, global financial market volatility resurfaced at the beginning of the year. In February, global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, completely erasing the significant gains made earlier in the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The sustained rally in global equity markets over the past two years amid low volatility was underpinned by market expectations of an ideal state of continued robust economic growth alongside low inflation and interest rates. However, this expectation now faces risks from tightened global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionism sentiment, and geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, but the market continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, the aggregate amount of RMB loans continued to increase, albeit at a slower pace. Following a modest slowdown earlier in the year, both property price increases and transaction volume rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, the resurgence of volatility in global and local financial markets may add to fluctuations in fund flows into and out of Hong Kong. Given uncertainties in financial markets, as well as the ongoing normalisation of US monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant against heightened fluctuations in interest rates and potential fund outflows. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of household debt servicing burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality should interest rates rise more than expected. After hovering at low levels for more than two years, the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) surged as global financial market volatility resurfaced at the beginning of the year. Global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, with the S&P 500 Index dropping by more than 10% at one point, completely erasing the significant gains recorded in early January. Market sentiment shifted due to signs that the global economic recovery could put pressure on long-suppressed US wages and prices, potentially prompting the Federal Reserve to accelerate its rate hike path. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rally in global equity markets over the past two years was predicated on market expectations of continued favourable economic conditions. In the second half of 2017, global economic growth drivers continued to strengthen, with economic activities in advanced economies and emerging market economies picking up in tandem. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package, which included tax cuts and comprehensive reforms to corporate and individual tax codes, raising market hopes that the robust US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite the pickup in activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained mild, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would stay low for an extended period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rallied significantly in 2017, with the US stock market in particular hitting record highs repeatedly. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. Following the short-term financial market volatility, the risk of tightened global monetary conditions may continue to cloud the global economic outlooks. In the US, as the economy has reached its output potential, the anticipated cyclical stimulus to domestic demand from tax cuts could accelerate a rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. Meanwhile, as tax cuts are expected to widen the budget deficit, the US may issue more government bonds in the future; this is expected to exert upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Federal Reserve continues to proceed with balance sheet normalisation. Outside the US, strengthening growth drivers in other major advanced economies have led markets to expect that their central banks may scale back their quantitative easing programmes. If implemented, this would result in a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks stemming from international political and geopolitical tensions could also cloud the global economic growth outlook. The US administration appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionism measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminium. These moves have raised concerns about whether trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. Furthermore, any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions could affect global trade and exacerbate financial market volatility. Given the aforementioned uncertainties surrounding the global economic outlooks, it remains questionable whether the currently elevated valuations in global asset markets can be sustained. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical increase in global demand and the expected widening of the US budget deficit due to tax cuts will push up the natural interest rate (R*); coupled with the expected rise in term premiums resulting from the Federal Reserve's balance sheet normalisation, this could drive up long-term interest rates, thereby weighing on asset market valuations. In East Asia, economies in the region also enjoyed a favourable environment of robust growth and mild inflation. Amid positive economic outcomes and optimistic outlooks, fund flows accelerated and financial markets rallied concurrently. However, this positive outlook faces downside risks due to several factors: global liquidity tightness caused by the synchronised monetary policy normalisation by major central banks; the inward-looking trade policy pursued by the US administration; geopolitical tensions; and the potential tightening of offshore US dollar liquidity as US corporations repatriate profits en masse in response to the one-off "deemed repatriation" provision under the country's tax reform. Should credit and financial markets face any shocks, a reversal of fund flows could be triggered, with sectors and economies with higher leverage being most vulnerable to the impact of tightened financial conditions. On Mainland China, supported by robust consumption, strong infrastructure investment, and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year, the Mainland economy performed well in the second half of 2017. Meanwhile, signs of the rise of the "new economy" became increasingly evident; over the past few quarters, high value-added industries such as manufacturing and services have demonstrated strong momentum in business expansion. Looking ahead, the near-term growth outlook remains positive, though uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressure on growth arising from the further advancement of structural reforms. The authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to adopt a proactive fiscal policy stance, which could help cushion adverse economic developments if necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in both structural reforms and the containment of system-wide risks. Notably, following the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland property market showed signs of cooling during the review period, particularly in first-tier cities. At the same time, as banks tightened lending standards, banks' exposure to enterprises in overcapacity industries remained contained, while shadow banking activities slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to these positive developments, our analysis also suggests that capital allocation efficiency in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) with weaker repayment ability appear to have tightened, possibly reflecting reduced support from local government (see Box 2 on page 28 for details). On external factors, amid a stabilising economic situation and receding risks, fund outflows remained mild for most of 2017. Hong Kong's economy maintained its quarter-on-quarter growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 3.8% for the full year of 2017, marking the fastest pace in nearly six years. Supported by favourable employment and income conditions as well as rising asset prices, Private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017. Aggregate investment also rebounded due to increased corporate capital spending. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further. Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on gross domestic product (GDP) growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018, with Private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports continuing to support the economy. Given that HKD interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayments on Private consumption. The Government and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2018 are 3–4% and 3.0%, respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook is still subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including those mentioned above regarding the external environment, the economic performance of Mainland China amid tightened financial conditions, and trends in the local asset market. Although the unemployment rate fell to a near 20-year low of 2.9%, Local inflationary pressures remained contained. That said, there were slight signs of increasing quarter-on-quarter Inflation momentum in recent months, with prices of both tradables and services rising. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may edge up slightly but remain mild, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of rising fresh-letting private residential rentals. Affected by funding demand from IPO fundraising activities and seasonal demand, liquidity positions tightened, and increased short-covering of the Hong Kong dollar prompted the spot Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to strengthen between September and November 2017. As liquidity positions eased and interest rate arbitrage activities resumed, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened again from December 2017 onwards. In early 2018, despite turbulence in global financial markets (especially equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar remained broadly stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened further in early March 2018, but the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) faced upward pressure between September and December 2017. This was mainly due to funding demand from IPO fundraising activities and banks' caution in managing their liquidity towards the end of the year. In December, the average overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively compared to six months earlier, reaching 0.25% and 1.26%. After dipping slightly in early January 2018, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained broadly stable and was largely unaffected by the recent adjustments in global financial markets. Despite intense competition in the housing loans business, the average lending rate for new mortgages offered by banks followed the rise in short-term HIBORs, increasing to 2.16% in December. On the other hand, Retail banks' funding costs remained generally low after a brief increase in October due to IPO fundraising activities, with the composite interest rate closing at 0.38% in December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure; should global financial market sentiment shift abruptly, volatility in fund flows may increase. For the full year of 2017, total loans grew steadily by 16.1%. Following robust growth of 10.2% in the first half, Loan growth slowed to 5.3% in the second half. Among them, growth in domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong decelerated across most sectors. Foreign currency loan growth slowed, partly due to rising USD funding costs. Meanwhile, driven by the improving local economic environment and relatively low HKD funding costs, HKD loans continued to record rapid growth. As HKD loan growth outpaced deposit growth, the Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio rose in the second half of 2017, reaching 82.7% at year-end, the highest level since March 2015. Conversely, due to the relatively slow growth in foreign currency loans, the foreign currency LTD ratio fell to 63.1% at year-end. Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar showed signs of stabilising between September and November 2017. Subsequently, as the US dollar weakened significantly against most major currencies, Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened from December onwards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi (CNH) liquidity pool (comprising total renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit) edged up in the second half of the year following a slight decline in the first half, largely reflecting changes in market expectations regarding the RMB exchange rate. As for other offshore renminbi business, although renminbi loans continued to decrease, the amount of renminbi trade settlement handled by banks in Hong Kong rebounded in the second half. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the advancement of the Belt and Road initiatives and the continued internationalisation of the renminbi.

The synchronized strengthening of the global economy since late 2016 has shown no signs of abating. The improved growth outlook drove global equity markets higher throughout 2017 and into early 2018. However, as market participants reassessed US inflation risks, global stock markets experienced a sell-off and significant volatility in February, marking the end of two years of calm in financial markets. Looking ahead, the risk of tighter global financing conditions, along with a range of policy and event risks, will continue to cloud the global outlook. Amid tight labour markets, US tax cuts could accelerate the cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Fed to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. As the Fed continues to advance balance sheet normalization, increased issuance of US Treasury bonds to finance tax cuts may add upward pressure on long-term US Treasury bond yields. The specter of rising trade barriers and any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, benefiting from robust export performance and stable domestic demand, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017. Nevertheless, while the economic outlook is optimistic, it faces multiple downside risks, such as a potentially greater-than-expected tightening of global monetary conditions, inward-looking US trade policy, and geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialize, the risk of a reversal in fund flows would also increase. Policymakers face multiple challenges: they must guard against risks to economic growth while limiting the impact of prolonged loose financial conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, economic outcomes were solid in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and containing system-wide risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, though uncertainties persist; this will depend partly on the extent to which rapid growth in the "new economy" can offset the short-term pressure on growth from further advancing structural reforms. With economic conditions stabilizing and risks subsiding, outflow pressures remained mild for most of 2017. As the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has become increasingly entrenched since late 2016, growth in advanced economies and emerging market economies accelerated synchronously in 2017. Among major advanced economies, the US saw robust increases in investment and exports, driven by improving private sector sentiment and a sharp depreciation of the US dollar, while the Euro area and Japan also recorded a broad-based cyclical recovery. Exports from emerging market economies also benefited from stabilizing global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the near term, following the passage of tax reform in the US, investment and consumption may receive a further boost from reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. Given the current cyclical economic upturn and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth estimates As growth drivers in the Euro area and Japan strengthened, market expectation suggested that divergence in global monetary policy would narrow. Coupled with a more optimistic global growth prospects, this stimulated higher risk appetite and net inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting pressure on the US dollar. Despite the Fed raising rates three times during the year and commencing balance sheet normalization, the US dollar index recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite a broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained weak and below central bank targets, leading markets to expect until recently that global rates would remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this background, global equity markets continued to rally through 2017 and into early 2018, with the S&P 500 Index hitting record highs repeatedly, pushing the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, the highest level since the "dot-com bubble" in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core inflation in major advanced economies However, since the second half of 2017, concerns that tax cuts would lead to larger budget deficits and higher inflation caused long-term US Treasury bond yields to climb steadily, raising questions about the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. After the US announced higher-than-expected average hourly earnings growth for January 2018, markets reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global equity markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 fell more than 10% from its peak on January 26, completely erasing its significant gains earlier in the year, and remained under stress after the US government announced a new round of trade protectionist measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility surged, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index briefly spiking to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the low-volatility environment that had persisted for the past two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, following the short-term stock market volatility, US inflation risks, upside risks to long-term US Treasury bond yields, and potential monetary tightening by other major central banks could all lead to tighter global monetary conditions, subsequently clouding global economic outlooks. First, regarding US inflation risks, the recently passed tax reform includes several provisions expected to provide short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. Key measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates; (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investments; and (3) a one-time "deemed repatriation" provision that helps reduce incentives for US corporates to park overseas earnings abroad. While it remains uncertain how tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the US economy now operating at its output potential, tax cuts could push US output beyond potential, leading to economic overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. If inflationary pressures rise more than expected, it could prompt the Fed to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. Currently, interest rate paths for the federal funds rate expected by financial markets are flatter than those projected by the Fed. However, should inflation unexpectedly rebound, the risk of a sudden repricing of rate hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal funds rate projections Second, given that tax reform could exacerbate the budget deficit, US Treasury issuance is expected to increase going forward. As the Fed continues its balance sheet normalization program, term premiums are expected to rise; under these circumstances, increased US Treasury issuance could intensify upward pressure on long-term US Treasury bond yields. Furthermore, as market expectations regarding the likelihood of passing US tax cuts increased, US inflation expectations have risen steadily since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). Consequently, after hovering at low levels for much of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns over increased supply pressure on Treasuries and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 5-year 5-year forward inflation expectations Moreover, whether the natural rate of interest (R*), a key component of long-term rates, will remain low for an extended period as widely recognised is a critical question. Although estimates of R* vary, it is widely recognised to have declined significantly since the Global Financial Crisis (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, due to (1) an expected decline in the national savings rate resulting from larger budget deficits, and (2) a potential rise in the investment rate driven by corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment for capital expenditure, US R* may face upside risks in the future. A rise in R*, combined with expected increases in term premiums from Fed balance sheet normalization, could signal higher long-term rates, thereby creating headwinds for asset market valuations. Chart 2.6 Estimates of US R* based on the Laubach-Williams model Third, strengthening growth drivers in the Euro area and Japan have led markets to expect their central banks may scale back monetary easing measures. Should this occur, it could signal a synchronized tightening of global monetary conditions. In the Euro area, member economies recorded a broad-based cyclical expansion (Chart 2.7). As for Japan, the economic recovery also accelerated, with real gross domestic product (GDP) recording its eighth consecutive quarter of positive year-on-year growth in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the ECB and the Bank of Japan continued to signal maintaining accommodative monetary policy amid weak inflation, clearer growth outlooks in Europe and Japan (and continuing tightening in Japan's labour markets) have led some market participants to predict further scaling back of quantitative easing programs in the near future. Chart 2.7 Real GDP of selected Euro area member states Policy and event risks stemming from international political and geopolitical tensions could also threaten the nascent global economic growth and trade recovery. The US administration appears more inclined toward inward-looking trade policy to protect domestic industries; recent examples include the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels and washing machines in January 2018, and import tariffs on steel and aluminum announced in early March, raising concerns about retaliatory measures from trading partners. Meanwhile, negotiations between the UK and other EU countries regarding post-Brexit trade arrangements are ongoing, with the process fraught with uncertainties. If these developments lead to increased trade tensions, they could hinder global trade flows and reduce global productivity. Furthermore, any unexpected escalation of geopolitical tensions (such as military conflict on the Korean Peninsula, political turmoil in the Middle East, and latent terrorist attack risks) could increase financial market volatility globally. In East Asia, growth drivers strengthened further in the second half of 2017, concluding the entire year with robust performance. Real growth accelerated to 4.3% in 2017, the fastest pace since 2012. External trade remained the primary driver of growth, while domestic demand provided steady support (Chart 2.8). Accelerated recovery in advanced economies, stronger-than-expected growth in Mainland China, and a rebound in global demand for technology products all boosted regional exports. Chart 2.8 East Asia: Domestic demand and exports Inflationary pressures have remained soft so far. In the second half of 2017, overall inflation in East Asia moderated, affected by declining food price inflation and stable energy prices (Chart 2.9). Meanwhile, due to slow wage growth in several economies, core consumer price inflation (excluding food and energy) remained at relatively low levels. Improving economic conditions accompanied by substantial net inflows caused financial asset prices to rise significantly in 2017 and early 2018 (blue and pink bars in Chart 2.10).
