Flows into regional markets rebounded significantly in 2017, with total portfolio investment inflows reaching a new high since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose alongside the market rally. Indeed, credit risk compensation in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, and benchmark equity indices across the region rose broadly. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the US dollar.

With robust domestic demand and improved export performance, Hong Kong's economy maintained robust growth drivers in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. The economic outlook for the domestic economy remains subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including monetary policy normalisation by major central banks, stability of the global financial market, rising protectionist sentiment, and heightened geopolitical tensions. In the near term, although Local inflationary pressures should remain mild, some upside risks still exist. Hong Kong's economy maintained growth drivers in the second half of 2017. The seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third quarter and fourth quarter, similar to the average growth of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half, Private consumption remained robust and continued to be one of the major drivers of gross domestic product (GDP) growth. Consumption growth was robust due to favourable employment and income conditions, sustained optimistic consumer sentiment, and the positive impact of rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activities weakened, corporate capital spending increased, causing aggregate investment to rise markedly in the last quarter after remaining broadly stable for three quarters. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance further improved (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net trade in goods still dragged on gross domestic product (GDP) growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to gross domestic product (GDP) growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component Chart 3.2 Real Export and import Sustained economic growth drivers drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. Total employment increased by about 0.7% during the period to over 3.85 million, with the most notable increases in the construction sector, financing and business services sector, and public administration, social and personal services sector. As real gross domestic product (GDP) growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from the improved global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. Domestically, Private consumption is expected to sustain its growth, mainly due to ideal labour market conditions. Given that HKD interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayments on Private consumption. As for local fixed capital formation, building and construction activities should see steady growth, benefiting from increased housing supply and the continued implementation of infrastructure projects. While the improved economic environment will stimulate business capital spending, possible increases in rates may have negative impacts. Government forecasts put real gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 2018 at ranges between 3% and 4%, while growth estimates by international organisations and private sector analysts range between 2% and 4%. However, the growth outlook for Hong Kong remains subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including the external environment mentioned in previous chapters, the economic outcomes of Mainland China amid tightened financial conditions, and trends in the local asset market. Local inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, but month-on-month Inflation momentum showed signs of a slight rebound in recent months. Year on year, the underlying composite consumer price index (CCPI) rose by 1.7% and 1.6% respectively in the third quarter and fourth quarter, similar to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the annualised three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects Inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Among them, prices of tradables and services both increased. The rebound in fresh-letting residential rentals since mid-2016 may also have partially added to Inflation momentum (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures remained mild in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Various indicators reflecting Consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and payroll per person With global inflation remaining mild and domestic costs rising steadily, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to remain mild in 2018, but the underlying inflation rate may gradually pick up from the eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For instance, due to the pass-through effect from rising fresh-letting private residential rentals, inflationary pressures may increase somewhat in the second half of 2018. Market consensus forecasts put the headline inflation rate at a mild 2.2% for 2018, while Government forecasts for the underlying inflation rate stand at 2.5%. Despite the mild inflation outlook, upside risks still exist. On the external front, any higher-than-expected surge in global inflation or commodity prices could add to local Inflation momentum. On the domestic front, the labour markets tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, falling below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero; if the labour markets tighten significantly, it could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate Following the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, low interest rates led to an increase in mortgage liabilities of Hong Kong households. As US dollar counterparts normalise, HKD interest rates will eventually follow suit and rise, leading to a corresponding increase in household mortgage repayments in the future, thereby weighing on household consumption. Therefore, this box examines the impact of increased mortgage repayments on Private consumption in Hong Kong. Mortgage repayments refer to the ratio of mortgage debt repayment (i.e. interest payments plus loan principal amortisation) to income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of mortgage repayments in the transmission of Interest rate shock to Private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, wealth effect and collateral effect arising from changes in asset prices mentioned in general economic theory, in the presence of mortgage repayments, Interest rate shock also affects Private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments, which in turn changes households' disposable income. This impact will be amplified as outstanding mortgages increase. Furthermore, loan principal amortisation varies with changes in outstanding mortgages, which also affects Private consumption by changing households' disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of Private consumption To measure the impact of mortgage repayments on Private consumption, we estimated the Outstanding Mortgage Debt Servicing Ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage liabilities. Unlike current mortgage repayment burden indicators that apply only to new mortgages, OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage liabilities of overall households, which are more closely related to total Private consumption. Broadly following the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we use the standard formula for fixed instalments to measure OMDSR: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are the average interest rate and tenor of outstanding mortgages respectively. To assess whether OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the entire household sector, it is appropriate to compare OMDSR with two commonly used debt servicing indicators. Chart B3.2 shows the OMDSR estimates from 1985 to mid-2017, alongside the median mortgage debt servicing and loan repayment to income ratios estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial Population Census. Both ratios showed a downward trend in the early 2000s, consistent with the decline in overall household mortgage lending following the bursting of the property bubble in 1997 and the sharp drop in mortgage rates during the same period. Despite the significant rise in property prices after the Global Financial Crisis, these two ratios remained stable, as macro-prudential measures adopted by the HKMA on bank housing loans curbed overall household mortgage leverage. Additionally, the extension of tenors for new mortgages also reduced the actual amount of mortgage repayments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and median mortgage debt servicing and loan repayment to income ratios We also compared OMDSR with the banks' debt-servicing ratio, which is the actual debt repayment to income ratio of applicants for new mortgages at banks. As shown in Chart B3.3, OMDSR is lower than the banks' debt-servicing ratio, partly because OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. Since existing mortgages were originated when property prices were lower, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage repayment burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e. OMDSR) is lower than the repayment burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e. the banks' debt-servicing ratio). Moreover, the higher banks' debt-servicing ratio is also due to banks complying with prudential supervisory requirements of the HKMA, taking into account non-mortgage loan repayments when calculating the debt-servicing ratio. After the Global Financial Crisis, both OMDSR and the banks' debt-servicing ratio remained stable, mainly due to the HKMA's implementation of prudential supervision on housing loans, setting a cap on the banks' debt-servicing ratio, a measure that also helped stabilise OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks' DSR for new mortgages Overall, OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt servicing indicators, but OMDSR has stronger Real Time relevance and can reflect the burden of overall outstanding mortgage liabilities, rather than just the burden of new mortgage liabilities. Therefore, we believe that using OMDSR can assess the impact of mortgage repayments on Private consumption. To assess the impact of mortgage repayments on Private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimated an error-correction model following the methods of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-run relationship between real Private consumption (proxied by real average Private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term in the short-run equation. Based on existing theoretical and empirical evidence, we include real income (proxied by median household income, deflated by the composite consumer price index (CCPI)), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by Residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index respectively, deflated by the composite consumer price index (CCPI)) and OMDSR as long-run determinants of Private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, but the pace of growth was softer than in the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Should global financial market sentiment change abruptly, volatility in flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened briefly during the period from September to November 2017 and remained at levels around 7.80. This was mainly due to increased funding demand from initial public offering activities and banks’ caution in managing their liquidity ahead of month-end and year-end dates, leading to tighter liquidity positions. Consequently, carry trade activities slowed and short covering of the Hong Kong dollar increased. As the tightness in Hong Kong dollar liquidity eased somewhat and commercial demand for US dollars rose towards the end of the year, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (especially equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar continued to function in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar weakened, but the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but has recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly consistent with the movement of the US dollar against most major currencies. Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners and its limited impact on the REER, the REER of the Hong Kong dollar continued to track closely the movements of the nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER). Chart 4.3 Nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) and real effective exchange rate index (REER) Non-residents recorded inflows in portfolio investment in the second half of 2017. The latest Balance of Payments statistics showed that both local and non-local residents recorded inflows in equity securities investment in the third quarter, reflecting an improved regional economic outlook and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-residents recorded inflows in debt securities investment in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows in debt investment by local residents. A survey of global mutual funds also indicated that both equity and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017, driven by optimistic market views on the economic outlook and firms’ earnings. In recent weeks, data from the same survey showed that despite adjustments in global financial markets, equity investments still recorded inflows, while bond investments saw slight net outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey on fund flows related to equities and bonds Looking ahead, as the normalisation of US monetary policy continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, potentially leading to increased carry trade activities. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Meanwhile, given the uncertain pace of US monetary policy normalisation and the rapidly changing global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment, volatility in HKD fund flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully guarantee the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Despite rate hikes by the Fed and its continued balance sheet reduction, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. The HKD Monetary Base increased further by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued for banknote issuance (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered, the Aggregate Balance and the total amount of outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) remained largely unchanged in the second half, standing at approximately HK$1,226.8 billion. Among these, the Aggregate Balance contracted somewhat, while outstanding EFBNs increased correspondingly. This was due to the additional issuance of EFBNs (totalling HK$80 billion) to meet banks' substantial demand for liquidity management. Entering 2018, despite stock market corrections, the Monetary Base remained stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Meanwhile, Hong Kong dollar money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace. Growth in broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased modestly by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Notably, demand deposits grew faster in the second half, partly due to buoyant asset markets and rising investment demand. Analysis of counterparts showed that the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was supported by robust growth in Hong Kong dollar loans on one hand (Chart 4.6), and dragged down by net outflows of HKD funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks’ net foreign currency assets on the other. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterparts On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits declined from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits rebounded significantly in the second half, rising by 8.4%, after declining continuously for more than two years. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in RMB customer deposits. Due to slower growth in both Hong Kong dollar and USD deposits, total deposits with AIs increased modestly by 3.0% in the second half, compared to a growth rate of 5.6% in the first half. For the entire year of 2017, Total deposits increasing modestly by 8.7%, broadly similar to that in 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth During the period from September to December 2017, increased funding demand from initial public offering activities and banks’ caution in managing their liquidity ahead of month-end and year-end dates exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, overnight and three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% respectively in December (monthly averages). The negative interest rate differentials between HKD and USD Interbank Offered Rates for tenors ranging from one month to three months also narrowed accordingly. Chart 4.8 HIBORs and USD Interbank Offered Rates Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upwards but flattened, broadly mirroring the trend of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half, yields on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at end-2017, while yields on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by a smaller margin of 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at end-2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields Composite interest rate and average lending rate on new mortgages Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. As funding demand subsided after the year-end, HIBORs retreated in early January. Thereafter, despite adjustments in global and local stock markets, HIBORs remained largely stable. Overnight and three-month HIBOR closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at end-February 2018. On the retail front, although banks’ lending rate increased somewhat alongside the spike in HIBOR, banks’ funding costs generally remained low due to the still large deposit base. Despite intense competition in the housing loans business, the average lending rate on new mortgages rose gradually by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly tracking the rise in one-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the composite interest rate, which measures retail banks’ HKD funding costs, rose briefly in October due to increased funding demand from initial public offering activities, but remained soft for most of the second half, closing at 0.38% at end-December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise and other major economies may embark on interest rate normalisation, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Meanwhile, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase volatility in fund flows. However, the sizeable HKD Monetary Base can serve as a buffer to help mitigate any excessively sharp increases in HKD interest rates. Furthermore, banks’ prudent liquidity management and access to the Discount Window for discounting will also help curb excessive volatility in Interbank Offered Rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. Loan growth reached 10.2% in the first half and slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). Growth in both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong slowed in the second half of 2017. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, supported by the improving local economic environment and relatively low HKD funding costs, while foreign currency loan increased only marginally by 0.1%. Specifically, growth in US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to elevated USD funding costs. For the entire year of 2017, total loans recorded robust growth of 16.1%, compared to 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan growth Growth in loans for use in Hong Kong (including trade financing) decelerated from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Loan growth in construction and property development and investment slowed in the second half, partly because authorities required banks to strengthen risk management regarding loans to developers starting from June 2017. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, loans for trade financing and the transport sector recorded only relatively modest increases, while loans to the wholesale and retail trade sector declined. Conversely, loan growth for financial and finance-related corporates remained strong, partially reflecting the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Chart 4.11 Domestic loan growth by selected sector Household debt increased by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared to a 5.0% increase in the first half. Within household debt, Personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal loans) accelerated further, growing by 12.4% in the second half. The robust growth in Personal loans was mainly driven by borrowings by private banking and wealth management customers collateralised loans to wealth management customers against financial assets. The growth of these loans was broadly in line with the sustained growth in customer assets under management by banks. The risks associated with such collateralised loans are manageable. Moreover, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks in January 2014 on risk management of Personal loans, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including imposing caps on loan tenor and borrowers’ debt repayment ratios. On the other hand, although residential transaction volume increased, the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio of newly approved mortgage loans declined, and growth in residential mortgage loan slowed slightly to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Largely benefiting from growth in net interest income, Retail banks’ profit improved in the second half of 2017 compared to the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained robust. After strong growth in the first half of 2017, credit growth moderated in the second half, while asset quality remained robust by historical standards. Despite a significant rise in Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs), the HKD funding cost for retail banks remained at a low level due to low retail deposit rates. However, banks should remain vigilant against risks arising from increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows amid US monetary policy normalization, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and the high level of personal debt servicing burden, banks should assess the impact on asset quality should interest rate increases exceed expectations. To enhance the resilience of banks against system-wide risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio in Hong Kong will be raised to 2.5% effective January 1, 2019. In the second half of 2017, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 13.6% over the same period last year. This was mainly driven by a substantial increase in net interest income and a decrease in loan impairment charges, which more than offset the decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets of retail banks edged down slightly from 1.17% in the first half to 1.15% in the second half of 2017. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 remained higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For the entire year of 2017, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks’ profit The net interest margins (NIMs) of retail banks further widened to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 from 1.34% in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.2). Observational evidence suggests that the improvement in NIMs is consistent with the rise in average spreads on HKD corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Net interest margins (NIMs) of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average spreads on HKD syndicated loans Since September 2017, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) has risen across the board, mainly due to initial public offering (IPO)-related and banks’ year-end liquidity demand, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. Notably, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose to a post-financial crisis high of 1.31% at end-December 2017, up 53 basis points from end-June, but still relatively low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Entering 2018, HIBOR appeared to have stabilized as banks’ year-end liquidity demand eased. Despite the recent rise in HIBOR, the HKD funding cost for retail banks remained stable. This was mainly due to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Under these circumstances, the composite interest rate, reflecting the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, remained at a low level of around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before edging up recently to 0.38% at end-December (green line in Chart 5.4). A similar trend was observed in the overall HKD and USD funding cost of locally incorporated licensed banks. In the second half of 2017, the average HKD and USD funding cost in the non-deposit market rose by 35 basis points, while the average deposit funding costs edged up by 12 basis points. Overall, the average overall HKD and USD funding cost of licensed banks increased by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 HKD and USD funding costs and tenors of licensed banks The rise in HIBOR exceeded the overall funding costs of the Hong Kong banking sector, which may help improve the spreads on banks’ HIBOR-linked assets. However, this improvement could be partly offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information indicates that some banks have lowered their mortgage rate spreads over benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. With further US interest rate hikes expected this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. Given the intense competition in the loan market, if the increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, this could put pressure on banks’ NIMs. The consolidated capital adequacy ratios of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) remained much higher than international minimum standards, indicating that the capital base of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong. At end-December 2017, the total capital ratio increased to 19.1% from 18.7% at end-June (Chart 5.6), while Tier 1 capital ratio also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.6 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) The HKMA recently published a consultation paper on proposed rules for loss-absorbing capacity requirements applicable to AIs under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of AIs helps reduce the likelihood of financial crises and thus benefits society, it inevitably entails costs. Box 5 presents a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing loss-absorbing capacity requirements would bring net benefits to Hong Kong's economy. Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity positions of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable to 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions edged down slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. AIs had sufficient liquidity, demonstrating that the Hong Kong banking sector is resilient to liquidity shocks resulting from potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), as part of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on January 1, 2018. This requirement aims to mitigate banks’ medium- to long-term funding risk by requiring them to maintain adequate stable funding sources to finance their business activities. Specifically, category 1 institutions must maintain an NSFR of no less than 100% at all times. Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for AIs, reflecting a stable liability structure in the banking system. At end-December 2017, customer deposits accounted for 56.2% of total liabilities of all AIs, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all AIs The Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio of all AIs rose from 77.1% at end-June 2017 to 82.7% at end-December (Chart 5.9), reflecting that HKD loans and advances grew faster than deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign currency LTD ratio declined from 65.5% at end-June 2017 to 63.1% at end-December. Overall, the loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio in all currencies rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the implications of the rising LTD ratios for their manage their liquidity. Chart 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a low level. We estimate that under an interest rate shock of a parallel 200-basis-point increase in interest rates, the decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would be equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base at end-December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nevertheless, given expectations that the Fed will continue rate hikes and commence balance sheet normalization, banks should assess the implications for their risk management of interest rate risk. Chart 5.10 Impact of Interest rate shock on locally incorporated licensed banks In the second half of 2017, amid a moderate yet favorable economic environment, the growth of total loans and advances of all AIs slowed to 5.3% from the robust 10.2% recorded in the first half. Following two years of softer growth, total loans registered solid growth of 16.1% for the entire year of 2017. The asset quality of bank loan portfolios remained robust and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At end-December 2017, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all AIs fell to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, compared to 0.84% and 0.61% respectively at end-June. For retail banks, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans also declined to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in loans for use outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks’ asset quality may become more sensitive to external developments, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risk. Chart 5.11 Asset quality of retail banks As banks have become more optimistic about near-term credit growth, strong credit growth is expected to persist. The HKMA’s Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook conducted in December 2017 showed that 29% of surveyed AIs expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected it to be the same (Table 5.A). During the review period, the credit risk associated with Personal loans remained low. Banks’ housing loan portfolios remained robust, with the delinquency ratio staying at a low level of 0.03% at end-December 2017. The average loan-to-value (LTV) ratio of newly approved mortgage loans further declined from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.12). This LTV ratio is well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA introduced the first round of counter-cyclical macro-prudential measures (i.e., September 2009).

The global economy maintained growth, but momentum has weakened as uncertainties increased amid persistent trade tensions, tightened financial conditions, and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds. The Fed adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience", leading investors to rule out the possibility of further rate hikes. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases, especially those that could prompt monetary tightening, such as rising US inflation. In Hong Kong, although the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered in March, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. In the second half of 2018, total loans growth edged down slightly, reflecting softer credit demand amid headwinds including the ongoing China-US trade conflict and global economic growth slowing. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with transaction volume falling markedly and property prices retreating, before showing signs of stabilising in early 2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector faces multiple headwinds due to increased uncertainties in the external environment. Should these uncertainties intensify and persist for a prolonged period, business sentiment and credit demand could be significantly dampened, thereby exerting downward pressure on bank profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the impact of a potential deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. In the second half of 2018, the global economy maintained growth. However, while the US economy grew steadily, growth momentum elsewhere slowed. Among advanced economies, Japan and several major Euro area countries saw slower growth and low inflation. Slowing global trade and a significant drop in oil prices posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In light of softer global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) lowered its global growth estimates for 2019 and 2020 in January by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively from its October 2018 forecasts. Due to the dimmer growth outlook and rising trade tensions, global equity markets experienced significant volatility at end-2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the Global Financial Crisis, sparking market concerns about an impending US recession. Nevertheless, US economic fundamentals remain solid, and the probability of a recession in the near term is low. Despite this, global economic outlooks remain fraught with uncertainties. On the US front, although mild inflation has given the Fed room to pause rate hikes, the Fed’s data-dependent policy stance suggests that financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases, particularly data such as rising US inflation that could prompt monetary tightening. Meanwhile, outcomes of trade negotiations between the US and China, as well as between the US and the EU, remain uncertain. In the UK, whether a "hard Brexit" can be avoided remains unknown. In East Asia, financial markets have stabilised as the US dollar rally moderated and market expectation of a Fed rate hike pause grew, but a deteriorating external environment could weigh on regional economic growth. Indeed, weakening global trade growth momentum has dragged down economic growth in several East Asian economies, and inflationary pressures have also eased. While this shift may ease the policy dilemma faced by regional central banks between supporting growth and containing inflation, financial imbalances such as high private sector leverage in some regional countries remain severe. As detailed in Box 1 (page 16), another challenge facing the East Asian region is that unexpected changes in the Fed's monetary policy could send shockwaves to sovereign bond markets in emerging market economies, including East Asian economies. In Mainland China, growth slowed further in the second half of 2018 due to increased uncertainties in the external environment and a slight moderation in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains uncertain pending the outcome of China-US trade negotiations. The significant contraction in shadow financing activities has exacerbated financing difficulties faced by private enterprises, especially small firms, over the past few quarters, which, coupled with weakening economic confidence, may also weigh on business activities. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers need to continue striking a balance between stabilising the economy and preventing potential system-wide risks through accommodative yet targeted measures, such as targeted reserve requirement ratio cuts. At the same time, authorities have adopted more supply-side measures to boost productivity growth, such as promoting competition among companies regardless of their ownerships, and providing a better social safety net for individuals. The official growth target for 2019 was also lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0% to 6.5%. In 2018, risk aversion dominated Mainland financial markets. Bank asset quality also deteriorated slightly during the review period, while leverage of listed non-financial firms edged up. However, bank loan impairment charges increased further in the second half of 2018, and exposure to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline; both developments help shield the banking system from potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development is that leverage of listed firms in overcapacity sectors — a key source of bank credit risk — declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Box 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of factors driving the recent improvement in business performance of overcapacity sectors. Compared with the first half of 2018, economic activities in Hong Kong softened in the second half. Gross domestic product (GDP) growth stalled on a quarter-on-quarter basis, and year-on-year growth also slowed, dragging full-year economic growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening in economic activities was mainly due to consumption and exports being dragged down by the direct or indirect impacts of the China-US trade conflict. Private consumption growth slowed, possibly reflecting increased economic uncertainties and the negative wealth effect arising from local asset price adjustments. Externally, Hong Kong's merchandise export performance also deteriorated, especially after the US and China implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines more closely the impact of the China-US trade conflict on Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance, and discusses the near-term outlook and associated risks. Mainly due to global economic growth slowing, economic growth is expected to slow further in 2019. Amid the interplay of multiple factors, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, against the backdrop of a low unemployment rate and rising household income, private consumption is expected to continue to support the economy, but the outlook for aggregate investment may become more uncertain. Government forecasts put real GDP growth for 2019 at 2% to 3%, while the latest average growth estimate by private sector analysts is 2.3%. These forecasts are subject to the various risks and uncertainties mentioned above. Local inflation edged up in the second half of 2018 but remained mild. The slight increase in inflation was partly driven by earlier rises in fresh-letting residential rentals. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, the lowest level in over two decades, total employment growth showed signs of slowing. Looking ahead, as local growth drivers weaken, local inflationary pressures are expected to remain mild in 2019. Following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered again four times in March 2019 (as of 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting carry trade unwinding amid liquidity tightness. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, partly due to the re-establishment of carry trade positions. Despite the re-triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Due to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) generally rose in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the three-month and 12-month HIBORs rose by about 30 basis points to 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December (monthly averages). Entering 2019, HIBORs generally fell due to waning seasonal demand. The composite interest rate, which measures the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks, rose from 0.62% at end-June 2018 to 0.83% at end-January 2019. In view of rising funding costs, following the upward adjustment of the US federal funds rate target range at end-September, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. At end-January 2019, the average lending rate for new mortgages followed the rise in Best Lending Rates to about 2.45%. Given persistent uncertainties related to China-US trade tensions and Brexit negotiations, volatility in flows may intensify. Moreover, the significant negative spread between Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates may stimulate arbitrage activities, leading to fund outflows. Under these circumstances, both fund outflows and the possible triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are normal operations under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Since early 2018, both offshore renminbi and onshore exchange rates have faced depreciation pressure due to market concerns over escalating China-US trade tensions. However, boosted by optimism driven by the resumption of high-level trade talks between China and the US, both offshore renminbi and onshore exchange rates stabilised in November. Although China-US trade tensions persist, they have not yet had a significant impact on the funding position in the offshore interbank market. Overnight CNH HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of 2018, while the three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, the offshore renminbi (CNH) liquidity pool in Hong Kong expanded steadily in the second half, with renminbi customer deposits growing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level, rising further to RMB 1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite lingering concerns over China-US trade tensions, with Mainland capital account liberalisation, the development of stock and bond connectivity, and regional economic cooperation promoted under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to continue expanding. The local equity market went through a roller-coaster ride over the past six months. During the early part of the review period, the market fell sharply due to ongoing global monetary tightening, significant differences between the two sides in China-US trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth in Mainland China. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Fed shifted to a "patient" monetary policy stance. Meanwhile, during the trade war truce, China took more measures to reduce its trade surplus with the US and open its markets to foreign investors. Although the US brought highly political legal proceedings against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides showed friendly gestures, indicating determination to reach a trade deal. Against this background, the local equity market rebounded sharply early this year. However, as discussions on the details of any agreement proceed, the future remains highly uncertain, and developments regarding the US federal government's prosecution could complicate matters, especially in the high-tech sector. The Hong Kong dollar debt market grew slightly last year. Yields fell, and performance improved towards year-end as market expectation of a slower pace of US monetary policy normalisation strengthened. Consequently, flows into bond funds reversed in the second half and increased slightly. New issuance in Hong Kong's offshore renminbi market rebounded significantly after three consecutive years of decline. However, as Mainland companies continued to deleverage, total new issuance remained lower than maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market remains challenging, and its outlook hinges on global economic developments, especially those in Mainland China.

During the review period, the global economy remained on a growth trajectory, but momentum weakened amid a confluence of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, especially outside the United States. Given the softer growth outlook, the Fed adjusted its policy stance, stressing that decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience," while ceasing to provide forward-looking guidance on further rate hikes. As the Fed’s policy becomes more data-dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases and perceive monetary policy as more uncertain. Meanwhile, heightened uncertainties over global trade policy and geopolitical risks may continue to cast a shadow over global economic outlooks. In East Asia, financial markets have largely stabilised since late 2018, as signs of a pause in the US interest rate hike cycle emerged and the US dollar stabilised. However, given the deteriorating external environment—namely the unresolved China-US trade conflict and softer growth in advanced economies—the region may face a broad-based slowdown. In Mainland China, growth drivers weakened further in the second half of 2018, and uncertainties over the growth outlook increased amid the China-US trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Consequently, policymakers adopted more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. Facing these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a prudent balance between continuing to contain system-wide risks and supporting corporates and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow broadly. However, while the US economy remained generally robust, some signs of slowing emerged. There were also clear signs that growth momentum outside the US had softened. Country-specific shocks—including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new auto emission standards in Germany, a spike in Italian Central Government bond yields due to a fiscal standoff with the EU, and social unrest in France—all weighed on economic activities in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). Moreover, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth posed headwinds to industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp drop in oil prices in the fourth quarter also presented new challenges to commodity-exporting emerging market economies. Given the waning growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) lowered its 2019 global growth estimates by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers’ Indices for Selected Advanced Economies Chart 2.2 Global Import Volume and Industrial Production in Emerging Market Economies In the fourth quarter, global equity markets underwent significant corrections amid softer global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainties, market concern over the sustainability of US firms’ earnings growth, and the Fed’s rhetoric suggesting continued monetary tightening. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels unseen since the Global Financial Crisis, sparking fears among some market participants of an impending US recession (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Spread Between 10-Year and Three-Month US Treasury Yields and Probability of US Recession Nevertheless, the probability of a US recession in the near term remains low. Fundamentals of the US economy remain solid; in particular, tight labour markets are expected to continue supporting Private consumption. Meanwhile, the US output gap is estimated to have turned positive only last year, making it less likely that economic overheating would prompt the Fed to tighten monetary policy aggressively. However, possibly reflecting the notable tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Fed officials began emphasising in early January that monetary policy would be data-dependent, noting that moderate inflationary pressures allowed them to exercise "patience" in determining future policy adjustments. Furthermore, following its January meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) ceased providing forward-looking guidance on further rate hikes and announced that it "is prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments." This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, MSCI World (ex-US) Index, and MSCI Emerging Markets Index Despite the Fed’s recent "dovish" signals, the US monetary policy outlook remains highly uncertain, hinging on inflation and other developments. Moderate inflationary pressures thus far have given the Fed room to proceed gradually with monetary normalisation. Stable inflation expectations in recent years support the view that the Fed can "remain patient" (Chart 2.5). Moreover, as Fed Chair Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including softer growth outside the US and trade policy uncertainties. Given these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more prudent policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-Based and Survey-Based Measures of US Inflation Expectations However, tight labour markets are expected to continue supporting overall US economic outcomes. Against this backdrop, wage growth may accelerate, which typically implies that inflation could heighten going forward (Chart 2.6). Therefore, market expectations that have largely priced out the possibility of Fed rate hikes in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average Hourly Earnings and Core PCE Inflation Chart 2.7 Futures-Implied Probabilities of the Federal Funds Rate Target Range Remaining Unchanged vs. At Least One Rate Hike in 2019 In sum, a prolonged pause in Fed rate hikes is not assured. To minimise policy errors, the Fed has increasingly emphasised that its decisions will be data-dependent as a risk management strategy. It follows that financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases, especially those that could prompt monetary tightening. Monetary policies of other major central banks are also uncertain. In the Euro area, the ECB ended its asset purchase programme in December while continuing to reinvest principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the programme in full, and reaffirmed its forward-looking guidance to keep policy rates unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, in January, the ECB downgraded its near-term growth assessment, stating that risks to the growth outlook had "moved to the downside." The implications of this downward revision to economic growth estimates for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its recent policy meeting that it would ease its policy stance if necessary amid increased downside risks. However, resistance to further monetary easing could be high, as its effectiveness is questioned and the drawbacks of maintaining an ultra-low interest rate environment for an extended period are becoming increasingly apparent; for instance, regional banks’ capital ratios declined from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018 as persistently low yields weighed on profitability. Consequently, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. Beyond uncertainties related to the global monetary policy outlook, uncertain outcomes of upcoming trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks represent two major sources of risk to global economic outlooks. The US administration announced in early December that it would not increase tariffs on imports from China for 90 days, and extended the deadline again in late February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the US and the EU have made little progress at this stage. Uncertain outcomes of these trade negotiations may continue to cast a shadow over global economic outlooks. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the US, partisan disagreements over border security funding led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be transitory, strained relations between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives could lead to further policy gridlock ahead. In the UK, after Prime Minister May’s Brexit deal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, risks associated with Brexit and its spillover effects surged, and it remains uncertain whether a plan can be devised at the eleventh hour to avoid a disruptive "hard Brexit." Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as renewed US sanctions on Iran, could also create uncertainties for oil prices, thereby affecting global growth prospects. In East Asia, financial markets largely stabilised in the fourth quarter after repeated volatility in the first three quarters of last year. The US dollar has stabilised since October, and signs that the Fed is exercising patience regarding further rate hikes have eased currency depreciation and fund outflow pressures facing East Asian economies. Several regional currencies edged up against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, and portfolio investment flows returned to net inflow (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: Currency Indices and Fund Flows Despite financial market stability, there are increasing signs that the region may face a broad-based slowdown. As global trade momentum weakened due to the China-US trade conflict, export growth in the region declined, causing real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in most East Asian economies to slow in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-index of the Purchasing Managers’ Indices for several regional economies—which reflects near-term external trade performance—has fallen into contraction territory since the fourth quarter, suggesting that near-term growth momentum may soften further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 Markit PMI New Export Orders Indices for East Asian Economies Amid softer growth and recent declines in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: Headline Inflation Rate and Oil Prices With both recent inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar relatively moderate, East Asian central banks face no pressing need for rate hikes, alleviating the policy dilemma of balancing fostering economic growth against curbing inflation and fund outflows. However, as private sector debt in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face challenges from financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

Hong Kong's economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting softer growth in private consumption and weaker trade performance amid the China-US trade conflict. With global growth slowing, real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 2019 is also expected to moderate. The domestic growth outlook is affected by numerous risks and uncertainties, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and economic outcomes in the Mainland economy. Local inflationary pressures should remain mild in 2019, though the inflation outlook faces potential risks on both the upward and downward sides. Economic activities in Hong Kong softened somewhat in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activities failed to sustain the strong momentum seen in the first half, and the quarter-on-quarter growth rate of gross domestic product (GDP) turned slightly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Year on year, economic growth also slowed, with the growth rate in the fourth quarter at 1.3%, below trend growth, dragging down the growth for the entire year from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018.* * Based on the seasonally adjusted GDP volume index compiled using the expenditure approach. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component The weakening of economic activities was mainly due to consumption and exports being dragged down by the direct or indirect impact of the China-US trade conflict. Private consumption growth slowed, possibly due to increased economic uncertainties and the negative wealth effect brought about by adjustments in local asset prices (Chart 3.1). Total investment spending declined notably amid fragile business sentiment. Hong Kong’s external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, especially after the implementation of additional tariffs by China and the US in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports decelerated faster than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines Hong Kong’s merchandise trade performance more carefully and discusses its near-term outlook and associated risks. Chart 3.2 Real Export and import As economic activities weakened, job growth appeared to have slowed in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to approximately 3,873,000 persons at end-2018, lower than the 0.8% increase in the first half of 2018. Due to weak output and employment growth, labour productivity remained broadly stable, showing no sign of significant improvement. With global economic growth slowing further, domestic economic growth in 2019 is expected to moderate. Facing challenges in the external environment, Hong Kong’s export performance is expected to remain under stress. Domestically, although a low unemployment rate and increased household income will continue to support Private consumption, its growth is expected to slow, partially affected by weaker consumer confidence and the negative wealth effect resulting from earlier asset price adjustments. As for fixed capital formation, the outlook may become more uncertain. While building and construction activities are expected to maintain steady growth as housing supply increases, corporates may become more prudent regarding capital investment amid increasing economic uncertainties. Business sentiment indicators, such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers’ Index, continued to hover in the contraction zone; forecasts of future economic growth based on this index suggest that the year-on-year increase in GDP will slow further in the near term. Government forecasts for real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 2019 range between 2% and 3%, while the latest growth estimates by private sector analysts range between 1.5% and 2.7%. The domestic growth outlook is affected by various risks and uncertainties discussed in the previous two chapters. Despite continuing to build up in recent months, Local inflationary pressures remained mild. Year on year, the underlying composite consumer price index (CCPI) recorded increases of 2.8% and 2.9% in the third quarter and fourth quarter of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half. Reflecting Inflation momentum, the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate has also bottomed out recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight increase in Inflation momentum was driven by increases in prices of certain services. Earlier rising housing rentals and accelerated price increases for meals out continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures have generally remained mild over the past few quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Various indicators reflecting Consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and payroll per person Looking ahead, Local inflationary pressures should remain mild in 2019. This mainly reflects weaker domestic growth drivers. However, the earlier uptrend in fresh-letting residential rentals will continue to transmit to consumer price inflation. Market consensus forecasts project a mild headline inflation rate of 2.2% for the entire year, while Government forecasts put the underlying inflation rate at 2.5%. The above inflation outlook faces risks on both the upward and downward sides. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at about 2.8%, the lowest level in over 20 years (Chart 3.6). If labour markets were to deteriorate unexpectedly, the current near-zero output gap would turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. On the other hand, if China-US trade tensions ease, leading to better-than-expected domestic economic performance, local inflation might be pushed higher. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate The China-US trade conflict gradually intensified in the second half of 2018: the US imposed higher tariffs of 25% on imports from Mainland China worth US$34 billion and US$16 billion on July 6 and August 23 respectively. Following these two measures, Mainland China responded by imposing retaliatory tariffs of 25% on an equivalent value of US goods. The US escalated further on September 24, imposing an additional 10% tariff on imports from Mainland China worth US$200 billion. Mainland China immediately responded by imposing tariffs of 5% to 10% on US goods worth US$60 billion. Subsequently, the two countries entered negotiations to avoid further tariff hikes. As Hong Kong has always been a re-export port between these two economies, the imposition of higher tariffs will inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through trade channels. Therefore, the China-US trade conflict has important implications for Hong Kong's macroeconomic and financial stability. This box reviews Hong Kong’s recent merchandise trade performance and explores its near-term outlook. We will also attempt to use more granular data to identify trade goods directly affected by the tariff hikes, thereby examining the impact of the tariffs more carefully. To analyse the impact of tariffs, we first extracted six sets of Hong Kong re-export data corresponding to the various rounds of tariff hikes described in the previous section. In the first two rounds of tariff hikes, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-finished products, while Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round, the scope of affected goods expanded to cover more consumer goods. For brevity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of tariff hikes as List 1, List 2, and List 3 respectively. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focused on analysing the year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong re-exports, adjusted for seasonal factors. In addition, readers should exercise caution when analysing data for September 2018, as trade activities in that month were partially disrupted by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the findings in this section should only be regarded as preliminary evidence of the impact of the tariff hikes. Hong Kong Re-exports of Mainland Origin Affected by Tariffs Shortly after the imposition of higher tariffs, relevant goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US via Hong Kong appeared to have decreased notably or seen slower growth (Chart B3.1). For instance, re-export growth for List 1 and List 2 slowed in the first month following the tariff hikes, while re-exports for List 3 recorded negative growth. Furthermore, re-exports for all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US via Hong Kong in 2018 Hong Kong Re-exports of US Origin Affected by Tariffs In contrast, goods re-exported from the US to Mainland China via Hong Kong showed mixed performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports for List 1 appeared to decrease notably in the months following the tariff hikes but bottomed out towards the end of the year. Re-exports for List 2 were largely in negative territory throughout the year, while growth for List 3 appeared broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the US to Mainland China via Hong Kong in 2018 Front-loading Due to the time lag between the announcement and final implementation of tariffs (or simply the threat of tariff hikes), corporates may increase shipments of affected goods before the anticipated effective date of the tariffs. Indeed, some information and news reports indicate that such front-loading behaviour was quite prevalent. Some private sector analysts also consider this behaviour to be part of the reason for the robust overall trade figures prior to the tariff hikes. More granular trade data show some signs of front-loading for certain listed goods, but this appears to involve only goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). Re-export growth rates for List 1 and List 2 both increased in the months preceding their respective tariff effective dates. On the other hand, the growth rate of re-exports from the US to Mainland China via Hong Kong (Chart B3.2) did not indicate any obvious front-loading behaviour by corporates. Hong Kong Re-exports Not Affected by Tariff Hikes It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports (by value) directly affected by the tariff hikes accounted for only about 4% to 5% of total Hong Kong re-exports. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong’s trade performance, we should also examine re-exports not affected by the tariff hikes. We found that re-exports not affected by tariff hikes recorded negative growth in the last two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). Moreover, the decline in growth of re-exports affected by tariffs (red line) was notably larger starting from the third quarter, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs. The slowdown in growth of re-exports not affected by tariff hikes partly reflects broader weakness in external demand. With increasing uncertainties caused by ongoing trade tensions, tighter global financing conditions, and rising geopolitical risks, external demand could come under more widespread stress. In particular, trade conflicts have weighed on global economic sentiment and activities, as reflected in corrections in major equity markets. Import demand from other economies has thus been dragged down, dampening Hong Kong’s external trade performance. Chart B3.3 Value of Hong Kong re-exports in 2018 Even if China-US trade tensions ease, the near-term outlook for Hong Kong’s merchandise trade remains challenging. Global growth may slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which is bound to further dampen Hong Kong’s export performance. Various business sentiment indicators suggest that businesses of all sizes are pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with sentiment in the trade sector particularly sluggish. Other trade-related sectors, such as logistics, may also be affected. Chart B3.4 Survey on Business Outlook of Hong Kong's Import and Export Sector

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid liquidity tightness driven by anticipated seasonal demand. Entering 2019, partly due to corporates repatriating proceeds from initial public offerings and the market re-establishing carry trade positions, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened, triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March. Nevertheless, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal demand, before some moderation in January 2019. Looking ahead, facing uncertainties such as continued China-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation, HKD fund flows may become more volatile. If the interest rate differential between Hong Kong and the US remains wide, market carry trade activities may persist, keeping the Hong Kong dollar on the weak side for some time and potentially triggering the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking again, which is consistent with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System. Following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499, until the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered four times in total in March 2019 (as at 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid liquidity tightness, but subsequently declined gradually in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilisation resumed after November, as year-end funding demand led to liquidity tightness and the unwinding of carry trades. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporates repatriating IPO proceeds and the market re-establishing carry trade positions. As the interest rate differential between Hong Kong and the US widened after the turn of the year, triggering market participants to buy US dollars and sell Hong Kong dollars in carry trades, the Hong Kong dollar gradually weakened, and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. The Aggregate Balance has remained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), declining slightly to HK$70.9 billion following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March (as at 19 March). Fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar since April 2018 represent only a small fraction of the approximately HK$1 trillion inflows since 2008. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked movements in the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation rate differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was minimal, having limited impact on the REER, the movement of the real effective exchange rate index (REER) broadly tracked that of the nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER). Chart 4.3 Nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) and real effective exchange rate index (REER) The latest balance of payments statistics showed that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and heightened equity markets volatility, outflows of equity securities investment by local residents accelerated, more than offsetting the inflows of portfolio investment by non-residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). In contrast, debt securities investment by both local residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, facing uncertainties such as continued China-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation, fund-flow volatility may heighten. Moreover, the significant negative interest rate differential between HKD and US dollar rates may stimulate carry trade activities, leading to fund outflows. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken, and the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking may be triggered again. Both fund outflows and the potential triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking are normal operations under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Despite the continued US interest rate normalisation process and the multiple triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking from April to August, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The HKD Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half, standing at HK$1,632.9 billion at end-2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, which caused the Aggregate Balance to decrease from HK$109.5 billion at end-June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at end-2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) increased slightly. The HKD Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with no significant change in the Aggregate Balance since August. Subsequently, due to the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to about HK$70.9 billion (as at 19 March). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base Regarding broader measures of Hong Kong dollar money supply, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half, partly reflecting increased macroeconomic and financial conditions uncertainties. Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 3.6% in the first half and edged up by only 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits changed little compared with end-June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand deposits and savings deposits declined, partly due to reduced investment-related transactions in the second half; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record robust growth as deposit rates were raised. Analysed by counterparts, the softer growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was attributable to changes in banks' capital and reserves (included in "net other items"). Chart 4.5 Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterparts Foreign currency deposits accelerated in the second half. Driven by an increase in deposits attracted after banks raised their preferential US dollar deposit rates, US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half, becoming the main driver of foreign currency deposits growth (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits edged up by 1.4% in the second half, with RMB customer deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits with AIs increased modestly by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit growth Although the HKD Monetary Base and deposit base remained large, HIBORs began to face certain upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term Interbank Offered Rates, causing them to be more volatile than long-term Interbank Offered Rates (Chart 4.7). The three-month and 12-month HIBORs averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, about 30 basis points higher than their June averages. Entering 2019, as seasonal demand subsided, HIBORs generally declined. The three-month and 12-month HIBORs fell to average 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Chart 4.7 HKD and US dollar Interbank Offered Rates The HKD yield curve shifted downwards in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2018, yields on 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds declined by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at end-February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate on new mortgages During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average HKD funding costs of Retail banks, edged up. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit funding costs, the composite interest rate rose from 0.62% at end-June to 0.89% at end-December 2018, before retreating to 0.83% at end-January 2019 (Chart 4.8). Given rising funding costs, following the upward adjustment of the US federal funds rate target range in September, Retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points.
