After the US federal funds rate target range was raised again in December, Retail banks did not adjust their Best Lending Rates further. Meanwhile, the average lending rate on new mortgages followed the rise in Best Lending Rates, reaching about 2.45% at end-January 2019. Looking ahead, US interest rate paths, fund flows, and local financial market activities (such as IPO subscription activities) will continue to be major drivers of HKD interest rates. Given the still large HKD Monetary Base and the substantial holdings of EFBNs by the banking system, as banks can use EFBNs as collateral to borrow HKD funds through the Discount Window, the pace of increases in HKD interest rates should be relatively moderate. Against this background of heightened China-US trade tensions, both offshore renminbi and onshore exchange rates depreciated against the US dollar since early 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, buoyed by optimism driven by the resumption of high-level China-US trade talks, both offshore renminbi and onshore exchange rates stabilisation resumed in November. Meanwhile, the spread between onshore and offshore renminbi was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Currently, the ongoing China-US trade tensions have not yet had a significant impact on the funding position in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity positions remained broadly stable, overnight CNH HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). Three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at end-February 2019, possibly reflecting recent monetary easing measures introduced by the People’s Bank of China (PBoC). Nevertheless, it remains to be seen how progress in China-US trade negotiations will affect liquidity in the offshore renminbi interbank market in 2019. Chart 4.10 The overnight and the three-month CNH HIBOR The offshore renminbi (CNH) liquidity pool in Hong Kong expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. Renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half, rising by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at end-2018 (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by renminbi customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and recorded a 5.2% increase in the second half. Among them, corporate customers’ deposits grew faster than personal customers’ deposits. However, certificates of deposit further declined by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to reduced issuance of certificates of deposit and a relatively larger amount of certificates of deposit maturing in October.

Largely supported by an increase in net interest income, Retail banks’ profit continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting the upward pressure on Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) and retail deposit rates amid US interest rate normalisation, the overall HKD funding costs of retail banks increased notably, but remained at a relatively low level. Against the backdrop of uncertainties in the external environment, bank credit contracted modestly in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilising since November, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds due to persistent uncertainties over China-US trade relations, global economic slowdown, uncertainties regarding the pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant about the potential impact on the credit risk of their related corporate loans should the external environment deteriorate further. The aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 14.3% from the same period in 2017, while the return on assets also rose to 1.23% from 1.14% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly driven by a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset increases in loan impairment charges and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 19.4%, while the return on assets rose to 1.27% from 1.16% in 2017. Chart 5.1 Retail banks’ profit The net interest margins (NIMs) of retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period last year (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Net interest margins of retail banks Largely reflecting further US interest rate hikes and some decline in interbank HKD liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking in August 2018, Hong Kong interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). As banks generally raised time-deposit rates to secure long-term stable funding, HKD retail deposit rates also increased during the review period. In addition, following the US rate hike decision at end-September, banks raised their Best Lending Rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Given the rise in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite interest rate (a measure of retail banks’ average cost of HKD funds) rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained at a relatively low level by historical standards. Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. On a broader front, the overall HKD and USD funding cost of licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to show an upward trajectory. In the second half of 2018, banks’ average overall HKD and USD funding cost rose by 36 basis points, following a 40-basis-point increase in the first half (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and USD funding costs and maturity profile of licensed banks The cumulative increase in HIBORs exceeded the rise in banks’ overall funding costs, which may have had a positive impact on retail banks’ HIBOR-linked housing loans, a segment that the industry has been actively promoting over the past few years. However, future improvements in NIMs may become more limited, as most HIBOR-linked housing loans have already reached their capped rates linked to Best Lending Rates. Given the uncertainty over the timing of future increases in Best Lending Rates, the continued upward trend in banks’ funding costs amid US interest rate normalisation may weigh on overall NIMs. Looking ahead, increased uncertainties in the external environment may cloud banks’ earnings outlook. In particular, against the backdrop of global economic growth slowing, persistent uncertainties over China-US trade relations may dampen business sentiment and reduce demand for bank credit. Should this lead to a significant decline in loans and deterioration in asset quality, it could weigh on banks’ profitability. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong, well above international minimum standards. At end-2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) rose further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated AIs 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Starting from 1 January 2013, locally incorporated AIs are required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012. In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III also introduced a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement came into effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs maintained at a robust level of 8.0% at end-December 2018, well above the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity positions of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable to 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions also rose from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated basis. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), as one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, indicated that the funding position of AIs remained stable. The average NSFR of category 1 institutions maintained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of category 2A institutions maintained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable to 2018. The sufficient liquidity and sound funding position of AIs indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is resilient to various liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for AIs, reflecting that the banking system maintained a stable liability structure. At end-2018, customer deposits accounted for 55.7% of total liabilities of all AIs, up slightly from 54.5% six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all AIs 1. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As total loans and advances declined during the second half of 2018 while Total deposits increased over the same period, the loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio of all AIs in all currencies fell from 75.7% at end-June 2018 to 72.6% at year-end (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign currency LTD ratio of all AIs decreased from 65.2% to 58.3% during the same period. In contrast, as Hong Kong dollar deposits grew much slower than Hong Kong dollar loans, the Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio edged up from 85.4% at end-June 2018 to 86.9% at year-end. We estimate that under a parallel 200-basis-point interest rate shock, the potential decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would be equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base at end-2018 (Chart 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty over the pace of further US interest rate hikes, banks should pay close attention to their interest rate risk management. Against the backdrop of persistent uncertainties over the China-US trade conflict, tightening global financial liquidity, and global economic growth slowing, credit growth slowed notably in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth has shown signs of stabilising since November 2018. On a semi-annual basis, total loans and advances of all AIs decreased by 0.9% in the second half of 2018, after a 5.3% increase in the first half (Chart 5.12). This decline was due to softer growth in domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and a decrease in loan volume for loans for use outside Hong Kong. Domestic loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loan volume for loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the preceding six months. For 2018 as a whole, total loan growth slowed significantly to 4.4% from 16.1% in 2017. Chart 5.12 Loan growth Looking ahead, credit demand may remain subdued in the near term. The HKMA’s Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook conducted in December 2018 showed that among all responding AIs, 82% expected loan demand to be the same over the next three months, while the proportion expecting a decrease in demand rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite a slight decline in total loans in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks’ loan portfolios remained sound. The gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all AIs edged down to 0.55% and 0.36% respectively at end-December 2018, from 0.61% and 0.40% respectively at end-June 2018. For retail banks, the gross CLR dipped slightly to 0.50%, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans rose slightly to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios were low by historical standards. Figures before December 2015 reflect the position of retail banks’ Hong Kong offices and overseas branches. From December 2015 onwards, coverage has been expanded to include major overseas subsidiaries of retail banks. On a semi-annual basis, Personal loans growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to softer growth in Personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal loans), which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loan (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP) grew at a slower pace than Personal loans, the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The outbreak of the coronavirus since early 2020 has hit both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economic that are distinct from previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have rolled out stimulus measures since early March to contain the economic shocks brought about by the epidemic, financial markets remained volatile and global financing conditions have also tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and domestic environments, Hong Kong’s foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. Amidst a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, the Aggregate Balance remaining largely stable, and total deposits increasing modestly, no significant fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. After a modest rebound in the first half of 2019, total loans growth slowed in the second half. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, though its trend was somewhat mixed. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a range of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt servicing burden, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has shown initial signs of stabilisation, supported by intensified monetary easing by major central banks, an easing of China-US trade tensions, and a reduced risk of a “no-deal Brexit” in the UK. However, since late January, the rising number of global coronavirus infections has caused market concerns and triggered significant volatility in the global financial market. To address the evolving risks of the epidemic, several major central banks have cut interest rates significantly and expanded liquidity facilities, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, amid widening credit spreads and plunging equity markets, global financing conditions have tightened. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlooks have increased. The coronavirus epidemic will dampen global economic activities, and the extent of the economic impact will depend on the severity and duration of the outbreak. Over the medium term, relations between the US and its major trading partners may become tense again, and trade negotiations between the UK and the EU post-Brexit could also be fraught with difficulties. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia.1 Exports from the East Asian region to various major destinations, including the US, European economies, and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported revenue growth, but it remains to be seen whether there will be a broad-based rebound in the technology products cycle. Financial markets reacted positively to the Phase One trade deal between China and the US announced in December 2019, and the trade truce has partially reduced uncertainties surrounding global trade. Nonetheless, the East Asian region will continue to face headwinds such as weak firms’ earnings and high private sector leverage. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies could come under further pressure amid sustained softer growth. Travel bans imposed by many regional economies could hit tourism in Asia, especially for economies more reliant on tourism service exports. Manufacturing may also be affected by the outbreak due to the region's close supply chains linkages with Mainland China. As for Mainland China, economic growth slowing continued in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade deal between China and the US helps temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressure persists amid the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing, and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 made stabilising the economy a priority for 2020, while also focusing on the control of financial vulnerabilities. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, authorities on the Mainland continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policy measures to support the private sector, especially small private-owned enterprises (POEs). Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed out that private industrial enterprises may have faced declining equity in recent years, seen as a sign of “private sector retreat”. Box 2 examines the drivers of changes in equity among Mainland industrial enterprises using data from listed firms in 2018, finding that POEs or small firms are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or “retreat”. While negative earnings were found to be the largest driver, other factors, especially structural ones, are also noteworthy (see Box 2 for details). Domestic economic activities contracted visibly in the second half of 2019. Real gross domestic product (GDP) declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the domestic economy has entered a recession. Dragged down by this, the economy contracted by 1.2% for 2019 as a whole, compared to growth of 2.9% in 2018, marking the first annual contraction since 2009. Sluggish domestic demand, especially the shrinkage of Private consumption, was the main factor dragging down GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, leading to a weak economic outlook, which in turn dampened consumer and business sentiment. With the resurgence of China-US trade tensions, global economic growth slowing, and a severe downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained sluggish. In view of the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government rolled out multiple rounds of stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To allow banks greater room to step up support for the domestic economy and help cushion the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion to enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic outcomes for 2020 are expected to face significant challenges, and the epidemic has recently brought about notable downside risks. As sectors such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism, and transport have yet to recover from the disruption caused by social incidents, the epidemic will deal a double blow to these industries. However, a range of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and businesses (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessional low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme (SFGS).2 The HKMA further reduced the CCyB ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020, which will allow banks greater room to step up support for the domestic economy, especially sectors and individuals under greater short-term pressure due to the epidemic. Analysed by gross domestic product (GDP) components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business sentiment. Although government consumption will support the economy, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued following the completion of some major infrastructure projects. On the external front, the Phase One trade deal between China and the US is expected to have a slight positive impact on the domestic economy in the near term.3 However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to weigh on Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. Government forecasts project real gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 2020 to be between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average of growth estimates by international institutions and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous risks and uncertainties, including global economic growth slowing, China-US trade relations, economic outcomes in Mainland China, and local social incidents. The labour markets came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment decreasing, the unemployment rate rising, and the real wage index declining year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social incidents and the coronavirus outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food service sectors. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak, the unemployment rate will rise further. Box 3 explores in greater detail recent developments and the near-term outlook for the labour markets. Local inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of elevated fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activities weakened, Inflation momentum also gradually eased. Due to weak economic conditions, consolidation in fresh-letting residential rentals, and moderate imported inflation, inflation is expected to moderate in the near term. Market consensus forecasts put the headline inflation rate for 2020 between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5%. Supported by increased Hong Kong dollar demand related to equities (including initial public offering (IPO) activity), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened gradually since mid-October 2019. Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened further, partly due to buoyant initial public offering (IPO) activity and partly due to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by liquidity tightness approaching year-end. Following the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, during the review period, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly, and the Convertibility Undertakings were not triggered. The Aggregate Balance remained largely stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) have been volatile, reflecting seasonal funding demand and increased capital market activities such as initial public offering (IPO)s. Box 4 examines how market attention to future initial public offering (IPO) activity affects the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate rose gradually from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020, reflecting banks continuing to raise preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding. As some banks raised the cap linked to Best Lending Rates, the average lending rate on new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October, but with Best Lending Rates in the market lowered starting from November, the average lending rate on new mortgages dipped slightly to around 2.5% in January 2020. Amidst a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, the Aggregate Balance remaining largely stable, and Total deposits increasing modestly, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact should the coronavirus epidemic worsen further amid uncertainties in the external environment. With substantial foreign reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to cope with fund outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. During the review period, amid market expectations of a trade deal between China and the US, both offshore renminbi and onshore RMB exchange rates strengthened, but they came under weakening pressure since late January 2020 due to the coronavirus outbreak. In late 2019, offshore renminbi generally traded at a premium to onshore renminbi; the discount widened briefly at end-January 2020, but the spread remained modest by historical standards. The offshore renminbi (CNH) liquidity pool in Hong Kong recovered slightly after a minor decline in the previous review period. As of end-January 2020, renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB 637.4 billion. Other renminbi businesses in Hong Kong also grew, with RMB bank loans and renminbi trade settlement in the city recording strong growth. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level of RMB 1,133.9 billion for 2019 as a whole. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, offshore renminbi business in Hong Kong is expected to benefit from the continuing liberalisation of Mainland’s capital account, increased asset allocation in renminbi assets by international investors, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives.

At the end of 2019, global economic activities showed signs of stabilisation, raising market hopes for a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the rising number of coronavirus infections worldwide has dashed hopes of recovery, deepening investors' concern over a global economic downturn and triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. To combat the economic shocks, major central banks and some governments have rolled out stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has clouded the outlook for many regional economies. The COVID-19 outbreaks are expected to drag on regional economic growth in the near term, with the tourism sector hit especially hard. Meanwhile, East Asia continues to face challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private-sector leverage. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US has helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressure persists amid the impact of the COVID-19 outbreaks, ongoing economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown, though monetary and fiscal policy responses by authorities will provide some buffer. Amid ongoing trade tensions and policy uncertainties, manufacturing and investment remained soft, and global economic growth stayed lacklustre in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, growth showed preliminary signs of stabilisation in the last quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from earlier policy easing by the Fed and the ECB, as well as an easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the "Phase One" trade agreement between China and the US. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Indices However, since the end of January, the rising number of coronavirus infections globally and the subsequent economic shocks have sparked market concern, leading to a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and plays a pivotal role in global supply chains, disruptions to production activities in the Mainland and the drag on its economic growth caused by the epidemic will result in significant spillover effects, potentially spreading worldwide (Chart 2.3). Since the end of February, the surge in coronavirus infections outside Mainland China may exacerbate disruptions to supply chains and pose risks of directly dragging on domestic economic activities. 5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread Chart 2.3 Exports of Goods and Services to Mainland China by Selected Major Advanced Economies in 2018 (% of GDP) To combat the potentially severe economic impact of the epidemic, some central banks (including the Fed, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England) have cut rates since early March, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and firms. However, financial markets still face immense selling pressure, leading to a notable tightening of global financing conditions, which may further intensify downward pressure on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index Beyond developments related to the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. Especially regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have declined following the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations may be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to proceed smoothly, thereby perpetuating uncertainties post-Brexit. Additionally, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will put stress on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economy activities remained lacklustre in the second half of 2019 due to sluggish global demand. Exports from the East Asian region to various major destinations, including the US, European economies and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Despite preliminary signs indicating that the downward cycle of technology products in the region is bottoming out, including reports from major regional electronics firms of improved earnings at the end of 2019, 6 it remains to be seen whether there will be a substantive rebound in regional exports of technology products. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise Exports to Major Destinations Persistent sluggish economic growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), potentially affecting potential economic growth in the region over the longer term. To support economic growth amid moderate inflation, central banks in Indonesia, the Philippines and South Korea cut policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after rate cuts in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross Fixed Capital Formation The COVID-19 outbreaks have raised concerns that regional economies may come under further stress amid persistently weak growth. As many regional economies have imposed lockdowns on Mainland China, the tourism sector has borne the brunt, with economies more reliant on visitors from Mainland China and tourism service exports being particularly affected by the epidemic (Chart 2.7). The persistence and intensification of the epidemic will also affect supply chains in the region that are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism Exports and Chinese Tourists In the near term, the epidemic will continue to impact economic activities and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the SARS outbreak in 2003, these impacts may be transitory, but the actual situation will hinge on the severity and scope of the epidemic and the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreaks. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, despite market expectation that corporate earnings will deteriorate in the near term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions have encouraged yield-seeking activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without support from fundamentals. Consequently, regional stock markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected Earnings of Constituent Stocks of Benchmark Equity Indices Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it harder for private-sector entities in the region to service debt. While lower domestic rates can provide breathing space for indebted corporates and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Furthermore, as discussed in Box 1, as more index-tracking flows enter regional financial markets, the risk of debt overhang in the private sector may also be heightened, although such impact may be confined to firms with stronger fundamentals and their long-term borrowings. Third, in terms of external factors, risks facing East Asian economies may increase amid increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite recent progress in the Phase One trade agreement between China and the US, China-US trade tensions persist as fundamental trade issues between the two countries remain. As evidenced by the widening net trade surpluses of many regional economies with the US (Chart 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to seek alternative supply sources outside China-centric supply chains to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the US had increased to approximately US$167 billion. If trade surpluses with the US continue to widen, relevant Asian economies may become the next targets of trade conflicts; for instance, the US government imposed massive tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In light of this, despite the China-US trade truce, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Merchandise Trade Surplus with the US Over the past decade, intensified integration of international financial markets has led to a notable increase in global cross-border securities investment flows. A recent study shows that as much as 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-tracking funds. 8 Index-tracking funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds) but also actively-managed funds that reference investment indices. 9 By bringing in overseas investors that relevant economies could not otherwise attract or access, these funds help promote financial market development in emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds enable emerging market economies to achieve a diverse investor base, supporting long-term market growth and stability. But is there really a free lunch? Regarding passive bond funds, there is market concern that investment by such funds may undermine the fiscal discipline of issuers of the corporate bonds they invest in, thereby leading to high leverage levels at relevant firms. 10 Moreover, some opinions suggest that the growth of index-tracking funds in recent years has exacerbated volatility in global securities investment flows, rendering emerging market economies—which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors—even more vulnerable. 11 This box assesses the impact of index-tracking investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to constituent bonds according to their weights in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared to actively-managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may leave issuers of index constituent bonds lacking the drivers to act in the interests of fund investors. 13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour may fuel excessive borrowing, posing significant credit and debt servicing ability risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, where leverage rose sharply after the Global Financial Crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate Leverage in Emerging Market Economies Using the weights of corporates in various emerging market economies within a mainstream index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as an estimate of their bonds' exposure to passive bond fund investment, 14 we find that increases in such investment raise the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to fostering the development of emerging market corporate bond markets, the expanded long-term bond investor base resulting from passive bond funds also benefits the development of firms in emerging market economies. We also find that the aforementioned effects are significant only for emerging market firms with relatively sound fundamentals (especially those with stronger debt servicing ability and lower leverage ratios) (solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged firms or those with weaker debt servicing ability do not appear to fall further into debt traps due to passive bond fund investment. In sum, the above research suggests that the growth of passive bond fund investment may not significantly increase debt servicing ability risks in the corporate sectors of emerging market economies.

Due to weakened private consumption, reduced investment spending, and poor export performance, Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. Economic outcomes for 2020 are expected to face significant challenges, and the recent coronavirus epidemic has also brought about notable downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous risks and uncertainties, including global economic growth slowing, China-US trade relations, economic outcomes in Mainland China, and developments in local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to climb further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease somewhat, although the outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. The domestic economy contracted visibly in the second half of 2019. Year on year, real gross domestic product (GDP) contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% respectively in the third quarter and the fourth quarter (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half, the economy shrank by 1.2% for the entire year, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis in 2009. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activities slowed markedly in the second half (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real gross domestic product (GDP) declined by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% successively in the second quarter, the third quarter, and the fourth quarter, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, weakening the economic outlook and dampening consumer confidence; consequently, private consumption contracted visibly from the third quarter onwards. 33 Due to increased economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment, overall investment spending remained subdued and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter. 34 On the external front, amid heightened China-US trade tensions, weaker global economic growth, and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals, Hong Kong’s external trade performance remained sluggish (Chart 3.2). 35 Affected by the sharp contraction in exports of services, net trade dragged down GDP in the third quarter but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Chart 3.2 Real Export and import Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government announced multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to relieve the financial burden on citizens, safeguard employment, and support corporates, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and hard-hit sectors such as retail, food services, transport, and tourism. 36 To allow banks greater room to step up support for the domestic economy and help cushion the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on October 14 a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion to corporates, including SMEs. Economic outcomes for Hong Kong in 2020 are expected to face significant challenges, and the recent epidemic has also brought about notable downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruptions caused by social incidents, the epidemic will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a range of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and firms (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and concessional low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee for firms under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme (SFGS). 37 The HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on March 16, 2020, which will allow banks greater room to step up support for the domestic economy, especially sectors and individuals under greater pressure in the near term due to the impact of the epidemic. Analysed by gross domestic product (GDP) components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain subdued due to fragile consumption and business sentiment. Although government consumption will support the economy, public investment spending is expected to remain relatively sluggish as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the Phase One China-US trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the domestic economy in the near term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to drag down Hong Kong’s external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may cause supply chain disruptions in the region and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong’s export performance. Government forecasts put real gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 2020 at between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average of growth estimates by international organizations and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous risks and uncertainties as described in previous chapters. The labour markets came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose to 3.3% in December 2019 from a multi-year low base of 2.8% in June 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). Notably, the unemployment rate for the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors rose to a decade-high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the heavy toll inflicted by social incidents. 39 As economic drivers weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued its downtrend to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly concentrated in the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction sectors. Real wages also declined by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in response to the weak economic outlook mentioned above, the labour markets will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is highly likely to climb further. Box 3 discusses recent developments and the near-term outlook for the labour markets in greater detail. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to elevated prices of fresh pork; thereafter, as economic activities weakened, inflation momentum gradually eased. Year on year, the underlying composite consumer price index (CCPI) grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, and the increase moderated slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also softened from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The easing of inflation momentum was due to reduced price pressures across several consumer price index (CPI) components. For traded goods, elevated prices of fresh pork kept basic food inflation visible, though price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear, as well as durable goods, remained mild. On the services side, following the earlier moderation in rising housing rentals for fresh-letting residential rentals, growth in the rental component of the CPI also showed a downtrend (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures edged up but remained mild in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the near term. Domestically, the weak economic conditions and the widened negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. With fresh-letting residential rentals continuing to moderate, the housing rental component in inflation should ease further. Externally, imported inflation is expected to remain mild due to weak global economic growth and softer energy prices. Market consensus forecasts put headline inflation rate for 2020 at between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5% and the headline inflation rate at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to risk factors on both the upside and downside. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economic deterioration is more severe than expected (e.g., due to a prolonged coronavirus epidemic), inflation could be further suppressed. On the other hand, if supply disruptions for fresh pork become more severe, it would bring upward pressure on inflation. Despite the marked slowdown in the domestic economy, the unemployment rate remained at a low level of 2.8–2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. It was only as social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate climbed more noticeably to 3.3% towards the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus epidemic, the labour markets will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this background, this box analyses recent developments and the near-term outlook for the labour markets, including exploring why the overall labour markets remained largely robust in the first three quarters of 2019 (with little change in the unemployment rate) and what implications this holds for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag behind the year-on-year growth of real gross domestic product (GDP) by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% even when real economic activities deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Chart B3.1 Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth and unemployment rate On the labour demand side, although China-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt heavy blows to employment in the trade and retail and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors managed to support the overall labour markets. Specifically, employment in financial, business, public administration, social, and personal services continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the impact of declining employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong’s financial system remained robust, and financial activities in fintech development and initial public offerings were also very active. These factors may have helped support the job market in the financial and business services sectors. Moreover, public administration, social, and personal services, including education, healthcare, and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real gross domestic product (GDP), public administration, social, and personal services exhibit a relatively neutral response to the economic cycle. In other words, even during an economic slowdown, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors. Chart B3.2 Changes in employment by industry in 2019 On the labour supply side, the labour force participation rate dropped from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against the rise in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 illustrates the various supply and demand factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped contain the unemployment rate. However, the visible economic contraction in the second half led to a decrease in employment, exerting upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment decreased during the economic downturn, the lower labour force participation rate helped alleviate the pressure of rising unemployment in the second half of 2019. Chart B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate Some structural changes in the labour markets are also noteworthy. In particular, the increased proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help firms retain staff. In fact, the shares of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment have declined to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, but the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group in total employment (about 7% in 2017). 42 Therefore, firms may be able to retain or hire more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to about 44 hours currently, partly reflecting a larger share of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has generally strengthened against the US dollar since October, with upward momentum further strengthening in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate at the strong side of the Convertibility Zone for most of the recent months. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was partly driven by equity-related demand and partly due to short-covering amid liquidity tightness towards year-end. Overall, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Despite heightened fund-flow volatility triggered by market sentiment amid an uncertain external environment and the COVID-19 outbreaks, Hong Kong’s substantial foreign reserves and robust banking system enable it to withstand pressures from fund outflows without compromising local financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related Hong Kong dollar demand, including initial public offering (IPO) activities, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened since mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar further strengthened, and from mid-December to February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained at the strong side of the Convertibility Zone. The stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was partly due to active IPO activities and partly due to short-covering amid liquidity tightness towards year-end. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity positions eased somewhat, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, during the review period, trading in the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. As neither the strong-side nor weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) The nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) of the Hong Kong dollar broadly tracked that of the US dollar, rising slightly during the review period (Chart 4.3). Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the movement of the REER broadly mirrored that of the NEER. Chart 4.3 Nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) and real effective exchange rate index (REER) In assessing fund flows in Hong Kong, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct yet interrelated concepts: (1) HKD fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. HKD fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows, which helps assess monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System. On the other hand, cross-border fund flows focus on the geographical movement of funds through the Hong Kong banking system, which helps assess the overall stability of Hong Kong's financial system. These two concepts require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring HKD fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert their HKD assets into foreign currency assets in large amounts, demand for the Hong Kong dollar would naturally decline, leading to a weaker Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking level of HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars upon banks' requests, thereby reducing the Aggregate Balance. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has largely remained unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been at the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months; therefore, no significant fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar were observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border fund flows, total deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) in Hong Kong serve as a useful indicator. Significant fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system would inevitably lead to a decline in bank deposits. During the review period, Total deposits increased modestly, indicating no significant cross-border fund outflows. The Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner, suggesting that the impact of the COVID-19 outbreaks on the local monetary environment remains limited. Nevertheless, risks arising from the COVID-19 outbreaks warrant close monitoring. With substantial foreign reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to cope with fund outflows and maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. Despite the uncertain external environment and local economic slowdown, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The HKD Monetary Base remained substantial, increasing by 4.0% since end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at end-January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As no Convertibility Undertakings were triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained largely unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs), Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, recorded steady growth. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, broad measures of Hong Kong dollar money supply remained broadly stable. Broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, before some moderation with a slight increase of 0.2% over the seven months since end-June 2019. Counterpart analysis shows that the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 since end-June mainly reflected increases in banks’ net foreign currency assets and the expansion of the Monetary Base (adjusted for increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins) (Chart 4.5). Over the seven months since end-June, Hong Kong dollar deposits (the major component of Hong Kong dollar M3) remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow modestly, partly reflecting rising interest rates on Hong Kong dollar deposits. Chart 4.5 Hong Kong dollar M3 and changes in counterparts Over the seven months since end-June 2019, foreign currency deposits increased modestly by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by US dollar deposits, which rose by 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits declined by 1.0% over the same period, with RMB customer deposits recording a slight decrease when valued in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits with AIs grew steadily by 1.2% since end-June. Supported by the increase in Total deposits, Hong Kong’s broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since end-June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may be subject to fluctuations due to various transient factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering (IPO) related funding demand and business and investment-related activities, these statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) by currency Chart 4.7 Broad money supply (M2) Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, Short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates exhibited volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities since the fourth quarter of 2019. In particular, as IPO activities in the Hong Kong equity market became more active, overnight CNH HIBOR experienced occasional larger fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 During the review period, other Short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates generally rose. Subscriptions for major new listings exerted significant pressure on overnight rates. Empirical analysis in Box 4 indicates that market attention to future IPO activities also affects the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. This occurs when market participants anticipate the subscription closing dates of major new listings and arrange medium-term funding in advance. Chart 4.8 HIBORs and US dollar counterparts As for the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it shifted downwards alongside the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2019, yields on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, yields on the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond dropped by 50 basis points to 1.00% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages On the retail front, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for Retail banks, rose gradually from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020. This increase mainly reflected banks continuing to raise preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding, resulting in higher weighted deposit rates. Following the reduction in the US Federal Funds target range at end-October 2019, several Retail banks lowered their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 basis points. Consequently, the Best Lending Rates of Retail banks currently stand in the range of 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding housing loans, for mortgages linked to the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR), major banks raised the cap determined by the Best Lending Rates, causing the average lending rate for new mortgages to rise to about 2.63% in October. 45 Following cuts in the Best Lending Rates in the market since November, the average lending rate for new mortgages declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to evolving risks posed by the COVID-19 outbreaks to US economic activities and to support the Fed in achieving its policy objectives, the Fed lowered the target range of the Federal Funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). While HIBORs track US dollar counterparts over the longer term, Short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates may be influenced by local factors affecting Hong Kong dollar demand, such as local IPO activities. Since the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has decreased since April 2018, the sensitivity of HIBORs to changes in HKD funds supply and demand may have increased. However, this does not imply that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet settlement needs among banks. In fact, the Hong Kong interbank market has continued to operate in an orderly manner. In case of short-term liquidity tightness, banks can use liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. Amid potential escalation of the China-US trade conflict, both offshore renminbi and onshore exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore renminbi falling to a decade low of 7.19 against the US dollar on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Entering October, amid expectations of resumption of China-US trade negotiations, the downtrend in the renminbi reversed. Both offshore renminbi and onshore strengthened in the fourth quarter, and following the signing of the Phase One trade deal between China and the US, briefly appreciated beyond the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020. However, since end-January, due to the COVID-19 outbreaks, both offshore renminbi and onshore have again faced weakening pressures. The offshore renminbi mostly traded at a discount to the onshore from May to August, while generally trading at a premium in later 2019; the discount widened briefly at end-January 2020, but the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates Despite fluctuations in the RMB exchange rate, liquidity positions in the CNH interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, three-month CNH HIBOR continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). Overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief volatility in late August and late November due to MSCI A-share adjustments, and again approaching the Lunar New Year holidays at end-January 2020.

Due to increased uncertainties in the global and domestic economic environment, Retail banks’ profit in Hong Kong edged down in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and sound as measured against international standards. Asset quality remained at a healthy level by historical standards. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the same period during the review period. Accordingly, the Average loan-to-deposit ratios in all currencies and the Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio of all AIs both increased. However, given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system remained stable and deposits were broadly flat, the liquidity positions of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt servicing burden, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks 59 edged down by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets dipped slightly to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% recorded in the same period in 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margins (NIMs) of Retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), the net interest income of Retail banks continued to record increased modestly during the review period. However, both loan impairment charges and operating expenses of Retail banks increased, resulting in a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1 Retail banks’ profit Chart 5.2 Net interest margins (NIMs) of Retail banks Despite three 25-basis-point cuts in the US Fed Funds target rate in the second half of 2019, the HKD wholesale funding market has not yet experienced significant downward pressure. On the contrary, affected by a number of local factors—including seasonal demand, increased liquidity demand due to large-scale initial public offering (IPO)s, and relatively tight liquidity positions in the interbank market—short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) have been on an upward trajectory since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, during the review period, longer-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) remained largely stable, with the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) standing at 2.43% as of end-2019, close to the level six months earlier (blue line in Chart 5.3). As for the retail front, since HKD savings deposit rates remained near zero, Retail banks had limited room to follow the US policy rate cut. 60 On the other hand, as HKD liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funding. 61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of HKD deposits, the composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average HKD funding cost of Retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% at end-2019, though it remained at a relatively low level by historical standards (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, given that the decline in USD funding cost of locally incorporated licensed banks offset the slight rise in their HKD funding costs, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost of locally incorporated licensed banks edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks’ net interest income benefited from the slight decline in overall funding costs and the relatively high level of Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs), supporting banking sector profitability during the period. Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding cost and maturity of licensed banks 1. Starting from June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local framework for interest rate risk in the banking book submit returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks continue to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost and maturity are calculated as weighted averages based on the relevant figures of these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Looking ahead, a number of downside risk factors in the external and domestic environments will continue to cloud banks’ earnings outlook. Relevant factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of China-US trade relations, and escalating geopolitical tensions. An intensification of these risk factors could dampen already weak global economic growth drivers and reduce credit demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of moderately loose monetary policy by major central banks, the global low interest rate environments are likely to persist, which may put pressure on banks’ future net interest margins (NIMs). On the domestic front, local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to weigh on business investment and business confidence. Against this background of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even intensifies further, it could deteriorate the credit demand outlook and banks’ asset quality. In terms of overall market developments, following the issuance of eight virtual banking licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector has begun to roll out virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to gain market share by launching more convenient products and offering more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this may exert upward pressure on incumbent banks’ funding costs. Although the near-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited business scale of virtual banks, the longer-term impact may hinge on whether incumbent banks accelerate fintech adoption to maintain competitiveness. Results from Box 5 indicate that the degree of fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically correlated with improvements in cost efficiency and higher profitability levels. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and much higher than minimum international standards. As of end-2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) further rose to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). Tier 1 capital also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) remained at a robust level of 8.2% at end-2019, well above the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). The average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines has raised hopes for an economic restart, boosting global growth prospects. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary policy easing, financial markets have repeatedly hit record highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery is expected to vary across economies. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels, and the long-lasting scars inflicted by the pandemic on the economy will pose challenges for policymakers in the period ahead. The Hong Kong dollar exchange and money markets continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings against the US dollar, mainly driven by equity-related demand. During the review period, Total deposits increased, with no signs of significant outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weaker economic activities and lower credit demand amid recurring COVID-19 outbreaks, total loans in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, although a modest increase was still recorded for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained generally stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties regarding the pace of recovery and lingering geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant about the impact of relevant downside risks on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as various places restarted their economies, but rising COVID-19 infections from the fourth quarter onwards led to softer growth globally. Nevertheless, following breakthroughs in vaccine development towards the end of 2020, market expectations that the pandemic would eventually come to an end bode well for the global economic return to normalcy and accelerated growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary policy easing, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, even as signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud global economic outlooks. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and the earlier aggressive policy easing could lead to higher-than-expected inflation, potentially prompting central banks to taper monetary easing earlier than anticipated and ending financial market expectations of a "lower for longer" monetary policy. Over the longer term, policymakers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the many economic legacies of the pandemic, including elevated global debt and long-lasting economic scars. In East Asia, domestic gross domestic product (GDP) growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a pickup in export demand. Amid increased risk appetite, portfolio inflows into the region recovered and search-for-yield activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, the East Asian region still faces persistent uncertainties arising from the pandemic. First, in the global race for vaccine procurement, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, potential variations in vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy, coupled with weakening government fiscal positions in the region, could dampen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of fund flows. As for Mainland China, the pace of recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive year-on-year growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook still hinges significantly on the COVID-19 situation and developments in Sino-US tensions. Latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. After depreciating for several months in early 2020, the renminbi strengthened for the rest of the year, driven by an accelerating economic recovery, a weak US dollar, and strong net inflows into the Mainland bond market. Detailed analysis suggests that during the COVID-19 outbreaks, fundamentals rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving RMB exchange rate movements (see Box 1 for details). Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real gross domestic product (GDP) remained well below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in domestic demand and further expansion in merchandise exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to about 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, marking the first-ever consecutive annual declines in history following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by industry show that consumption- and tourism-related industries experienced deeper contractions than the overall economy during the pandemic. To cope with the persistent pandemic, the Government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to assist affected industries and citizens and enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost its economy, including the issuance of one-off HK$5,000 electronic Consumption Vouchers and the provision of 100% guaranteed personal loans for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, announced in March 2021 the extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, as well as the extension of the repayment periods for trade financing loans under the Scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines expected to facilitate a return to normal economic activities, the local economy is projected to resume positive year-on-year growth in 2021 (as a whole), though the strength and pace of recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the COVID-19 situation and the progress and efficacy of vaccine rollouts. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. On external factors, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's merchandise and service exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their mass vaccination programmes. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of 3.5–5.5% for 2021, while the average of growth estimates by international institutions and private sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021.
