The unemployment rate climbed further to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. To address worsening labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (from June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support hard-hit sectors. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Box 2 examines the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Underlying consumer price inflation declined significantly year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further fell to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects Inflation momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months but remained at a low level. As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, local inflationary pressures are likely to stay mild in the near term; in particular, local inflation will continue to be contained by the earlier slowdown in fresh-letting residential rentals. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation rate at a moderate 1.4% for 2021, while the Government forecasts underlying and headline inflation rates at 1.0% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings against the US dollar, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that from buoyant IPO activities and buying flows through the Southbound Stock Connect via Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar on the stronger side. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings were triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in net inflows of HK$263.3 billion. For 2020 as a whole, the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings were triggered 85 times, with cumulative inflows reaching HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. From a geographical perspective, Total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to the COVID-19 situation, the pace of recovery, and lingering Sino-US tensions may exacerbate fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong’s ample foreign reserves position and robust banking system enable it to withstand such volatility. As the Aggregate Balance increased following triggers of the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) generally stayed at very low levels. The composite interest rate, reflecting the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.23% at end-February 2021. Driven by lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also dropped from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, Best Lending Rates at major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Following the strengthening of the onshore (CNY) exchange rate, offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium to the CNY rate, with an average premium of about 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB 826.3 billion by end-January 2021. As for other renminbi business, renminbi bank loans in Hong Kong decreased, while renminbi trade settlement grew, and the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system remained high at RMB 1,191.5 billion throughout 2020. With its efficient financial infrastructure providing investors with numerous cross-border fund flow channels linking to the Mainland, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening up of the Mainland’s capital account, growing demand for renminbi assets from international investors, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. Supported by rising global equity markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors via Stock Connect, the local equity market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. Global equity markets rose due to unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies; market optimism over positive progress in vaccine development, which was seen as conducive to accelerating the recovery of economic activities; and reduced global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recovered from its steep decline in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period and briefly surpassing the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021 to reach a 32-month high. Supported by steady issuance, both the Hong Kong dollar and CNH debt markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following massive net outflows in the first half of 2020, business confidence recovered swiftly as governments worldwide rolled out unprecedented economic stimulus measures, leading to a rebound in inflows into bond funds investing in the local market. Despite a moderate rebound in yields during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained hovering near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, markets expect the COVID-19 pandemic to eventually end, paving the way for accelerated global economic growth thereafter. Coupled with expectations of a "lower for longer" global monetary policy, investors were not deterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at end-2020, and financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021. However, the high hopes in financial markets have diverged from the still-challenging macroeconomic environment. Should the recovery prove less robust than expected, or should policy support be withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for instance due to higher-than-expected inflation), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers face the difficult task of determining when to withdraw policy support and addressing the many legacies of the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and long-lasting economic scarring. Persistent uncertainties surrounding the pandemic continue to cloud the economic recovery in East Asia, with less developed emerging market economies in the region potentially facing greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in vaccination programmes could reverse the current optimism, destabilising net inflows and financial markets. As for Mainland China, the pace of recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the growth outlook remains fraught with uncertainties, hinging significantly on the COVID-19 situation and developments in China-US tensions. Therefore, the government has announced that it will maintain its supportive policy stance while emphasising the importance of containing system-wide risks. Benefiting from pent-up demand released by the re-opening of economies, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, rising COVID-19 infections have prompted local governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, weakening global growth momentum once again. At end-2020, the emergence of more transmissible variants, which subsequently spread worldwide, further aggravated the situation. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of several vaccines for use at end-2020, markets expect the pandemic to eventually end, allowing the global economy to return to normalcy and accelerate its growth. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery has been sustained policy stimulus measures. These include commitments by major central banks to a "lower for longer" monetary policy amid subdued inflation, as well as continued fiscal easing in major advanced economies, notably the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, in January 2021, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) raised its 2021 global gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast to 5.5%, an increase of 0.3 percentage points from its October 2020 projection (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts made by the IMF in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this background, market sentiment strengthened, with cyclical sectors—typically benefiting from economic recovery—seeing share price gains, driving global equity prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices However, the strong performance of financial markets stands in contrast to the still-challenging macroeconomic landscape, and this disconnect may lead to volatility in the asset market amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the pandemic under control hinges on widespread vaccine distribution, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although global mechanisms such as COVAX aim to foster fairer vaccine distribution, limited vaccine supply is expected to exacerbate the issue of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies. If containment efforts fall short, prolonged social distancing and other restrictions may be necessary, thereby undermining the global growth outlook. Chart 2.3 Share of population having received at least one vaccine dose in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021) Second, the rebound in financial markets has been underpinned by sustained monetary and fiscal policy support, especially the "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn faster than expected. For instance, driven by supply bottlenecks, strong money and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already heated up (Chart 2.4). Should future inflation turn out stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back their policy-easing plans, and above-expected inflation data could also heighten volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates in the US and Euro area Third, significant uncertainties exist regarding future China-US relations. The trend of China-US "decoupling", particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the COVID-19 outbreaks. Given the increasingly tough bipartisan stance towards Mainland China in the US, this trend may not necessarily be reversed under the Biden administration. Any unexpected escalation in China-US tensions could trigger turmoil in financial markets going forward. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the dilemma of whether and when to withdraw anti-pandemic support measures. While premature withdrawal could jeopardise the recovery and create a "cliff effect", these measures are costly over the longer term, imposing fiscal burdens and delaying necessary post-pandemic resource reallocation—for example, by keeping unviable "zombie firms" alive through continued government support. Moreover, policymakers must address the many legacies left by the pandemic. First, global debt levels surged in 2020 due to declining corporate revenues and soaring government spending (Chart 2.5). Although the immediate risks posed by the sharp rise in debt may not be imminent given the currently ultra-low global interest rates, continued debt accumulation in both public and private sectors could raise concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt-to-GDP ratio Another legacy involves the potential long-term economic losses or scarring caused by the pandemic. For instance, heightened uncertainties may discourage business investment, while workers suffering from prolonged unemployment may permanently exit the labour markets, leading to significant wastage of manpower. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after a sharp contraction in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The recovery was primarily driven by a rebound in exports, with demand for electronics and technological equipment being particularly strong. Meanwhile, the hardest-hit services sectors (such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face contact) remained in distress. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020 Despite lingering uncertainties over the recovery, portfolio investment flows have resumed. Since the second half of last year, improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to bonds in advanced economies have attracted increased bond fund inflows into the region (Chart 2.7). Amid signs of economic recovery and the rollout of vaccination programmes, equity fund inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the fourth quarter of 2020. Regional currencies appreciated correspondingly due to portfolio inflows, lifting the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index by about 10% from its trough in March last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment flows The East Asian region continues to face persistent uncertainties related to the pandemic. First, while the vaccine rollout offers hope to the region's battered services sectors and economies, global competition for early vaccine supplies has raised procurement costs, and vaccine distribution poses logistical and public health capacity challenges within the region. Consequently, less developed economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination progress across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, as investor optimism is largely driven by the vaccine rollout, any significant shortfall in vaccination progress or efficacy could bring an end to the current capital inflows and the rebound in financial asset prices. A sudden reversal of flows could trigger another wave of market turmoil. With the successful containment of COVID-19 and a gradual pickup in consumption, the Mainland economy recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, exports maintained their growth, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products such as medical supplies and technology products (Chart 2.8). For 2020 as a whole, despite the unprecedented shock from the COVID-19 pandemic, Mainland GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contributions to GDP growth by demand components Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to become a key driver of economic growth. However, whether the continued recovery can be sustained will hinge partially on the evolution of the pandemic. Although industrial production in the Mainland has normalised, the services sector has faced partial disruptions following renewed outbreaks in several northern provinces. On the external front, despite the resumption of export growth in the second half of 2020, uncertainties remain regarding global demand amid fresh waves of infections in most advanced economies. Furthermore, China-US tensions are unlikely to ease in the near term, but the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the agreed-upon EU-China Comprehensive Agreement on Investment will help foster deeper integration between China and other economies, potentially offsetting partially the adverse effect of China-US decoupling on the recovery. Given that the economic outlook remains fraught with uncertainties, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that there would be no new changes to the existing policy stance in 2021, so as to support economic growth while emphasising the importance of controlling system-wide risks, such as maintaining macro leverage stability and local government debt sustainability. In addition, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. Over the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan prioritises technological self-reliance and dual circulation strategies, aiming to raise per capita GDP to the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on the repayment ability of bond issuers appears to have been limited, with the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remaining relatively low in the second half of 2020. However, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 due to a notable rise in defaults by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) (Chart 2.9). While the rise in SOE defaults mainly reflects the Central Government's determination to break the implicit guarantee for SOEs to promote more rational market risk pricing, constrained fiscal space among some local governments, particularly in less developed regions, may also be a contributing factor. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Scale and ratio of onshore Mainland bond defaults In the second half of 2020, funding costs for corporate issuers increased, especially for higher-risk issuers. Although the continued recovery and gradual normalisation of rates led to rising funding costs for lower-rated issuers to some extent, several corporate default incidents in the fourth quarter of 2020 resulted in a significant widening of credit spreads (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: Yields on 5-year corporate bonds In the property market, housing prices in the Mainland continued to rise in the second half of 2020, especially in tier-1 cities. In contrast, price increases in lower-tier cities were much slower (Chart 2.11). The oversupply issue that plagued tier-3 cities in previous years was essentially contained in 2020, partly because tier-3 cities recorded robust sales amid buoyant market sentiment. By end-2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in tier-3 cities stood at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real gross domestic product (GDP) remained well below the pre-pandemic level, Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020 as domestic demand bottomed out and merchandise exports expanded further. With the prospect of COVID-19 vaccination enabling a return to normalcy in economic activities, the domestic economy may resume growth in 2021 after recording its most severe contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the COVID-19 situation and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the domestic economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. Therefore, labour markets are expected to remain under stress in the near term, while Local inflationary pressures should remain mild. Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activities remained well below the level before the COVID-19 outbreaks. The year-on-year decline in real gross domestic product (GDP) narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, for the entire year of 2020, real gross domestic product (GDP) fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, marking the first time in history that two consecutive years of decline were recorded following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data across industries also showed that economic activities in the vast majority of industries recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related sectors experiencing deeper contractions than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real gross domestic product (GDP) began bottoming out from the third quarter of 2020, ending the downtrend of the preceding five consecutive quarters (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Domestic Private consumption returned to positive year-on-year growth in the third and fourth quarters; however, consumer sentiment remained weak as the authorities re-imposed social distancing measures amid the third and fourth waves of local epidemics. Following a brief improvement in business sentiment, aggregate investment spending also increased in the second half. Partly benefiting from stronger export performance (especially to Mainland China), Hong Kong's merchandise trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak as global tourism was still stagnating. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) dragged down GDP in the second half, partly reflecting that the revival of merchandise exports was slower than that of imports. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component Chart 3.2 Real Export and import To cope with the persistent epidemic, the Government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund totaling HK$30.4 billion between September and December 2020 to assist affected industries and citizens and enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional countercyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost its economy, including the issuance of one-off electronic Consumption Voucher Scheme worth HK$5,000 and the provision of 100% guaranteed personal loans for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the "Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism", announced in March 2021 that the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme would be extended to October of the same year, and also announced an extension of the moratorium period for trade financing loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate clients. With COVID-19 vaccines expected to enable a return to normalcy in economic activities, Hong Kong's economy is forecast to regain positive year-on-year growth in 2021 (for the entire year combined), but the strength and pace of recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the COVID-19 situation and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the domestic economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. On external factors, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's merchandise and service exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their mass vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong's merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts real gross domestic product (GDP) growth for the entire year of 2021 to range between 3.5% and 5.5%, while the average of growth estimates by international organisations and private sector analysts is 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed further to 7.2% in February 2021, a 17-year high (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low base (Chart 3.3), while government figures showed a continued decline in job vacancies. The nominal wage index per person engaged, reflecting labour earnings, saw its growth slow to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. To address worsening labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain staff. After the Employment Support Scheme ended, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support hard-hit industries. In the short term, labour markets are expected to remain under stress due to weak economic conditions. Box 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on local labour markets. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Local inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying inflation rate declined notably to 0.3% and 0.2% year-on-year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). Reflecting Inflation momentum, the three-month annualised underlying inflation rate remained at a relatively low level despite slight fluctuations in recent months. Specifically, price pressures on basic food eased, and costs of dining out decreased notably, reflecting more restaurants offering takeaway food discounts during periods when dine-in services were restricted. Price pressures on other traded goods (such as durable goods) remain mild. On the services front, the rental component of the composite consumer price index (CCPI) remained soft as housing rentals consolidated (Chart 3.5). Labour cost pressures have also eased in recent quarters (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.5 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.6 Unit labour cost As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, local inflationary pressures should remain mild in the near term. In particular, local inflation will continue to be contained by the earlier softer growth in fresh-letting residential rentals. Market consensus forecasts put the headline inflation rate for 2021 at a moderate 1.4%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate for 2021 at 1% and the headline inflation rate at 1.6%. As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, inbound tourism quickly fell into depression, raising market concerns about scarring effects on the future recovery of labour markets. To this end, this box empirically analyses the impact of the boom in inbound tourism on local labour markets to explore the potential impact of the current tourism depression. Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced ups and downs (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals decreased during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) epidemic in 2003. Following the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of the same year, visitor arrivals began to surge. Under the initial IVS, Mainland residents could apply to visit Hong Kong in their individual capacity once or twice a year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded from April 2009, enabling eligible Shenzhen household registration holders to apply for a multiple-entry IVS visa valid for one year ("one trip per week"). Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased significantly. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure connecting Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached a historic high from late 2018 to early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved visitor arrivals in the second half of 2019, and under the COVID-19 pandemic, inbound tourism has been stagnating since late January 2020. Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies Using the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example, we examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We consider the IVS launched in 2003 akin to a random economic shock, as it was nearly exogenous in timing and unanticipated by local residents. Our primary data source is population data from Hong Kong Population Censuses or By-censuses. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. Furthermore, we define tourism-related industries as catering, retail, hotel and transport industries. First, we adopt a "difference-in-differences" analytical framework to compare differences in employment outcomes between younger workers (aged 20-40) in the "treatment group" and older workers (aged 41-65) in the "comparison group" before and after the implementation of the IVS. We classify the younger cohort into the "treatment group" because they were still in the early stages of their careers and could make significant adjustments to their employment choices more flexibly in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the impact of the IVS-induced tourism boom on labour markets may change over time, we also employ an "event study" approach to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical analysis results show that compared to the older cohort, younger workers (especially females and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the IVS. Notably, the effect of the IVS on the probability of young women entering tourism-related industries was particularly significant and persistent, remaining at nearly 5 percentage points (in terms of average difference in entry probability relative to the older cohort) from 2006 onwards (Chart B2.2). We also used a similar methodology to compare earnings of those in tourism-related industries (treatment group) versus non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). Estimation results indicate that after the implementation of the IVS, earnings growth for workers in tourism-related industries exceeded that of employees in non-tourism-related industries. Moreover, compared to similar employees in other industries, female workers and lower-educated workers in tourism-related industries experienced higher earnings increases showing an upward trajectory (3-20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3). Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on earnings of female and lower-educated workers The above findings are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women and lower-educated workers. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses, indicating that robust growth in inbound tourism increased demand for lower-skilled labour, enhancing the resilience of the lower-skilled segment of labour markets. As inbound tourism falls from boom to bust, these worker groups may be disproportionately affected, warranting close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to stay close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings level, which was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that from buoyant initial public offering (IPO) activities and buying flows through the Southbound Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) retreated across the board. Despite uncertainties related to the COVID-19 situation, the pace of recovery, and lingering tensions in Sino-US relations, which could exacerbate fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong’s ample foreign reserves position and robust banking system are capable of withstanding the volatilities in fund flows. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings level, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that from buoyant IPO activities and buying flows through the Southbound Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although part of the amount raised from some IPOs was transferred out, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December, as market sentiment in the local equity markets turned positive and market expectation pointed to rising funding demand towards year-end. With fundraising activities remaining active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar closed at 7.7568 on 26 February 2021. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings were triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, reflecting significant net inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings were triggered 47 times. Under the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, causing the Aggregate Balance to increase from HK$193.1 billion at end-August to HK$457.5 billion at end-February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side Convertibility Undertakings were triggered a total of 85 times throughout 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, Total deposits increased, indicating no signs of significant outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments statistics showed that non-residents’ direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, without showing any abnormal fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised at HKEX Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) of the Hong Kong dollar generally declined, tracking the weakening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation rate differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER), the movement of the REER broadly followed that of the NEER. Chart 4.4 Nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) and real effective exchange rate index (REER) Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the COVID-19 situation, the pace of recovery, and lingering tensions in Sino-US relations could exacerbate fund-flow volatility. As an international financial centre, various fundraising activities (such as IPOs) take place in Hong Kong, resulting in substantial fund flows in and out of the city. On one hand, these fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, the amount raised by listed firms may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong due to business needs. Hong Kong possesses an ample foreign reserves position and a sound banking system, capable of withstanding the volatilities in fund flows without affecting financial stability. Amid continuous inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since end-June 2020, the HKD Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). Analysed by components, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the rise in the Aggregate Balance due to the multiple triggers of the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings. On the other hand, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs), remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large-scale IPO activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits derived from subscription loans, causing Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposits component to rise significantly between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). Following the conclusion of IPO activities and the repayment of subscription loans by customers, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at end-2020. Entering January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 surged again, mainly driven by large-scale IPO activities at end-January. Overall, over the seven-month period since end-June, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of the IPO activities at end-January, Hong Kong dollar M3 increased modestly by 9.1%. Based on counterpart assets analysis, excluding subscription loans, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly attributable to the expansion of the Monetary Base driven by the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertakings (Chart 4.7). As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the impact of the IPO activities at end-January, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased modestly by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits recorded a decline due to low deposit rates, this was fully offset by the rapid growth in demand and savings deposits, partly driven by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) by currency Chart 4.7 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and counterpart assets Overall foreign currency deposits increased steadily by 3.6% over the seven-month period since end-June. US dollar deposits dipped slightly by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in RMB customer deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO activities, total deposits with AIs rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the IPO activities at end-January, Total deposits increased modestly by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various transient factors (such as seasonal and initial public offering (IPO) related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), and therefore the statistics should be interpreted with caution. With the increase in the Aggregate Balance, HIBORs generally remained at very low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large-scale IPO activities in the second half of 2020, HIBORs did not exhibit significant volatility due to sufficient liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 HIBORs and US dollar Interbank Offered Rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly followed the movement of the US dollar yield curve, steepening during the review period, with yields on short-term bonds declining and yields on long-term bonds rising (Chart 4.9). Compared with end-June, the yield on the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond dipped slightly by 4 basis points to 0.23% at end-February, while the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate for new mortgages Retail front HKD interest rates mainly followed the decline in HIBORs. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June to 0.23% at end-February 2021 (Chart 4.9). Due to lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgages also decreased from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the movement of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, HKD interest rates are influenced by US interest rates. Given the prolonged low level of US interest rates, HKD interest rates are expected to remain low and may experience occasional fluctuations due to capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. Facing a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, the ample liquidity in the banking system should provide a sufficient buffer to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. The exchange rates of offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore (CNY) against the US dollar strengthened since end-May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the better economic outlook in Mainland China compared to the rest of the world, as well as the weakness of the US dollar. FTSE Russell announced at end-September the inclusion of Mainland government bonds in the World Government Bond Index, and investment demand further supported the strengthening of the renminbi. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium relative to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, with an average premium of about 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates During the review period, liquidity positions in the CNH interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, it stayed below 4% for most of the time (Chart 4.11). The three-month CNH HIBOR followed onshore renminbi interest rates to retreat in late December, and then rose again in late January, partly due to tightening onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 The overnight and the three-month CNH HIBOR In the second half of 2020, the offshore renminbi (CNH) liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued its growth trend. Since the fourth quarter, the growth rate of RMB customer deposits accelerated, partly reflecting the appreciation of the renminbi and its relatively higher interest rates compared to other currencies. Compared with end-June 2020, the growth rate of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit accelerated, reaching RMB826.3 billion at end-January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among them, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. On the other hand, certificates of deposit decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong As for other renminbi businesses, over the seven-month period since end-June 2020, the outstanding amount of renminbi loans decreased by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion. On the other hand, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. During the seven-month period from July 2020 to January 2021, transactions handled by Hong Kong banks amounted to RMB3,769.5 billion, up 16.7% from the same period last year. Among the relevant transactions, the growth in outward trade remittances to the Mainland from Hong Kong was higher than that of remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong has a sizable renminbi liquidity pool, sufficient to continue supporting substantial renminbi payments and financial transactions. Throughout 2020, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system reached RMB1,191.5 billion, compared to RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

As the COVID-19 pandemic continued to cause an economic downturn and the prolonged low interest rate environments persisted, Retail banks in Hong Kong saw a further decline in profitability and a slight deterioration in asset quality in the second half of 2020. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust, underpinned by its strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, to continue supporting the economy through these difficult times, the HKMA decided to extend various relief measures. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines has raised hopes that the global pandemic may be contained and economic activities can resume, the pace of recovery remains uncertain. The aforementioned uncertainties and ongoing geopolitical tensions will weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic weakens the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant about the impact of relevant downside risks on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks declined by 38.5% compared to the same period in 2019. Accordingly, the return on assets fell to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, down from 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margins (NIMs) of Retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), resulting in a decrease in net interest income that outweighed the slight increase in non-interest income, leading to lower earnings. For the entire year of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of Retail banks fell by 29.4%, and the return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of Retail Banks Chart 5.2 Net Interest Margins of Retail Banks HKD liquidity became more ample, largely driven by substantial net inflows associated with equity market activities. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate declined by 43 basis points in the second half to 0.35% at end-2020 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate, a measure of the average HKD funding cost for Retail banks, followed a broadly similar trend, falling significantly from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.28% at end-2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and cuts in time-deposit rates by some major Retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest Rates From a broader perspective, the average overall HKD and USD funding cost of locally incorporated licensed banks declined moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and USD Funding Costs and Maturity Profile of Licensed Banks Looking ahead, as the global low interest rate environments are likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks' NIM performance, the earnings outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging. Moreover, despite breakthroughs in vaccine development boosting market optimism about global economic outlooks, the trajectory of recovery remains highly uncertain given considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. Capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and was much higher than minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions (AIs) stood at 20.7% at end-December 2020, well above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). Tier 1 capital stood at 18.7% during the period, of which Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital accounted for 16.7%. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a robust level of 8.2% at end-December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of Locally Incorporated AIs Chart 5.6 Leverage Ratio of Locally Incorporated AIs Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity positions of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average LCR of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), far above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. Over the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratio figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirement also indicated stable funding positions of AIs. The average NSFR of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of category 2A institutions remained high at 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), both well above their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of AIs suggest that the Hong Kong banking sector is resilient to liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for AIs, reflecting the banking system's stable liability structure. At end-2020, Customer deposits accounted for around 56.1% of total liabilities of all AIs, broadly unchanged from six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability Structure of All AIs As total deposits with AIs increased while total loans decreased in the second half of 2020, the Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all AIs across all currencies declined from 76.0% at end-June 2020 to 72.3% at end-2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in Total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Accordingly, as of end-2020, the average Hong Kong dollar LTD ratio and foreign currency LTD ratio fell to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratios of All AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Assuming an Interest rate shock of a 200-basis-point rise in HKD and USD interest rates, the estimated potential decline in the economic value of locally incorporated licensed banks’ interest rate positions would be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at end-December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of HKD and USD Interest Rate Shocks on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks Against this background of a persistent economic downturn caused by recurring waves of the pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, total loans and advances recorded a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. However, for the entire year of 2020, bank credit still posted positive year-on-year growth, although the growth rate slowed markedly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a semi-annual basis, after growing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, total loans and advances of all AIs contracted by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was due to decreases in both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade financing) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. Specifically, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with increases of 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the preceding six-month period. Chart 5.12 Loan Growth Analysed by currency, after declining by 2.0% in the first half, HKD loans remained broadly stable at end-2020 compared with end-June. Following a significant increase of 10.6% in the first half of 2020, foreign currency loan declined by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting weaker demand for US dollar loans amid improved global liquidity conditions. The banking sector turned slightly more optimistic about the near-term credit demand outlook compared with six months ago. The HKMA’s Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook conducted in December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed AIs expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while those expecting a decline fell to 13% (Table 5.A). Due to the adverse effect of the pandemic on the repayment ability of households and firms, bank loan quality deteriorated slightly but remained robust by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality slowed in the second half of 2020. The gross CLR of all AIs rose moderately from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at end-2020, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all AIs increased from 0.49% at end-June 2020 to 0.57% at end-2020. For Retail banks, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, the global economic performance was weak, but inflationary pressures continued to intensify across various places, especially in the US. Looking ahead, global economic outlooks face significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale COVID-19 outbreaks, and the possibility that monetary tightening could be more aggressive than expected if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than anticipated. Should the Federal Reserve tighten monetary policy significantly, leading to tighter global financing conditions, pressure would be placed on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may have significant impacts on the global economy through trade and financial channels, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened against the US dollar, but trading continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no significant signs of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For 2021 as a whole, the growth of total bank loans accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the continued recovery, and coupled with the possibility that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation may be faster than expected, these risk factors will pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impacts of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. Global economic growth began to slow in late 2021, and the weakness extended into 2022, as the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant led to increased restrictions on mobility globally, while persistent supply bottlenecks continued to weigh on production. Meanwhile, amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify, spreading to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the US. Recently, following the outbreak of the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, the sharp rise in commodity prices could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility could lead to a less desirable tightening of global financing conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, there are significant uncertainties surrounding global economic outlooks. In the near term, should large-scale COVID-19 outbreaks occur, the reimposition of lockdown measures and a renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out. In the US, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected grows, the Federal Reserve has turned hawkish, accelerating the timetable for tapering asset purchases and interest rate hikes, and beginning discussions on balance sheet reduction. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy significantly, global financing conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers’ repayment abilities, and disorderly capital outflows would put pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may expose global commodity prices to the risk of sustained increases, aggravating shortages of industrial supplies and increasing financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economy continued its recovery in the second half of 2021, although the momentum slowed temporarily in some Southeast Asian economies due to the reimposition of strict pandemic containment measures in the third quarter, while technology product exporting economies in the region (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although there is a market consensus that emerging Asia will see a broad-based recovery in 2022, the region’s near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, especially for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and strained public health resources. Second, the Federal Reserve’s accelerated policy normalisation could trigger capital outflows from the region and exacerbate currency depreciation pressures; for regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activities will become more difficult. Third, softer growth in major economies, coupled with a possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on the trade growth outlook. Fourth, rising prices of various commodities triggered by the conflict between Russia and Ukraine will feed into regional inflation and simultaneously dampen consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainties, regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalisation will become more complex. Central banks in some economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the longer term, to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is affected by firms’ environmental performance. Mainland China’s economic growth slowing in the second half of 2021 was affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures, and tightening measures in the real estate market. Looking ahead, due to the continued downturn in the property market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the near term. Accordingly, authorities have made stabilising growth their top priority this year and have introduced a series of fiscal and monetary supportive measures. The total amount of onshore Mainland bond defaults and state-owned enterprises (SOEs) onshore Mainland bond defaults both decreased in the second half of 2021; Box 3 discusses whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. Overall risks in the banking sector remain manageable, as Mainland banks (especially systemically important banks) have limited exposure to developer loans, low non-performing loan (NPL) ratios, and high provision coverage ratios. The domestic economy continued its recovery in the second half of 2021, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Supported by the continued recovery of the global economy, improved local labour market conditions, and the Government’s Consumption Voucher Scheme, which benefited merchandise exports and private consumption, seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product (GDP) increased modestly. Year on year, economic growth was 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared to 7.8% in the first half. For 2021 as a whole, economic growth was 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local COVID-19 outbreaks and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures have weighed on economic activities in Hong Kong. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund, and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme (SFGS) will be enhanced, with maximum loan amounts increased, and application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, has also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to end-October 2022. The Scheme also provides borrowers with an option for partial principal repayment over a one-year period, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme (SFGS). The domestic economy is expected to continue its recovery for 2022 as a whole, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting softer global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong’s merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government’s push for various capital works and infrastructure projects will also render support to the economy. Government forecasts project real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% for 2022, while the average growth estimates from international organisations and private sector analysts stand at 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the recovery are subject to a number of uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, notably the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. Alongside the economic recovery, the labour markets further improved in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end. Total employment rebounded but remained below the pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressures re-emerged amid the new wave of local COVID-19 outbreaks. Moreover, the decline in online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local COVID-19 outbreaks and tightened pandemic containment measures will exert some pressure on the local labour markets in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on the development of the local COVID-19 situation and the pace of recovery of the domestic economy. Local inflationary pressures have generally increased in recent months but remain mild. Year on year, underlying consumer price inflation edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also picked up in recent months, partly due to elevated airfare and prices of some energy-related items. Looking ahead, with rising import prices and logistics disruptions caused by the pandemic, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the near term. However, soft rentals and mild local labour cost pressures should contain overall inflationary pressures. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation rate to reach 2.4% in 2022, while The Government projects headline inflation rate to be 2.1% and underlying inflation rate to be 2.0% for 2022. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk aversion in the local stock market. Despite a slight rebound in October 2021, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar subsequently lost steam, mainly due to weak southbound net buying flows via Stock Connect and market expectation that the US dollar would strengthen alongside the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy normalisation. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar stayed mostly on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertakings, and trading continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no significant signs of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Due to ample interbank liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained low during the review period. The average lending rate for new mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Offshore renminbi business continued to thrive. In particular, the offshore renminbi (CNH) liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to expand, with renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit rising to RMB 1,113.5 billion by end-January 2022. While the outstanding amount of renminbi loans decreased, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. The average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system rose to RMB 1,522.6 billion in 2021. Looking ahead, leveraging Hong Kong’s efficient financial infrastructure and the two-way Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connects, the continuing liberalisation of Mainland’s capital account, increasing demand for renminbi assets from international investors, and deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong firms’ earnings drove major global stock markets generally higher in the last quarter of 2021, pushing the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022. However, growing concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid surging inflation risks, soaring commodity prices, and escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict have led to consolidation in major global stock markets since early January 2022.

Due to the rapid global spread of variants (Delta and Omicron) and persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed markedly in late 2021, and growth drivers remained weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and had broadened to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, especially the US. Rising inflation concerns prompted a shift toward a more hawkish monetary policy stance by the Fed, heightening the risk that premature tightening of global financing conditions could put pressure on currently elevated asset valuations, which would also be detrimental to emerging market economies where recoveries are generally still lagging. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up energy and other commodity prices and triggered volatility in the global financial market, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant in the region, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, with major regional exporters of technology products continuing to outperform other economies. While the current Omicron variant is unlikely to severely derail the regional economic recovery, any uncertainties associated with new variants will continue to cloud the regional economic outlook. In addition, US policy normalization could trigger adjustments in regional asset prices, while softer growth in major economies could weigh on regional growth in goods exports. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on the one hand, leads to increases in commodity prices and heightens inflation risks; on the other hand, it dampens consumption and increases global economic uncertainties, making regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalization more complicated. Economic growth in Mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a fresh wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing, and tightening measures in the property market. Looking ahead, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from a cooling property market and Omicron outbreaks. In light of this, the government has made stabilizing growth its top priority for this year, and macroeconomic policies will provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed noticeably in the last quarter of 2021 as the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a fresh wave of infections and leading to tightened mobility restrictions worldwide. Moreover, supply chain issues, such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs including semiconductors, continued to put stress on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected in January that global gross domestic product (GDP) growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy supports in the US and other major advanced economies, and slowing growth drivers in Mainland China offsetting the expected rebound in growth in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 IMF real GDP growth estimates Alongside the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressures continued to build during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, particularly in the US, which had implemented larger-scale policy stimulus since the onset of the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, pent-up demand being released, and labour shortages, inflationary pressures have broadened to a wide range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). Furthermore, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up prices of various commodities, potentially exacerbating already elevated global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2 Core consumer price index (CPI) inflation rates of selected economies (1) Latest data for the US, UK, and Euro area are for January 2022; others are for December 2021. (2) "Advanced Asian economies" include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Singapore. (3) "Emerging Asian economies" include Mainland China, IDR, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties and considerable downside risks, and will hinge on the evolution of the COVID-19 situation and related supply chain disruptions, how geopolitical tensions affect global trade, inflation, and financial market sentiment, and the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. On the pandemic front, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work, and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdowns, these relatively looser measures should help mitigate supply chain disruptions, which have shown preliminary signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, should large-scale COVID-19 outbreaks occur, lockdowns cannot be ruled out, which could lead to a renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers' Index – Supplier Delivery Times Sub-index If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to ease gradually, providing some relief to goods inflation. However, several developments could make the current elevated global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia push up commodity prices, the delayed pass-through of rising production costs to final selling prices, the earlier sharp rise in global residential property prices potentially driving subsequent rent increases, upside risks to wage growth from tight labour markets, and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation recorded its largest increase in decades, the Fed shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting in December 2021, no longer characterizing high inflation as "transitory," and doubled the pace of tapering asset purchases from USD 15 billion per month to USD 30 billion, aiming to conclude the asset purchase program before March 2022 and begin discussions on balance sheet reduction. Indeed, recent market pricing suggests that the Fed may implement multiple rate hikes in 2022. In contrast, given the Euro area's closer trade and financial linkages with Russia and Ukraine, the ECB may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this background, coupled with global debt levels and asset valuations remaining elevated following prolonged policy easing, if persistent inflationary pressures necessitate faster-than-expected policy tightening by the Fed, borrowers’ repayment abilities could face deterioration risks, triggering financial market volatility. Recently, amid heightened geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe, risk aversion in financial markets has risen, and signs of US dollar shortages have emerged, including widening cross-currency basis swaps. Under premature tightening of global financing conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals still impacted by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation, and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing—a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds—can reduce these funds' liquidity risks during market stress, and examines the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant dampened growth drivers in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, as major regional exporters of technology products, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, further widening the unevenness of recovery across the region. Additionally, inflationary pressures in many emerging Asian economies remained mild. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Indices Markets broadly expect a widespread recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, but the near-term regional economic outlook faces multiple headwinds: First, although the Omicron variant has spread in the region since late 2021, its economic impact has been milder than previous infection waves; however, some regional economies with lagging vaccination rates and relatively constrained public health resources will continue to face threats from the emergence of new variants. Second, US policy normalization could trigger capital outflows and exert depreciation pressure on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery will face more difficult trade-offs between containing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activities. At the long end of the yield curve, due to their historically high correlation (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden spike in long-term US yields could spill over to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, heightening the risk of adjustments in regional asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation Between 10-Year Asian Sovereign Bond Yields and Corresponding US Treasury Yields Third, the regional merchandise trade outlook faces uncertainties stemming from softer growth in major economies and the potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, factors that could dampen regional export growth. Chart 2.6 US: Imports from Emerging Asia and Real GDP Fourth, although regional economies have relatively limited trade and financial linkages with Russia and Ukraine, the conflict-induced increases in commodity prices will feed into regional inflation while dampening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainties, regional central banks’ decisions on monetary policy normalization will become more complicated. Central banks in some regional economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic also serves as a reminder that regional economies need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models in the long term to prepare for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines whether equity market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporates’ environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic caused massive shocks to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds experienced substantial outflows (Chart B1.1), putting stress on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Outflows from Selected Open-Ended Funds During the March 2020 Episode Beyond investors’ liquidity needs, another reason for substantial outflows could be investors exercising a "first-mover advantage" to redeem funds early, thereby avoiding redemption costs that could soar under market stress. To curb outflows induced by the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds adopted swing pricing—a pricing rule for open-ended funds designed to reduce investors’ first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, no empirical studies have indicated whether swing pricing effectively reduces outflows from open-ended funds. Against this background, this box conducts an empirical study to understand whether swing pricing reduced outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby lowering their liquidity risks. In addition, this box identifies factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during market stress. Based on these assessments, we propose policy recommendations regarding financial stability. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of others, thereby passing redemption costs onto them. The first-mover advantage primarily exists in open-ended funds using traditional pricing rules, where subscription and redemption costs borne by fund investors (such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund price after trades are executed. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem shares first do not bear these transaction costs. This creates an incentive for them to redeem funds early, especially when large redemption costs are anticipated. Therefore, during market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced as anticipated redemption costs rise. This amplifies redemption pressures and liquidity risks faced by open-ended funds.

With merchandise exports and private consumption continuing to grow, Hong Kong's economy continued its recovery in the second half of 2021, achieving positive year-on-year growth for the entire year since 2019. Entering 2022, a fresh wave of local epidemic and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on domestic economic activities.
