The economy is expected to continue its recovery for 2022 as a whole combined, but its strength and pace of recovery will be affected by risks and uncertainties such as the COVID-19 situation and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These adverse factors may also affect the labour market outlook following the significant improvement in 2021. Although local inflation may edge up slightly in the near term due to elevated import prices, soft local rental and labour costs should contain overall inflationary pressures. Hong Kong's economy continued its recovery in the second half of 2021. Year on year, real gross domestic product (GDP) increased further by 5.5% in the third quarter and grew by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), but its growth slowed compared to the first half. For 2021 as a whole combined, real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 6.4%, marking the first positive year-on-year growth for the entire year since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contribution by major expenditure component Quarter-on-quarter, economic activities increased modestly by 0.6% and 0.2% respectively in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 (Chart 3.1). Domestically, improved labour market conditions, coupled with the Government's Consumption Voucher Scheme, drove up private consumption. However, aggregate investment retreated in the last quarter after strong rebounds in the two preceding quarters. On the external front, amid the continued recovery of the global economy, Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance remained robust, while trade in services remained subdued, partly due to inbound tourism remaining stagnant (Chart 3.2). In net terms, external trade dragged down GDP in the third quarter but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Export and import volume A fresh wave of local epidemic and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on domestic economic activities in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional countercyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, enhancements were made to the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme (SFGS), with maximum loan volumes raised and application periods and moratorium periods extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to end-October 2022. The Scheme also provides borrowers with an option for partial principal repayment over one year, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme (SFGS). Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue its recovery for 2022 as a whole combined, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global economic growth amid the persistent pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's merchandise exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government's push for various capital works and infrastructure projects will also render support to the economy. Government forecasts for real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 2022 range between 2.0% and 3.5%, while the average of growth estimates by international organisations and private-sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of recovery of Hong Kong's economy are clouded by numerous risks and uncertainties mentioned in previous chapters. In particular, the recent COVID-19 situation, the accelerated pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the Russia-Ukraine situation) have clouded the near-term economic outlook for both Hong Kong and the global economy. On the other hand, if quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and Mainland China resumes earlier than expected, it could boost local economic growth. Alongside the economic recovery, the labour market further improved in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining to 3.9% at year-end (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from the recent low in February 2021, though it remained below the pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market pressures re-emerged amid the fresh wave of local epidemic. Moreover, the decline in online job advertisements reflected a reduction in new vacancies. Looking ahead, the fresh wave of local epidemic and tightened COVID-19 restrictions will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, especially in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over a longer horizon, labour market conditions will hinge on the local COVID-19 situation and the pace of recovery of the domestic economy. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures generally increased in recent months but remained mild. Year on year, underlying consumer price inflation edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% respectively in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The annualised three-month-on-three-month underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, has also bottomed out in recent months. Specifically, amid the recovery in local demand and elevated external prices (Chart 3.5), prices of meals out and some energy-related items accelerated. Meanwhile, the housing rental component of the CCPI continued to decline broadly, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). Despite remaining soft, real unit labour costs edged up in recent quarters, partly due to improvements in real average wages (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4 Different measures of consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Hong Kong Import Prices Chart 3.6 CCPI rental component and market rental Chart 3.7 Unit Labour Costs Looking ahead, with elevated import prices and logistics disruptions caused by the pandemic, local inflation is expected to edge up slightly in the near term. However, soft rentals and mild local labour cost pressures should contain overall inflationary pressures. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation rate for 2022 at 2.4%, while the Government forecasts headline inflation rate for 2022 at 2.1% and underlying inflation rate at 2.0%.

Amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over US monetary policy normalisation, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period. With sufficient liquidity in HKD funds, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained at low levels. Overall, Hong Kong dollar exchange and money markets continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Looking ahead, although uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the COVID-19 situation and heightened geopolitical tensions could exacerbate fund-flow volatility, Hong Kong’s ample foreign reserves position and robust banking system are capable of withstanding the volatilities in fund flows. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar stayed mostly on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertakings, and trading continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021 as market sentiment improved, its upward momentum subsequently faded, mainly due to weak net buying flows via Southbound Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectation that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, initial public offering (IPO) fundraising activities continued to provide support to the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits increased modestly during the review period, with no significant signs of outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments statistics showed that non-residents’ direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, and there were no signs of abnormal cross-border fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Net buying flows via Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect Chart 4.3 Equity funds raised at HKEX Despite the strengthening of the US dollar during the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) remained stable as the renminbi appreciated against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index (REER) broadly followed the movement of the NEER. Chart 4.4 Nominal effective exchange rate index (NEER) and real effective exchange rate index (REER) Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the COVID-19 situation and heightened geopolitical tensions could exacerbate fund-flow volatility. As US dollar counterparts rise, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), outflows of HKD funds (the pace and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions) could lead to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking. Hong Kong also possesses an ample foreign reserves position and a sound banking system, which are capable of withstanding the volatilities in fund flows without affecting financial stability. During the review period, the monetary environment stayed accommodative in Hong Kong. The HKD Monetary Base rose by 1.4% over the eight months since end-June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting the additional issuance of bills to meet banks’ ongoing demand for Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) amid sufficient liquidity in the banking system, EFBNs increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, while the Aggregate Balance (before discount window operations) decreased correspondingly by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued currency notes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) Over the six months since end-July 2021, total deposits with AIs increased modestly by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various transient factors, such as seasonal and initial public offering (IPO) related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities. It is therefore advisable to observe longer-term trends. For 2021 as a whole, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions (AIs) by currency Overall, Hong Kong’s interbank market continued to trade in a smooth and orderly manner. With sufficient liquidity in the banking system, HIBOR remained at low levels despite market concerns over monetary tightening in the US (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of rising funding demand towards year-end, HIBOR picked up slightly in December 2021. The average lending rate for new mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, Best Lending Rates at major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Looking ahead, sufficient liquidity in the banking system can provide an adequate buffer against large-scale capital market activities or financial market volatility. Chart 4.7 HKD and USD Interbank Offered Rates During the review period, the CNH interbank market continued to function normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced slight fluctuations in late December 2021, while the three-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 The overnight and the three-month CNH HIBOR In the second half of 2021, the offshore renminbi (CNH) liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to see steady growth. Over the six months since end-July 2021, renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased by 30.3%, reaching RMB 1,113.5 billion at end-January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among them, renminbi customer deposits rose by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in certificates of deposit. Chart 4.9 RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong Over the six months since July 2021, although the outstanding amount of renminbi loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB 167.6 billion, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. Between end-July 2021 and end-January 2022, transactions handled by Hong Kong banks amounted to RMB 3,763.0 billion (Chart 4.10), an increase of 18.3% from RMB 3,181.0 billion in the same period last year. Hong Kong’s substantial renminbi liquidity pool continued to support a large volume of RMB payments and financing transactions. For 2021 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the renminbi Real Time Gross Settlement system rose from RMB 1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB 1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 Renminbi trade settlement remittances Looking ahead, with the establishment of the two-way Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connects, the continuing liberalisation of Mainland’s capital account, increasing demand for renminbi assets from international investors, as well as deepening regional economic and financial co-operation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, Hong Kong’s offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Major global equity markets continued to rally in the fourth quarter of 2021, but have consolidated since January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict. The Hong Kong stock market remained subdued in the fourth quarter of 2021, mainly dragged down by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties regarding the COVID-19 situation in Hong Kong caused the Hang Seng Index to fall to a nearly two-year low in late February. Meanwhile, the CNH debt market in Hong Kong continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weaker asset market sentiment and a new wave of local COVID-19 outbreaks. Major global equity markets generally continued to rally in the last quarter of 2021, pushing the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022 (Chart 4.11). Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, the global economic recovery and strong firms’ earnings supported the rally in major global equity markets, but the pandemic remained a key risk concern for investors throughout the year. However, major global equity markets have consolidated since early January 2022, amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amidst surging inflation risks, soaring commodity prices, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict. In contrast, at end-2021, the Hong Kong stock market continued to lag behind other major global markets. The Hang Seng Index hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, closing at 23,398 points at end-2021, down 14.1% from 2020. In early 2022, buying interest from value investors returned to the Hong Kong stock market, pushing the Hang Seng Index back to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties regarding the COVID-19 situation in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index down to a nearly two-year low of 22,713 points in late February. Over the entire review period from end-August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index declined by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11 Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index Due to the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, option-implied volatilities in the stock market fluctuated significantly in late November 2021 before retreating somewhat. Although the SKEW Index has retreated from its historical high in late June 2021, it remains elevated, reflecting investors' concerns about a correction to the prolonged stock market rebound since the COVID-19 outbreaks, and their willingness to spend more on hedging against downside protection in the stock market (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Option-implied volatilities of the Hang Seng Index and S&P 500 Index, and the SKEW Index Against the backdrop of ample global liquidity, the Hong Kong stock market has continued to record net buying flows from international investors since the last report (Chart 4.13). In contrast, Southbound Stock Connect recorded significant net outflows in the third quarter of 2021, mainly due to concerns over the impact of regulatory changes in the Mainland on technology stocks. However, buying interest via Southbound Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, recording fund inflows of HK$98.3 billion by end-February. During the review period, cumulative net buying flows increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233.0 billion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13 Net inflows into Hong Kong's equity market Chart 4.14 Net flows via Stock Connect After raising a record amount in the first half of 2021, Hong Kong’s primary market slowed down in the second half. For 2021 as a whole, there were 98 initial public offerings (IPOs), raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), representing a 17.8% decrease in total funds raised compared to the previous year. In 2021, HKEX ranked fourth in the global IPO market, trailing only Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15 Hong Kong's IPO market The outlook for the local stock market remains uncertain. Easing of monetary policy in the Mainland and more Chinese concept stocks coming to Hong Kong for secondary listings in the primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market. However, the stock market still faces many headwinds, including uncertainties regarding the local COVID-19 situation, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Retail banks’ profit in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio edged up slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained at a low level by both historical and international standards. Supported by robust capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust. During the review period, to further assist the economy in weathering the difficult times, the HKMA extended various support measures. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the pace of recovery, which, coupled with the risk of a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, will pose challenges to banks’ credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impacts of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks declined by 16.1% from the same period in 2020. The weak profitability was mainly attributable to decreases in net interest and non-interest income, as well as an increase in operating expenses. Consequently, the return on assets declined to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period in 2020 (Chart 5.1). For 2021 as a whole, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% from 2020, while the return on assets declined from 0.77% to 0.59%. Chart 5.1 Retail banks’ profit Reflecting the continued impact of the low-interest-rate period, retail banks’ net interest margins (NIMs) also remained at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Chart 5.2). Chart 5.2 Retail banks’ NIMs Reflecting year-end funding demand and the decline in the Aggregate Balance following the HKMA’s issuance of additional EFBN, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) edged up in the fourth quarter of 2021. However, as liquidity in the banking system remained very ample, HIBOR continued to stay at relatively low levels. Specifically, the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate edged up by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at end-December 2021 (blue line in Chart 5.3). Retail banks’ funding costs remained stable during the review period. Among them, the composite interest rate (a measure of retail banks’ average HKD funding cost) rose moderately by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at end-2021 (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-period figures. (b) Period-average figures for newly approved loans. (c) Starting from June 2019, the composite interest rate has been calculated based on the newly implemented local “interest rate risk in the banking book” framework. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not strictly comparable with those of previous months. From a broader perspective, the overall HKD and USD funding cost of locally incorporated licensed banks edged up by 6 basis points in the second half of 2021 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks Starting from June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks continue to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding cost is calculated as the weighted average of the relevant figures of these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Although US monetary policy normalisation may herald some improvement in bank profitability, such improvement in the near term could be partly offset by two factors. First, despite the Fed’s indication of multiple rate hikes in 2022, past experience suggests that movements in local interest rates may lag behind US dollar counterparts (especially when liquidity among local banks remains very ample). As such, it may take more time for improvements in banks’ NIMs to materialise. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases may also bring uncertainties to the pace of recovery, thereby putting pressure on banks’ asset quality and profitability. Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its impact. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted substantial efforts to advancing Hong Kong’s climate targets and contributing to enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA 2021 Annual Report last year, we have published the 2022 Sustainability Report as a standalone document for the first time this year. I hope this report will enable readers to gain a deeper understanding of the HKMA’s strategies and priorities in strengthening the ability of the Hong Kong banking system to combat climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our role as a responsible investor and sustainable entity. During the year, we made visible progress in advancing sustainability across the HKMA’s key functions. Readers will find details of our concrete measures and work in this report, with highlights including the following: Banks’ day-to-day operating processes are confronted with climate risk. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete measures to strengthen banks’ ability to combat climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into supervisory processes and conducted studies on how to leverage tech to assist banks in evaluating the impact of physical risks. Given the increasing range of green and sustainable products introduced by banks, we also shared good practices with the industry on properly managing these products to foster enhancements in banks’ climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various co-operation initiatives related to combating climate risk and fostering sustainable finance development. Domestically, through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), we are working with other financial regulators to develop a local green taxonomy; the framework will increase transparency in the financial market and make green finance policy more consistent. At the international level, we are actively participating in various international organisations to help formulate policies to combat climate change and evaluate their impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia’s demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite 2022 being a challenging year for global bond markets, the volume of green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to record strong growth, with an increase of 42% and total issuance rising to US$80.5 billion, making Hong Kong the largest centre for arranging international green and sustainable bonds in Asia². Relevant issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government and the People’s Government of Hainan Province, whose offerings once again demonstrated Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable funding flows between the Mainland and international markets. The vibrant development of Hong Kong’s green bond markets is partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the government in issuing nearly US$16 billion worth of green bonds, with proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. We also assisted the government in achieving two "firsts", including facilitating the issuance of the first batch of HKD 20 billion Government Green Retail Bonds in May 2022, which was the largest green retail bond offering globally at that time. Furthermore, we assisted the government in issuing the first tokenised green bond in February 2023. This was the first tokenised green bond issued by a government globally, and the issuance marked a milestone in successfully combining our edge in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and fintech. Standards, datasets, and talent are indispensable elements for fostering a healthier climate finance ecosystem, and their establishment relies on the efforts and co-operation of various sectors. To this end, the HKMA works primarily through the Steering Group to collaborate with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions, and the financial industry to expand these elements. In addition to the aforementioned development of a local green taxonomy, the Steering Group, through its established Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance, is promoting skills training for the industry and improving Hong Kong’s data resources. Moreover, the Steering Group has made good progress in other areas such as mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund’s responsible investment efforts, in particular setting a target for the Exchange Fund portfolio to achieve net-zero GHG emissions by 2050. Meanwhile, we have also implemented enhancements to risk management to improve the Exchange Fund’s climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term yield. Furthermore, to fully capitalise on potential opportunities arising from climate change, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment within the Exchange Fund, seeking investment opportunities that support climate transformation and mitigation to enhance the portfolio’s long-term return. By end-2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio had decreased by 43% compared to 2017 levels. In fact, the Exchange Fund’s exposures to high-carbon assets have remained consistently lower than those of the overall market. Looking ahead, we will continue to move towards the net-zero target by continuously strengthening the integration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into investment management processes, proactively exercising asset ownership, maintaining continued co-operation with stakeholders, and focusing on decarbonisation and transformation of the portfolio. At the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, chaired by myself, is responsible for formulating the HKMA’s sustainability strategies. Our strategic direction is based on three pillars: Environment, Staff, and Community. On the environmental front, we strive to promote a green workplace and advocate for a more environmentally friendly market; regarding staff, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthier and inclusive working environment; and in terms of social responsibility, we are dedicated to raising public financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion, and giving back to the community. Compared to the levels when we started tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, our per capita GHG emissions, energy consumption, and paper usage in 2022 all achieved double-digit reductions. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or before. In the near term, our target is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or before, using 2015 as the baseline. Combating climate change and fostering sustainable development requires sustained efforts and co-operation from multiple parties. On this key global issue, we understand that we have to lead by example and work alongside like-minded interbank participants and international organisations. The next section outlines the HKMA’s short-term plans and priorities in combating climate change across its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or before is an arduous task, and we will go all out to reach this target. We are confident that with the joint efforts of all staff, the financial industry, and the community, we can successfully combat future climate challenges. Chief Executive Eddie Yue

In 2023, the HKMA will continued to foster the sustainable development of Hong Kong’s financial sector and fulfill its responsibilities as a responsible investor and sustainable entity. Meanwhile, through participation in international and regional organizations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As regulators of the banking sector, we will strive to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support banks’ green transformation. Specifically, the HKMA will communicate with banks to understand their progress in implementing supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and make amendments to the Common Assessment Framework on “Green Baseline” for the banking sector. At the same time, the HKMA will support banks in their efforts to enhance climate resilience and risk management ability, for instance by examining various actions and technology solutions to help banks identify, calculate and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also co-operate with banks to undertake the next round of climate risk stress-tested, as part of the regulator-led regular stress testing for 2023 to 2024. Participating banks will be required to evaluate their ability to withstand climate risk under an enhanced stress testing framework; this framework covers multiple stress scenarios including extreme climate and adverse economic environment. To foster the healthier development of banks in providing green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, and maintain communication with the industry to provide guidelines on sales processes in a timely manner. We will also conduct off-site Box assessments to gain a full understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to strengthen the building of a green finance ecosystem to support the green transformation of the finance sector, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of developing a local green taxonomy. In terms of market developments, to foster Hong Kong as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA will assist the government in expanding the issuance scale of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broaden the scope of the Programme to cover sustainable bonds; meanwhile, attract more green financing activities to take place in Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA also assists in introducing the government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Scheme to expand the talent pool for green finance in Hong Kong. Moreover, the HKMA will continued to encourage more Mainland local governments, entities and corporates to undertake green financing through Hong Kong, and examine the feasibility of integrating green finance with tech. On the other hand, we will continued to co-operate with other agencies and departments through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group on cross-sectoral topics such as skills training and dataset, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosure and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA will jointly introduce various dedicated programmes with the International Finance Corporation in Asia, including conducting green finance studies, providing unique market analysis, providing targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidelines to assist banks in formulating roadmaps to develop green finance as core business. Looking ahead, the Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners and knowledge partners to introduce a membership programme to expand the Alliance’s impact in the Asia region. Meanwhile, the Alliance will also strengthen the upgrading of professional capabilities of industry participants, foster knowledge sharing on green finance, and lead projects in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target for the Exchange Fund portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or before, as its promise to participate in global efforts to combat climate change and implement the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continued to incorporate environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into its investment management processes, strive towards the net-zero target, and fully support global efforts to combat climate change. As a responsible and sustainable entity, the HKMA cares about its staff, as well as the community and the surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and imposed climate targets on our own operating activities, as our promise to participate in global decarbonisation and climate action. The HKMA will continued to prioritise reducing carbon emissions and encourage staff to fully support energy saving and waste reduction. Furthermore, we will provide further guidelines to staff to incorporate sustainability principles into the procurement process. To drive digital transformation and increase operating flexibility, the HKMA will examine methodologies to modernise internal systems and applications to further enhance work efficiency, while mitigating potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process as much as possible.

Climate change represents a key risk confronting the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong’s financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong’s climate targets as well as the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are confronted with the impact of various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their key functions in the financial system and channel more funding towards green and sustainable projects, banks have to proactively manage climate risk. As the regulator of the banking sector, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks’ ability to combat and manage climate risk, and accelerating banks’ efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in upgrading their capabilities in detecting environmental crimes, and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas including environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)1 published principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to frequently asked questions, clarifying how the existing Basel framework covers such risks. In light of these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related factors into its supervisory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management” in 2021, the HKMA has also maintained communication with banks to exchange opinions on expectations, progress and challenges regarding the implementation of relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks’ climate risk management, the HKMA has formulated a two-year Programme to incorporate climate risk factors into bank supervisory processes, which was communicated to the banking sector in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year Programme, the HKMA issued the revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 “Risk-based Supervisory Approach”, and strengthened the CAMEL2 rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. Meanwhile, drawing on experience gained from the pilot exercise in 2021, the HKMA refined the climate risk stress-tested scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA has also formulated a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into the regular supervisor-led stress testing, enabling a more full assessment of the banking sector’s resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year Programme, the HKMA is also strengthening its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related topics, including climate risk management and transition planning. At the same time, the HKMA is reviewing the Supervisory Review Process used to evaluate and monitor banks’ capital adequacy levels and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, aiming to encourage banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks related to combating climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the increasing prevalence of banks offering green and sustainable products, the HKMA undertook a round of thematic reviews focusing primarily on banks’ development and ongoing management of these products. During the thematic reviews, the HKMA identified some good practices and issued a circular in December to share them with the industry, enabling banks to gradually strengthen their ability to manage climate risk. The adoption of technology can improve data availability and enhance banks’ ability to manage climate risk. The HKMA has started the development of a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on property. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub network, examining how technological solutions can assist in physical risk assessment. The HKMA also attaches great importance to fostering sustainable and globally leading anti-money laundering operational practices; this work adopts advanced analytics and compliance tech, supplemented by fully automated supervisory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the anti-money laundering supervisory data collection process to reduce banks’ manual burden and paper usage. To enhance transparency across financial markets and foster greater consistency in green finance policies, the HKMA is collaborating with other financial regulators to establish a local green taxonomy framework. The green taxonomy framework, commonly referred to as a green taxonomy, classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA maintains engagement with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to examine in depth the features and challenges of the framework, and is prepared to make proposals and conduct consultations on the structure and core elements of the framework in the first half of 2023. Recognising that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial vulnerabilities analysis and studies to strengthen current monitoring efforts. In its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks, the HKMA takes into account climate change and includes analysis of climate-related risks in various Financial Stability Reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Workstream under the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helps further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the impact of climate change on the macroeconomic and financial landscape. On the research front, the HKMA undertook various applied research projects in 2022, examining in depth two major topics: greenwashing behaviour in corporate green bond markets3, and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures4. The findings of these studies help inform the formulation of policy and measures to address the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Domestically, these studies help strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research seminars and the HKMA’s Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA’s Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralised backstop funding arrangement designed to provide timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the incorporation of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and fostering sustainable finance into the mainstream. Through such engagement, the HKMA contributes to fostering policy dialogue at international and regional levels on combating climate change and its impact on financial stability, and draws insights to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA has stepped up efforts to enhance market awareness and participation, provide necessary infrastructure and drivers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), coordinates the financial sector’s actions to combat climate and environmental risks, accelerates the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supports the Government’s climate strategy1. The work of the Steering Group is primarily guided by its Strategic Plan, which sets out six key focus areas and five action plans to strengthen Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem and build a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). Strengthen climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong’s position as a global risk management centre Facilitate the flow of climate-related information at all levels to ease risk management, capital allocation and investor protection Enhance relevant skills of industry practitioners and raise public awareness and understanding Encourage product innovation and research measures to direct fund flows towards green and sustainable projects Capitalise on opportunities from the Mainland to develop Hong Kong into a green finance centre for the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (Greater Bay Area) Strengthen regional and international co-operation Actions taken to date to advance the development of sustainable finance in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. Current priorities include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), the green taxonomy (see “Developing a Green Taxonomy Framework to Facilitate Green Financing” in the chapter “Building a Sustainable Financial System” on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Specifically, the Steering Group announced in March a preliminary feasibility assessment on carbon market opportunities in Hong Kong, and will support Hong Kong’s development as a regional carbon trading centre, including developing an international high-quality voluntary carbon market and seizing opportunities arising from Greater Bay Area co-operation. In December, the Steering Group announced a partnership with CDP2 to enhance data availability and strengthen sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of this collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting unlisted firms and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which facilitates corporate sustainability reporting and assists financial institutions in collecting and analysing company-level data for risk assessment and relevant business decisions. This marks an essential step for the Steering Group to expand the coverage of its data work to include SMEs, a previously less accessible yet vital segment of the economy. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021 to coordinate efforts among financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions in training and policy formulation, and to build resources and a database. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three repositories covering data, training information and internship opportunities respectively, to assist the financial sector and other sectors in accessing data and learning resources related to green and sustainable finance. The resource repository provides data sources for assessing physical risks in Hong Kong To support talent training in the industry, the Centre assisted the Government in launching the “Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme” in December, providing subsidies to practitioners, students and graduates participating in training and skills upgrading related to green and sustainable finance. Other measures to foster skills training include the launch of the “Sustainable Finance Internship Programme” to create more internship opportunities for students, and the introduction of a new Module on “Green and Sustainable Finance” under the HKMA’s “Enhanced Competency Framework” for banking practitioners. “Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme” The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the “Alliance for Green Commercial Banks”4, bringing together regional financial institutions, banking industry organisations, research institutions and innovative technology providers to jointly develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banks. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realise their potential in developing green finance as a mainstream core business and fostering the financial system’s participation in global climate change-related activities. It operates by providing a one-stop peer learning platform for financial institutions to acquire the necessary knowledge, tools and information to formulate their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions Convening green finance leaders to connect green financial institutions across different emerging markets to facilitate communication and examine frontier issues Advancing the global green finance agenda and unlocking vast green and climate-related investment opportunities In June, five globally leading financial institutions5 became Cornerstone Members of the Alliance, working closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage customers to adopt green strategies, promote best practice guidelines for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities to facilitate the transition to a green economy. Moreover, three Global Partners and one Knowledge Partner6 committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version): Cornerstone Members, International Finance Corporation and HKMA sign Memorandum of Understanding Separately, since March 2021, the Alliance has organised 18 training sessions and roundtables, attracting over 6,000 participants from APAC, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, the Alliance, together with the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (HKIMR)7, published its first frontier issue research report in June 2022 entitled “Climate Risk: Definition, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulation”. The HKMA has been fostering the issuance of green and sustainable debt and building a local ecosystem of related professional services. Total green and sustainable debt issued in Hong Kong in 2022 (including bonds and loans) reached US$80.5 billion, representing growth of 42%. +42% Green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion) To demonstrate the Government’s commitment to combating climate change, promoting green finance and striving to develop Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government introduced the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in implementing the relevant green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued nearly US$16 billion equivalent of green institutional and retail green bonds, with proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and recycling, energy efficiency and energy conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the Programme, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report detailing the allocation of proceeds raised from green bonds and the expected environmental benefits. To allow the public to participate in Hong Kong’s sustainable development through investment and share the resulting benefits, the first batch of retail green bonds totalling HK$20 billion was issued in May, receiving enthusiastic public support and becoming the largest retail green bonds issuance globally at that time. This issuance also expanded the product offerings of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, consolidating Hong Kong’s position as a premier regional and international green and sustainable finance hub. The Government continued its regular issuance of green institutional bonds in the 2022-23 fiscal year, issuing US$5.75 billion equivalent of green bonds in January 2023. This triple-currency offering covered US dollars, Euros and renminbi, with tenors ranging from 2 to 30 years, continuing to provide an important Baseline for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The issuance was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not participated in previous Government Green Bond issuances, reflecting investors’ confidence in Hong Kong’s long-term credit profile and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of renminbi bonds to RMB10 billion. The share of international investors and Mainland investors participating via the Southbound Bond Connect also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong’s role as a premier CNH business hub and further consolidating Hong Kong’s leading position as an international financial centre. The HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing a tokenised institutional green bond in February 2023 to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This was the first tokenised green bond issued by a government globally. This primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis on a private blockchain network, and subsequent processes (including coupon payments, secondary market trade settlement and redemption at maturity) were also digitalised. The experience from this Government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and accessible market information, the HKMA continues to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt markets in Hong Kong and the region respectively. The International Capital Market Association report shows that in 2022, Hong Kong became the largest hub for arranging international green and sustainable bonds in Asia, with total bonds arranged through Hong Kong reaching US$27.8 billion, accounting for over one-third of the regional total. Largest arrangement hub for international green and sustainable bonds in Asia US$27.8 billion Following its initial green bond issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government issued RMB5 billion offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong again in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion of green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the People’s Government of Hainan Province also issued RMB5 billion offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, including blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuance activities have repeatedly highlighted Hong Kong’s unique role in facilitating green and sustainable fund flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring status as a premier regional fundraising platform. The HKMA continues to promote and implement the “Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme” introduced in 2021, using the scheme to attract more relevant professional service providers (including financial institutions, green advisory firms and external reviewers) to establish and expand their businesses in Hong Kong. The scheme has been well received by the industry. By end-2022, the scheme had covered expenses for pre-issuance, post-issuance or both external review services for over 180 green and sustainable debt instrument issuers, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate stringent adherence to market best practices and international standards. Starting from March, enhancements were made to the scheme, lowering the minimum loan volume threshold for applying for external review fee subsidies from HK$200 million to HK$100 million to help smaller firms access green financing. Following the successful completion of the proof-of-concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA collaborated again with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre under Genesis 2.0 to examine the technical feasibility of digitalising carbon forwards (also known as Mitigation Outcome Interests, or MOIs), thereby enhancing the transparency, objectivity and environmental benefits of the green bond markets. Completed in October 2022, the project successfully developed two prototypes to track, deliver and transfer digitalised MOIs using blockchain and other relevant technologies.

As one of the world’s largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in fostering the development of green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment, having taken the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets as early as 2015. It requires its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership promulgated by the Securities and Futures Commission, and to incorporate environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Guided by the principle of "Capital Preservation First, Long-term Growth," the HKMA invests prudently, believing that emphasizing ESG factors can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate related risks. Facing increasingly severe climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting a "net-zero by 2050" target in 2022 and enhancing risk management strategies to improve portfolio resilience, thereby seeking better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulators to jointly promote responsible investment, and collaborating with international organizations to develop ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risk. To fulfill its commitment to supporting the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to greening the global financial system, the HKMA has made climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment c. NGFS — Network for Greening the Financial System d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, has established a responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is for the HKMA to prioritize ESG investments with risk-adjusted long-term returns comparable to other options, consistent with the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Details of the HKMA’s responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website: The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for monitoring ESG and climate-related risks associated with Exchange Fund investment projects. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors the progress of integrating ESG factors into investments and the ESG status of the Exchange Fund through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Compliance Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Chart 1, the ESG Committee established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office is chaired by the Chief Risk Officer and is responsible for coordinating and monitoring various ESG initiatives of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Motions and work progress discussed at each meeting of the ESG Committee are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Monitoring and Governance Framework for Responsible Investment Dedicated teams within the Risk Management and Compliance Division work closely with various investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on integrating ESG factors, and assist senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across various investment projects: Open Markets Investments The Credit, Regulatory and Compliance Committee, composed of senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG status of the fixed income portfolio through regular reporting by the Risk Management and Compliance Division. In addition, the Risk Management and Compliance Division participates in the selection, appointment, and monitoring processes of external investment managers for equity portfolios from an ESG perspective (see the section "Striving for Active Exercise of Asset Ownership" in the "Risk Management" part on page 27). Private Market Investments The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers ESG-related assessments made by the Risk Management and Compliance Division and private market investment teams for each investment proposal. Concrete evidence² continues to show significant impacts from climate change and related risks. According to the latest report³ of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even assuming full implementation of announced Nationally Determined Contributions targets across regions, global temperature rise is estimated to reach 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius by 2100, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement goal of limiting global average temperature rise to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. If regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to narrow the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴ and asset repricing by markets based on anticipated future trends, coupled with inherent physical risks, will heighten stress on asset valuation. Given updates to global warming trajectories and model assumptions, the HKMA leveraged the expertise of external consultants to further evaluate the resilience of the Exchange Fund's "portfolio" under a "Rapid Transition" scenario (Chart 2), beyond the scenarios assessed in 2021. The "Rapid Transition" scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors in the short, medium, and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments jointly drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets face sudden divestment to keep average temperature rise before 2100 within 1.5 degrees Celsius. This scenario broadly aligns with the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The "portfolio" remains resilient in the medium to long term due to a larger proportion of asset allocation in sovereign bonds, which have lower sensitivity to transition impacts. Sector distribution is key. Low-carbon power and renewable energy assets may benefit from the relevant transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may cause shocks to performance (especially equity assets) in the near term. The overall "portfolio" will be subject to heightened impacts from physical risks that gradually manifest over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors. Climate scenario analysis, like other modeling methodologies, has its limitations. The analysis is based on market benchmark sector distributions at the strategic asset allocation level and does not consider the effects of active selection of specific securities within a sector. More in-depth studies indicate that investment projects within the "portfolio" are generally better able to withstand transition shocks or suffer milder impacts compared to the market benchmark of strategic asset allocation. This result reaffirms that the HKMA’s responsible investment focused on combating climate change can enhance portfolio resilience. The trajectory of climate change remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methodologies will continue to evolve with improvements in data quality and policy developments. The HKMA will regularly review relevant scenarios and optimize assessments to better ascertain the Exchange Fund's resilience to climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully understands the risks and opportunities that climate change may bring. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and seizing opportunities targeting climate transition, mitigating climate risks, and improving long-term portfolio returns. Building on strong momentum in 2022, the HKMA increased its holdings of green, social, and sustainable bonds by another 50%. Regarding equity investments, the HKMA invested in actively managed equity portfolios with a governance theme and adopted a decarbonization strategy favoring low-carbon companies for passive equity portfolios. Furthermore, the HKMA is exploring with dedicated partners of the Exchange Fund's "Long-Term Growth Portfolio" the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio to foster green and sustainable development in Asia (Chart 3). Chart 3 Continued Implementation of Measures to Increase ESG Investments The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator which, in addition to producing clean energy, places great emphasis on social and biodiversity factors. Before the wind farm was established, local villagers used poisoned bait to prevent predators from preying on their livestock, inadvertently endangering certain endangered vulture species. Livestock represents important property for local villagers; to help them protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect animals from natural predators. Additionally, the operator employs bird monitoring teams to issue warnings when vultures are attracted by animal carcasses occasionally left by predators, enabling the shutdown of wind turbines to avoid vultures being struck by blades. Reduced livestock predation creates a win-win situation: protecting villagers' livelihoods on one hand, and reducing vulture fatalities from turbine strikes on the other, thereby protecting endangered species. Sound ESG practices can bring more business opportunities and open up income sources for corporates, as illustrated by the following supply chain-related operations. The investee company is an integrated logistics and warehousing operator in Mainland China, specializing in cold chain pharmaceuticals, chemical products, and high-end consumer goods logistics services. The company faces continuously rising ESG operating standards, primarily driven by multinational corporate customers requiring their service providers to meet high decarbonization targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to these demands, the company engaged external consultants to help formulate a "Three-Year ESG Plan" to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% by 2030. This comprehensive decarbonization plan yielded significant results in 2021 alone. These ESG measures earned the company a "Low-Carbon Green Management Case" award from the China Federation of Logistics & Purchasing. These achievements and accolades enable the company to secure considerable business opportunities from multinational consumer and chemical product clients who especially value ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and upgrade industry skills. In 2022, the HKMA successfully held the 4th Annual ESG Workshop, exchanging sound ESG practices with nine participating private market entities (including dedicated partners, limited partners, and corporates), and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the APAC region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. In Open Markets, the HKMA urged trade partners (mainly investment banks) to expand ESG staff and research capabilities, especially in Hong Kong. Mr. Darryl Chan, Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, delivered opening remarks at the 2022 HKMA ESG Workshop At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in developing industry ESG investment standards and practices: As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participated in joint signatory actions coordinated by the PRI to develop standardized responsible investment due diligence questionnaires for private equity and venture capital investments⁵,⁶, assisting private market investors in conducting ESG assessments of dedicated partners and investment proposals. The HKMA participates in several working groups to support FCLTGlobal's research; this research aims to examine major market practices regarding long-term portfolios and decarbonization of private assets, and their application to long-term investors. As a member of the NGFS and a supporter of the TCFD, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS Guidelines for Climate-related Disclosure by Central Banks, demonstrating its determination to adopt sound ESG practices. The HKMA also leads a working group under the NGFS "Central Banks Net-Zero" workstream, participating in formulating sustainable and responsible investment approaches for the central banking community. The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars to share insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies. Ms. Wai-kuen Lau, Chief Risk Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office (center), spoke at an ESG Investment Opportunities Sharing Session Building internal capability is crucial to continuing the ESG journey. In addition to encouraging staff to take sustainability-related courses and obtain relevant qualifications, the HKMA has gained relevant knowledge and practical experience from the process in which external consultants provided advice in 2021 on major industry practices for portfolio climate transition. Meanwhile, the HKMA utilizes ESG datasets compiled by reputable external information providers to supplement its ongoing analysis of the portfolio, helping to reinforce the ESG resilience of the Exchange Fund.

The HKMA is committed to reducing the carbon footprint of its own organisation, with the aim of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, and contributing to Hong Kong's overall climate targets. While striving to foster environmental sustainability, the HKMA also honours its promises to care for staff physical and mental health, promote financial inclusion, and fulfil social responsibilities. The HKMA is committed to conducting its day-to-day operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, the HKMA puts into practice the concept of sustainable development under three key pillars: environment, staff, and social responsibility (Figure 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Commission is responsible for leading the HKMA in formulating and implementing sustainable development strategies. Chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, the Commission comprises three Deputy Chief Executives and representatives from the Risk Management and Compliance Department and the Corporate Development and Operations Department; it submits regular reports to the Governance Sub-Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the leadership of the Commission, various teams and working groups are responsible for planning and executing actions within their respective areas. In 2022, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Commission reviewed and approved the climate targets for corporate operations, and examined the transformation roadmap towards achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. During the year, the Commission continued to review progress on the HKMA’s green measures, including proposals to strengthen the HKMA’s sustainable procurement policy, procedures, and methodology. Sustainable Development Governance Framework The HKMA’s Corporate Sustainability Journey In recognition of the HKMA’s commitment to caring for the environment, staff, and the community at large, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service has awarded the HKMA the "15 Years+ Caring Organisation" logo for the 16th consecutive year. The HKMA attaches great importance to the carbon footprint of its own organisation and has formulated internal "Green Office Guidelines" to manage the environmental impact of operating processes. Environmental considerations have been integrated into the interior design, operations, and maintenance of the HKMA’s offices. In 2022, the HKMA was awarded Gold certification under BEAM Plus for certain renovated office areas. This marks the second green building certification received by the HKMA, following the LEED Gold certification obtained in 2021. Awarded BEAM Plus Interiors v1.0 Gold Certification The HKMA has introduced various energy-saving measures. Total energy consumption in 2022 was 4,996.4 MWh (2.8 MWh per capita), representing a downtrend of 24.4% compared to 2015 (Chart 1). Total Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions in 2022 amounted to 2,996.4 tonnes of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e) (1.7 tCO2e per capita), down 38.2% from 2015 (Chart 2). Chart 1 Chart 2 GHG Emission Intensity (Scope 1 and 2) The HKMA encourages paperless internal operations. Moreover, the HKMA has implemented a print management arrangement whereby staff must log in to printers to confirm each print request, helping to reduce unnecessary paper prints and toner use. Where printing is necessary, double-sided printing and black-and-white printing are encouraged. The HKMA is also preparing to introduce an internal electronic records keeping system. Total paper consumption in 2022 was 20.5 tonnes (0.0114 tonnes per capita), down 65.3% from 2015 (Chart A). Chart A: Paper Use Intensity The HKMA’s waste management continues to adhere to the "4R" principles. In addition to traditional waste, the HKMA reduces electronic waste through the adoption of technology solutions such as server virtualisation and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external firm for the first time to conduct a waste audit to analyse the composition of waste generated from offices. The audit revealed that food waste accounted for a significant share of total waste, prompting the HKMA to launch a food waste recycling programme (see page 41, "Strengthening Waste Management"). The total amount of non-hazardous waste generated in 2022 (including general waste and recyclables) was 242.0 tonnes (0.135 tonnes per capita), down 4.8% from 2015 (Chart 3). The volatility in the trend was mainly due to work-from-home arrangements implemented during the peak of the pandemic and the resumption of office operations after the fifth wave of the local epidemic. Chart 3 Non-Hazardous Waste Intensity The HKMA prioritises waste reduction at source and is committed to reducing, reusing, and recycling. In 2022, the HKMA engaged a firm for the first time to conduct a waste audit to better understand the composition of waste (plastics, paper, metals, glass, wood, electronics, etc.) arising from day-to-day operations and to provide waste reduction recommendations. Based on the findings of this audit, the HKMA introduced a food waste recycling programme in November, installing food waste collection bins in all pantries. Food waste collected daily is transported to an organic resources recovery centre in Hong Kong for conversion into renewable energy for power generation. Residues generated from the conversion process can also be turned into compost for landscaping and agricultural staple food production. Furthermore, recycling bins are placed at various locations throughout the office for ease of use. The HKMA shares recycling tips with staff and places greater emphasis on further improving source separation of recyclables, as well as highlighting precautions when handling recyclable items such as cardboard boxes, food containers, and beverage bottles. In addition, we continue to organise activities to raise staff environmental awareness, explain waste management policies, and encourage staff to make good use of recycling facilities in the office. Daily collected food waste transported to organic resources recovery centre Recycling plastic items The HKMA operates two data centres (primary and backup respectively). As they account for a major part of the organisation’s overall energy consumption, the HKMA has adopted green design and various energy-saving measures, including rack-mounted air conditioning systems, LED lighting, and 24-hour monitoring of power efficiency. Following the completion of a consultancy study on the green performance of the aforementioned data centres in 2022, the HKMA is prepared to implement recommendations to enhance overall energy efficiency. Preparations have also started to obtain green data centre certification. Understanding the importance of building a sustainable culture, the HKMA regularly introduces various programmes and activities to educate and encourage staff to develop habits conducive to sustainable development and adopt green and digitalising working styles. The HKMA shares green living tips with staff, along with annual office-wide energy consumption and paper usage statistics, reminding them to help combat environmental issues at the personal level; staff are also encouraged to submit suggestions on sustainability matters. Led by a Senior Manager of the Administration Division, a task force brings together staff from different departments to brainstorm ideas and concrete measures to foster a green workplace. Task force members also serve as ambassadors when new green measures are introduced. The HKMA encourages the wider community to adopt greener practices and has introduced various measures to improve the operational efficiency of the HKMA, the financial sector, and the economy as a whole, thereby minimising resource consumption. The HKMA’s "Submission Through Electronic Transfer System" (STET) is a one-stop platform enabling banks to submit documents electronically to the HKMA, covering various types of regular returns required on a weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annual basis. Another system, the "e-Delivery System", is a secure electronic communication channel for the HKMA to disseminate information such as circulars and guidelines to banks. Both systems help save a substantial amount of paper every year. In handling bank complaints and enforcement work, the HKMA has taken measures to support paperless document submission, allowing bank customers to lodge complaints via electronic channels and online forms. The HKMA is also developing a next-generation management information system to facilitate complaint handling and the transition from paper records to digital records. To reduce paper use, the Central Moneymarkets Unit (CMU) has adopted digital signatures in its day-to-day communications with participants, including the issuance of circulars, account opening and closure letters, and responses to audit confirmations.
