Looking ahead, the CMU will continue to examine more green measures, including the adoption of automated electronic processes for internal and external communications. By promoting the use of the Faster Payment System (FPS) and stored value payment tools, the HKMA encourages the public to adopt electronic payments more frequently in place of cash and physical cheques. More information on FPS and stored value payment tools can be found in the chapter "Hong Kong's Status as an International Financial Centre" of the HKMA Annual Report 2022. Sending electronic red packets is simple and convenient, reducing the use of physical red packet envelopes and banknotes, and fostering sustainable development in Hong Kong. To this end, the HKMA continued to actively promote this practice across various social media and traditional platforms, encouraging the public to send electronic red packets via online or mobile banking services using FPS or other e-wallet services during the Lunar New Year. Major banks and e-wallet operators also organised various activities to attract users to send electronic red packets, such as providing user interfaces full of festive sentiment, upgrading functions for greater ease of use, and launching lucky draws or cash rebates. HKMA promoting electronic red packets on social media For those who choose to give physical red packets during the Lunar New Year, the HKMA continues to encourage the use of "Good-as-New Banknotes", i.e., used but crisp banknotes, for packing red packets. Good-as-New Banknotes reduce the need for printing new banknotes, thereby mitigating environmental impact. Feedback from note-issuing banks shows that the public has become increasingly accepting of Good-as-New Banknotes in recent years. The Coin Collection Programme reflects the HKMA’s efforts in promoting coin recycling. Coins collected through the programme are recirculated to meet public demand, improving the efficiency of coin circulation and reducing the need for minting. The programme operates two coin collection vehicles and has served over one million person-times to date, collecting a total of over 800 million coins with a total face value of approximately HKD 1.3 billion. In 2022, about 78% of users chose to top up some or all of the collected value to their stored value payment tool accounts. The HKMA has maintained co-operation with the Hong Kong Council of Social Service, deploying coin collection vehicles on NGO flag days to collect coins in support of social services. Coin counting machines on board the coin collection vehicles Launched in 2014, the Coin Collection Programme is the world’s first systematic coin collection programme adopting the concept of mobile vehicles. It has won multiple local and international awards over the years, gaining recognition for its innovative and environmentally friendly coin handling methodology. The programme features two coin collection vehicles, each equipped with two high-speed coin counting machines to collect coins exchanged by the public. Users may choose to exchange coins for banknotes, top up their stored value payment tool accounts (such as Octopus cards or e-wallets), or donate the proceeds to the Community Chest. In addition to collecting coins, the vehicles are occasionally deployed for various educational activities (e.g., student visits).

Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency has undertaken an independent verification of the climate target (the “Climate Target”) of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (“HKMA”). The Climate Target was prepared based on the requirements reported in the SBTi Corporate Manual (the “SBTi Corporate Manual”). The objective of this verification engagement is to verify whether the Climate Target was developed based on the SBTi Corporate Manual. This verification engagement was conducted in accordance with the International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised), “Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information,” issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were specifically designed to express opinions and a Balance to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification processes were established based on the requirements of the SBTi Corporate Manual. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and reporting of the relevant data. Our verification work is absolutely independent and impartial. Based on the results of this verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency provides reasonable assurance and concludes that: • The Climate Target was developed based on the SBTi Corporate Manual. Shen Xiaoyin Audit Manager Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency March 2023 Verification Statement Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency has undertaken an independent verification of the 2022 environmental dataset (the “2022 Dataset”) of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (“HKMA”). The 2022 Dataset includes total energy consumption, Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emission intensity, paper consumption intensity, non-hazardous waste generation intensity and recycling rate for 2022, and the change in these data compared to 2015 levels. The GHG emission data of the HKMA was compiled in accordance with the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (“GHG Protocol”) jointly published by the World Resources Institute (“WRI”) and the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (“WBCSD”). The verification scope covers relevant data for the periods from January 1, 2022 to December 31, 2022, and also covers relevant data for the periods from January 1, 2015 to December 31, 2015 used for comparison of annual performance. The verification scope covers a total of 6 office and warehouse assets, comprising 4 offices at 1) Two International Finance Centre, 2) Hopewell Centre, 3) Pacific Place Phase 1, and 4) Kowloon Trading Hub, and 2 warehouses at 5) Lok Sing Industrial Centre and 6) Chung Lee Centre, located in Kwai Chung and Tsuen Wan respectively. The purpose of the verification is to provide reasonable assurance on the accuracy and reliability of the 2022 Dataset, and to confirm the adequacy of the HKMA’s data collection mechanisms. Within the verification scope, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency examined representative data and supporting evidence selected from the 6 assets. This verification engagement was conducted in accordance with the International Standard on Assurance Engagements 3000 (Revised), “Assurance Engagements Other Than Audits or Reviews of Historical Financial Information,” issued by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board. The verification procedures were specifically designed to express opinions and a Balance to obtain a reasonable level of assurance. The verification processes were established based on the requirements of the GHG Protocol. The verification processes tested the completeness and accuracy of the data by tracing the selected sample data to its Source, and also reviewed the underlying processes of data collection, aggregation, estimates, calculation and internal checks, and performed reliability testing. The verification processes also included verifying Domestically data collection and management mechanisms, conducting interviews with proxies responsible for preparing the 2022 Dataset, and selecting representative data and information for examination. Relevant raw data and supporting evidence were also reviewed in detail during the verification process. The HKMA is responsible for the collection and reporting of the relevant data. Our verification work is absolutely independent and impartial. The Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency verification team has not participated in the preparation processes of the 2022 Dataset. Based on the results of this verification, Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency provides reasonable assurance on the 2022 Dataset and concludes that: • The 2022 Dataset is materially accurate and reliable; • The HKMA’s headline data collection mechanisms are strong. Shen Xiaoyin Audit Manager Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency March 2023

Expanding and accelerating climate action has become the most pressing issue of our time. We are already nearly halfway through the critical decade for addressing the climate crisis. To have any hope of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, we need to cut global carbon emissions by more than 40% within this decade. That said, GHG emissions continue to hit record highs. The latest climate science studies highlight that the window for keeping global temperature rise within 1.5 degrees Celsius is rapidly closing. The impact of a 1.1-degree Celsius temperature increase is already being keenly felt by all — record-breaking heatwaves and droughts, severe flooding, storms, and other extreme weather events are occurring with increasing frequency and severity around the world. Hong Kong is no exception. Last September, following a violent super typhoon, we were hit by a once-in-a-century rainstorm. Despite our robust infrastructure and rapid disaster response capabilities, the impact was still very severe — widespread flooding, transport disruptions, and damage to roads in many areas. All these serve as stark reminders that decisive and proactive actions to combat climate change are urgently needed. Asia faces particularly significant challenges on its path to low-carbon transition, especially in balancing economic development with sustainability. We need credible transition strategies that can appropriately balance climate action with economic growth and social inclusion. This is by no means an easy task. Due to rapid economic development and population growth in the region, its carbon emissions account for more than half of the global total. Meanwhile, the Asia Pacific region is highly densely populated and, due to its geographical location, is also vulnerable to sea-level rise and extreme weather. Given the varying stages of development among economies in the region, while the low-carbon transition will bring new opportunities for some, securing the necessary transition funding remains a huge challenge for others. Market estimates suggest that the Asia Pacific region will require over US$3 trillion annually in low-carbon transition investment over the next 30 years. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong has both the capability and the responsibility to leverage the power of finance to support the low-carbon transition across Asia. As a regulator of the banking sector, a market facilitator, and a responsible investor, the HKMA has been making significant efforts towards the sustainable development agenda. Readers can understand the various concrete measures and work introduced by the HKMA over the past year from the different chapters of this report. Moreover, to strengthen the HKMA’s internal governance structure and enhance coordination of sustainability work across different functional areas, we established the Green and Sustainable Steering Committee last year. For detailed information on the Steering Committee, please refer to the newly added chapter on "Governance for Sustainability". Hong Kong banks play an important role in supporting Asia's transition to net-zero. In addition to fulfilling our traditional functions as a banking sector regulator, ensuring banks properly manage climate risk in our day-to-day supervisory work, we also act as a facilitator to support the banking sector in providing financing for the low-carbon transition. One example is the development of a green taxonomy framework to assist banks and other financial institutions in identifying environmentally sustainable activities, thereby aligning their business decisions with global climate targets. We introduced a prototype of the green taxonomy framework for consultation in May and are now upgrading the framework based on opinions collected during the consultation period. Furthermore, as there is an increasing need for higher quality and globally comparable sustainability disclosure information, the HKMA is working with other regulators to formulate a clear roadmap for Hong Kong to adopt the disclosure standards issued by the International Sustainability Standards Board in June, which serve as a comprehensive global baseline for sustainability reporting. The HKMA’s role as a facilitator extends beyond setting frameworks and rules; we are also committed to addressing pain points faced by the industry. Currently, many banks face difficulties in conducting physical risk assessments due to data limitations. In light of this, the HKMA will introduce a cloud-based physical risk assessment platform in the near term. By simply entering a property address, banks can assess the impact of physical hazards on residential and commercial buildings in Hong Kong under different climate scenarios, thereby helping banks manage related climate risks. As a major international financial centre and sustainable finance hub in Asia, Hong Kong has consistently played a bridging role, channelling international investment into sustainable development projects in Asia to support the region's low-carbon transition. In recent years, the total volume of international green and sustainable bonds arranged in Hong Kong has accounted for more than one-third of the Asian market, significantly leading other regions. It is especially worth noting that the Shenzhen Municipal Government and the Hainan Provincial Government issued green and sustainable bonds in Hong Kong in 2023 for the third and second consecutive years respectively, reaffirming Hong Kong's pivotal role as a green gateway connecting the Mainland with the rest of the world. The vibrant development of sustainable bond activities in Hong Kong is partly attributed to the demonstration effect of the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the government in issuing approximately US$25 billion worth of green bonds to institutional and retail investors. We have seized every offering opportunity to continuously innovate and expand the features of green bonds, including currency, tenor, and distribution channels, laying the foundation for other public and private green bond issuers in the region. Following the issuance of the world’s largest government retail green bonds in 2022, we issued the first tokenised Government Green Bond in February 2023. In February 2024, we completed the second batch of tokenised green bond issuance; denominated in four major currencies and issued in digital native format, these were the first multi-currency digital green bonds globally. Meanwhile, we have proactively introduced various actions to enhance the vitality and competitiveness of Hong Kong's sustainable finance ecosystem. This covers work in multiple areas including skills training, data enhancements, green fintech, and transition finance. Particularly in talent training, we introduced a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module under the Banking Professional Qualification Framework in 2023, providing systematic courses for banking practitioners to enhance their understanding and professional knowledge of green and sustainable finance. Transition finance is another key area of our work. It provides funding for decarbonisation activities in high-carbon and hard-to-abate sectors, preventing these industries from failing to transition due to lack of funding support. To support the robust development of transition finance, the HKMA will expand the local green taxonomy framework to cover transition activities. We will also expand the scope of the "Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme", which provides funding support to eligible bond issuers and borrowers, to include transition bonds and loans, encouraging corporates in the region to raise transition capital in Hong Kong. Moreover, we will strengthen communication with relevant stakeholders to attract private sector investment in sustainable development projects that have traditionally found it difficult to secure financing, through public-private partnerships and blended finance models. Some of the above work requires cross-sectoral co-operation and is primarily coordinated by the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group, co-chaired by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission. Regional co-operation is equally important. In addition to our long-standing partnership with the International Finance Corporation on the "Alliance for Green Commercial Banks", the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office became a founding member of the "Sustainable Investment Capacity Building Alliance" and the "Green Development Investment and Financing Partnership" in 2023. Furthermore, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero announced plans to establish a chapter in Hong Kong. Through these partnerships, we aim to foster skills training and knowledge sharing, thereby supporting the channelling of capital to sustainable development projects in the region and globally. To foster new business development and knowledge exchange, the HKMA also helped organise the inaugural "Hong Kong Green Week" earlier this year, attracting over 1,600 participants from nearly 30 jurisdictions, including top decision-makers from global business and financial sectors, to discuss ways to scale up climate finance in the region and forge new partnerships. Chief Executive Mr Eddie Yue delivered a speech at the flagship event of "Hong Kong Green Week", the "APAC Climate Business Forum". As the manager of Hong Kong's official reserves and a significant global asset owner, the HKMA leads by example as a responsible investor. Since 2015, the HKMA has been pioneering investment in green and sustainable assets, progressively expanding the Exchange Fund’s ESG and green asset portfolio in both Open Markets and private markets. With respect to the target of achieving net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund’s "portfolio" by 2050 or sooner, the HKMA added a new active global equity portfolio themed on sustainability and climate transition last year, and extended the application of customised low-carbon equity indices to another Open Markets portfolio. Additionally, green, social, and sustainable bonds prioritised for investment by the HKMA have outperformed the investment benchmark, demonstrating the proposition of "doing good while doing well". In private markets, we continue to pursue green-related investment opportunities and have become an anchor investor in two Asia-focused transition investment funds. At the end of 2022, the weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of the Exchange Fund’s equity portfolio decreased by 6% and 46% compared to 2021 and 2017 levels respectively, and has consistently remained below the headline market level. As a sustainable entity, the HKMA will continue to strive for progress, formulating our sustainability goals and plans based on three pillars: environment, staff, and social responsibility. Specifically, in our journey towards low-carbon transition, the HKMA continues to strengthen our capacity to combat climate change by assessing our environmental performance and implementing various internal measures. These measures cover emission reduction, energy efficiency improvements, and waste management, with the ultimate goal of fulfilling our promise to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or sooner. We have formulated plans to fully eliminate Scope 1 emissions in the near term and have made good progress towards our interim target of reducing Scope 2 emissions by 2030. To attract and retain top talent to fulfill the HKMA’s key functions, in addition to green targets, the HKMA is committed to fostering a healthier physical and mental well-being for our staff. Furthermore, we contribute to building a caring society by collaborating with various stakeholders to promote financial inclusion, enhance the public’s financial literacy, and raise awareness against financial fraud. The climate challenges are immense and exceptionally urgent. Economies around the world are moving towards a more sustainable future, a process that is expected to bring significant changes to financing activities and asset allocation. This transition carries potential risks, but will also be accompanied by unprecedented access to opportunities. As a major global sustainable finance hub, Hong Kong has a responsibility to take the lead in taking actions to address these challenges. At the same time, we are well-positioned to capitalise on this momentum. The HKMA will fully support the industry in providing financing for the low-carbon transition; continue to lead by example as a responsible investor and sustainable entity; and collaborate with like-minded partners to advance this critically important global agenda. Chief Executive Eddie Yue

Climate change risks and other sustainability issues are of global concern. The HKMA’s objective in its sustainability work is to play a leading role through its own policies and operations, ensuring that both the Hong Kong financial system and the HKMA itself can withstand climate change risks, and supporting the transformation towards more sustainable economic development. Through active participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to contribute to the formulation of green and sustainable finance policies and standards at both regional and global levels. As the regulator of the banking sector, the HKMA will further strengthen the banking sector’s climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. Specifically, key priorities include: launching a new round of thematic reviews on banks’ climate risk management practices and conducting a new round of consultation sessions as part of the assessment of banks’ progress in implementing supervisory requirements on climate risk management; continuing the work on incorporating climate factors into the HKMA’s supervisory review process; completing the second round of industry-wide climate risk stress testing, providing guidelines to participating banks throughout the process, and sharing observations and lessons learned with the industry; enhancing sustainability disclosures, including working with local relevant authorities to align relevant requirements with the global baseline International Financial Reporting Standards Sustainability Disclosure Standards, and preparing for the implementation of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision’s Pillar 3 framework on climate-related financial risks; and sharing guidelines on best practices for transition planning with the industry. To foster the healthy development of banks in offering green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will continue to keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, and maintain contact with the industry to ensure that banks adopt appropriate sales processes. Moreover, the HKMA will also act as a facilitator, striving to foster the development of the green finance ecosystem and support banks in providing financing for economic transformation. We will soon publish a local green taxonomy and continue expanding its coverage to encompass more activities, including transition activities. Meanwhile, we will also continue to examine the application of tech solutions to assist banks in identifying, measuring and monitoring their climate risk exposures; one example is the upcoming launch of a cloud-based platform to facilitate banks’ physical risk assessments. To enhance the professional competence of practitioners, we will also develop the “Green and Sustainable Finance” module under the Professional Level of the “Banking Professional Qualification Framework” in 2024. Hong Kong is well-positioned to serve as a regional and international sustainable finance hub. To fulfil this role, the HKMA is assisting the government in implementing the proposals set out in the 2023-24 Budget to expand the scope of the Government Green Bond Programme to cover sustainable finance projects, thereby deepening the development of the local green and sustainable bond market; meanwhile, attracting more green financing activities, including transition finance activities, to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. We will also continue to encourage more governments, entities and corporates to raise green funding through Hong Kong, and explore potential synergies between green finance and technology. Furthermore, we will continue to assist in implementing the government-funded Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Scheme to expand the talent pool for green finance in Hong Kong. As co-chair of the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), we will continue to work closely with other agencies and departments to coordinate cross-sectoral policies and efforts related to fostering the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. The Steering Group will focus on three areas of work in 2024, including sustainability disclosure, application of technology and transition finance. As another key area of work, through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation will continue to jointly launch various dedicated initiatives in Asia, including conducting green finance studies, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidelines to assist banks in supporting financial institutions in establishing their distinctive green transition pathways. In 2024, we will also strive to deepen co-operation with the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero, the Sustainable Investment Capacity Building Alliance and the Green Development Investment and Financing Partnership. As a responsible investor, the HKMA promises that the Exchange Fund portfolio will achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. We will continue to enhance the sustainability of the Exchange Fund’s investments through a three-pronged responsible investment approach, ensuring that the portfolio remains resilient during the progress towards net zero. Recognising that achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement requires the transformation of the real economy, we are refining our net-zero strategy to focus on assets that can bring positive climate benefits to the real economy, while taking into account the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. As an environmentally supportive organisation, the HKMA’s decarbonisation strategy will continue to evolve to reflect the latest developments in markets, regulation, technology and other climate-related areas. To further strengthen the HKMA’s climate resilience and risk preparedness, we will examine the feasibility of using tech solutions to assess the impact of physical risks on our offices. In addition, we will continue to actively encourage staff to participate in our sustainability efforts, including launching promotional campaigns to cultivate sustainable habits and optimising office processes and practices. Furthermore, the HKMA will continue to maintain consistent, efficient and sustainable procurement practices, including evaluating suppliers’ ESG practices during selection and contract renewal. Building on the green data centre certification obtained in 2023, the HKMA promises to adhere to designated certification standards. Regarding regular upgrades of data centre facilities, in addition to keeping pace with the latest technological developments, we will also incorporate green design and operational practices. Meanwhile, we will continue to reduce electronic waste through the application of technology and convergence, and actively modernise internal systems to improve efficiency and mitigate potential risks as far as possible. Finally, regarding social focus areas, the HKMA will identify more community service opportunities for colleagues, collaborate with the industry to promote financial inclusion and enhance financial literacy levels, and raise public awareness of financial fraud prevention.

Climate change has an impact on every aspect of human life, and everyone can make a contribution to mitigating its related impacts. Through its multiple roles as a central bank institution, banking sector regulator, market facilitator, responsible investor, and sustainable development entity, the HKMA contributes to fostering and accelerating the transformation towards net-zero in Hong Kong and across Asia. The HKMA has established a robust sustainable development governance framework to lead the formulation of its related strategies and policies; oversee the implementation of related actions; and ensure that sustainability factors are incorporated into the HKMA’s own operating processes and methodologies. In pursuit of good corporate governance, the HKMA has put in place a robust sustainable development governance framework with clear accountability arrangements and high transparency for its sustainability-related work. This governance framework ensures that sustainability factors are effectively integrated into the HKMA’s strategic planning and decision-making processes, and establishes effective mechanisms for monitoring and evaluating the progress and effectiveness of sustainability initiatives. The HKMA’s sustainable development governance framework comprises: the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee and its relevant sub-committees, which oversee the HKMA’s work, including its sustainability efforts, and provide recommendations; the Green and Sustainable Steering Committee (Steering Committee), chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, which leads the HKMA’s overall environmental, social and governance (ESG) strategies and policies at the management level; regarding responsible investment, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office is responsible for coordinating and overseeing ESG-related work within the Exchange Fund Investment Office; and for other functional areas, relevant teams and working groups are responsible for planning and implementing sustainability-related actions concerning banking and market developments as well as the HKMA’s own operations. At the cross-sectoral level, the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-established by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the efforts of financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders, and other stakeholders to accelerate the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. Given the visible expansion in the scope of the HKMA’s various sustainability initiatives over the past few years, we established the Steering Committee in October as a new central platform to lead and more effectively coordinate all sustainability work across different functional areas of the HKMA1. It provides guidelines on the formulation of strategies, policies, and programmes related to ESG matters across four functional areas: banking sector, market developments, Exchange Fund investments, and domestic operations; oversees the implementation of ESG-related programmes by various functional departments of the HKMA; evaluates the HKMA’s performance and effectiveness in achieving its ESG targets; and oversees external communication strategies. The Steering Committee is chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, with three Deputy Chief Executives serving as standing members. In addition, Assistant Chief Executives in charge of major functions related to green and sustainable development will be invited to attend meetings of the Steering Committee to report on key outcomes of their work and future plans. The Steering Committee meets regularly and is supported by relevant working groups under the Banking Department, Institutional Development and Operations Department, External Affairs Department, and Exchange Fund Investment Office of the HKMA. In addition to formulating and implementing its own sustainability actions, the HKMA co-established the Steering Group with the SFC in May 20202. As a cross-agency platform, the Steering Group provides strategic direction and coordinates cross-sectoral efforts for the financial sector to combat climate and environmental risks, thereby strengthening Hong Kong’s position as a leading green and sustainable finance centre in Asia and globally. For details on the work of the Steering Group, please refer to the chapter “Strengthening the Green and Sustainable Finance Ecosystem”.

Climate change represents a major risk to the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong’s financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong’s climate targets as well as the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are subject to the impact of various sustainability- and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue performing their critical functions in the financial system and channel more funds towards green and sustainable projects, banks have to proactively manage climate risk. As the regulator of the banking sector, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks’ ability to combat and manage climate risk, and accelerating their efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA is committed to formulating various policy measures to strengthen the banking system’s ability to combat climate risk. In August, the HKMA issued a circular on net-zero transition planning, setting out high-level principles to help banks remain safe and sound during the economic transition to net-zero emissions. Following the issuance of the circular, we conducted a survey of selected banks in the fourth quarter to understand their transition planning measures. Based on the survey results, we will share observations and best practices on transition planning with the industry, and organise seminars or workshops to foster experience sharing within the sector. On disclosure requirements, in light of the latest international developments, including the International Financial Reporting Sustainability Disclosure Standards announced in June and the consultation launched by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee) in November on the Pillar 3 disclosure framework for climate-related financial risks, the HKMA is stepping up its efforts to enhance the sustainability-related disclosure framework for banks in Hong Kong. Specifically, the HKMA is working with local authorities and stakeholders to develop a full roadmap for Hong Kong that is consistent with the International Financial Reporting Sustainability Disclosure Standards. During the year, the HKMA strengthened its supervision of banks’ climate risk management and provided guidance to banks to help them further upgrade their climate resilience and climate risk management capabilities. Significant progress has been made in implementing the two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the bank supervisory process. Climate risk management has now been included as a standing agenda item in prudential meetings with bank management. Bank supervisors have also adopted the enhanced CAMEL rating system1, which incorporates climate risk factors, to assess banks’ risk status and risk management systems. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the bank supervisory process, the HKMA revised the “Green” assessment framework to focus on banks’ transition planning measures. The HKMA is also reviewing the Supervisory Review Process used to assess and monitor banks’ capital adequacy levels and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with a view to encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address climate risk. Key work priorities under the 2023 two-year plan Following the completion of the 12-month implementation period for compliance with Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management”, the HKMA launched a round of thematic reviews on climate-related risk governance in the second quarter. The thematic review covered four key areas, namely the governance structure for climate-related risks, oversight of climate strategies, oversight of climate-related risk management, and organisational culture, awareness and communication. The HKMA made various enhancements to its climate risk stress-testing framework, including the introduction of a new five-year scenario to assess the potential impact on banks arising from simultaneous shocks to the economy and climate change. With these enhancements and as part of the HKMA’s regular supervisor-led stress testing programme, the second round of climate risk stress testing was launched in June to conduct a full assessment of banks’ climate risk exposures and further enhance banks’ ability to manage climate risk. A total of 44 banks participated in this stress test, representing an increase of over 60% compared to the first pilot exercise in 2021. The HKMA also organised a Climate Risk Stress Testing Forum in November, which was attended by as many as 300 banking practitioners. By fostering experience sharing among banks, the event helped deepen the industry’s overall understanding of climate risk measurement. The HKMA also conducted a range of consultation meetings to review banks’ progress in implementing the HKMA’s Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 “Climate Risk Management”. The HKMA held meetings with bank management to discuss their work on climate risk management and common challenges faced by the industry, and reviewed information provided by banks and other public information to assess their relevant progress. The HKMA provided targeted recommendations to banks to encourage and support them to continue strengthening their climate risk management capabilities in line with the HKMA’s supervisory expectations. With increasing global attention to climate change and concerted efforts to combat the issue, the HKMA has noted a growing demand for green and sustainable investment products, and some banks have offered related products to meet customer needs. In view of this, the HKMA completed a thematic review of banks’ sale of green and sustainable investment products and issued a circular in November, setting out the standards expected by the HKMA and sharing observed good practices. The circular covers multiple areas including product due diligence, disclosure, governance and controls, staff training and record-keeping, aiming to mitigate potential greenwashing risks and enhance investor confidence, thereby fostering the sound development of related investment activities. The HKMA will continue to keep abreast of the latest trends and market developments. The HKMA is committed to fostering the application of technology in green and sustainable banking. For instance, technology can improve data availability and risk analytics, enhancing banks’ ability to manage climate risk. The HKMA will soon introduce a pilot version of a cloud-based platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on residential and commercial buildings under different climate scenarios. Moreover, the HKMA continues to co-operate with other central banks and regulators to examine how technological solutions can assist in physical risk assessments. Separately, the HKMA also encourages the adoption of sustainable anti-money laundering (AML) approaches through the use of advanced analytics and artificial intelligence to reduce the consumption of compliance-related resources. In 2023, the HKMA launched an online shared data submission platform to fully automate the financial crime risk data collection process, thereby enhancing banks’ operational processes for submitting AML-related data in a sustainable manner. In September, the HKMA organised the “Green Fintech Competition”, aiming to seek market-ready solutions to help the banking sector address challenges in the following areas: (i) net-zero transition or transition planning; (ii) climate risk management; (iii) green and sustainable finance; and (iv) sustainability or climate-related disclosure and reporting. The competition attracted over 85 entries from around 70 firms. In December, the HKMA hosted the “Green and Sustainable Banking Conference”, providing a platform for the banking sector and the tech industry to examine the role of low-carbon technology and green fintech in the net-zero transition in Hong Kong and the Mainland, alongside the announcement of the results of the “Green Fintech Competition”. The event attracted approximately 400 participants from banks, tech companies, regulators and academia. To enhance transparency across financial markets and promote greater consistency in green and sustainable finance decision-making, the HKMA developed a local green taxonomy framework with the assistance of consultants. In May, the HKMA published a discussion paper on the “Prototype Hong Kong Green Taxonomy” to solicit opinions from stakeholders on the establishment and implementation of a green taxonomy. Based on the feedback received, the HKMA is fine-tuning the prototype framework and identifying other areas for the next phase of framework development. The HKMA participates in the work of the Financial Action Task Force, which has identified environmental crime as a predicate offence for money laundering; given the nexus between AML and environmental, social and governance (ESG), this area is receiving increased attention from regulators. Recognising that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and studies to enhance current monitoring efforts. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks and includes analysis of climate-related risks in various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the Scenario Design and Analysis Workstream under the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helps further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impact of climate change. As a member of the Financial Stability Board’s Transition Planning Working Group, the HKMA participates in analysing the interplay between transition planning by financial and non-financial corporates and financial stability, enabling policymakers to develop forward-looking and dynamic perspectives on climate-related financial vulnerabilities. On the research front, the HKMA conducted various applied research projects examining the impact of climate change and broader ESG issues on the financial sector and the economy. Research topics included climate risk exposures of the banking sector and investment funds2, ESG fund flows3, the impact of climate change on housing prices4, and the ripple effects of corporate ESG performance in global supply chains5. The findings of these studies have enhanced the HKMA’s understanding of the impact of climate change and ESG issues on financial stability, facilitating the formulation of relevant policies. Domestically, these studies have helped strengthen the HKMA’s ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has also shared research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through international events on climate-related matters and various channels such as the HKMA Research Memorandum. The HKMA’s Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralised backstop funding arrangement designed to provide timely liquidity support to banks in need. In line with NGFS recommendations, the HKMA has incorporated sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such engagement, the HKMA helps foster international and regional policy dialogue on combating climate change and its impact on financial stability, drawing insights to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong’s financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a leading regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA is committed to enhancing market awareness and participation, providing the necessary infrastructure and drivers, and supporting international initiatives to align with global standards. During the year, the HKMA worked closely with local and international partners to build a richer ecosystem and foster the further development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial sector’s actions to combat climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the government’s climate strategies. The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. In January 2024, the Steering Group announced key measures to support Hong Kong in seizing opportunities in sustainable finance, covering major work areas including sustainability disclosure, strengthening the ecosystem, transition finance, and green fintech. Specifically, a Sustainability Disclosure Working Group has been established to formulate a roadmap for the adoption of IFRS Sustainability Disclosure Standards in Hong Kong. The roadmap will cover four key areas: sustainability reporting, assurance, data and technology, and skills training. A Transition Finance Working Group has also been set up to examine methodologies to support financial institutions and corporates in transition planning and reporting. The Steering Group has also strengthened the sustainable finance ecosystem through cross-sectoral skills training and data enhancements. On data in particular, we continued to promote the adoption of the Climate and Environmental Risk Questionnaire for Non-listed Companies 2, launched by the Steering Group in collaboration with CDP in 2022. The Steering Group will continue to keep abreast of the latest developments in green and sustainable finance and enhance Hong Kong’s status as a regional and global green and sustainable finance hub. In January 2024, the Steering Group announced three new key work streams to capture investment and financing opportunities arising from the low-carbon transition in the Asia Pacific region. To facilitate skills training in the industry, the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance under the Steering Group implemented the Government’s “Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme”, which provides subsidies to practitioners, students, and graduates who undergo relevant training and obtain relevant qualifications in green and sustainable finance. As of December 2023, a total of 46 international and local training programmes or qualifications were registered as eligible training or qualifications under the scheme, and over 560 funding applications were approved. The HKMA also introduced a new Foundation Level module on “Green and Sustainable Finance” under the Banking Professional Qualification Framework. This module aims to foster talent development in the banking sector and enhance the overall professional competence of practitioners. In 2024, the HKMA will continue to work with the banking sector to develop the Professional Level of this module to meet the rapidly growing demand for professionals in green and sustainable finance. To help financial institutions and corporates, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), better understand key climate and sustainability-related topics, including climate risk management, sustainability reporting, GHG emission calculation, and transition planning, the HKMA collaborated with relevant government bureaux and departments, as well as global partners such as CDP, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ)3, and the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF)4 during the year to organise a range of seminars and thematic workshops, attracting participants from the financial services and corporate sectors. For students, following the launch of the “Sustainable Finance Internship Programme” in 2022, training sessions were held in January and February 2023 to enable interns and university undergraduate graduates to deepen their understanding of sustainable finance. Recognising the potential of technology in bridging climate-related data gaps and improving data quality, the HKMA is committed to making relevant data more accessible and enhancing data quality to support informed decision-making and effective climate action. In February 2024, the Steering Group introduced a series of website enhancements to provide a one-stop source of green and sustainable finance information for financial institutions, corporates, and the public. Key enhancements include an electronic platform for sustainability disclosure, GHG emission calculation and estimation tools, as well as more centralised, user-friendly, and searchable data and resources. During “Hong Kong Green Week”, the Steering Group co-organised the “Leveraging Technology to Catalyse Sustainable Finance” event with Cyberport and InvestHK, showcasing leading green innovative solutions and Hong Kong’s edge in green tech. “Hong Kong Green Week – Finance Theme” was held from 26 February to 1 March 2024, during which various sustainability-themed activities attracted over 1,600 guests from nearly 30 jurisdictions, including representatives from financial institutions, corporates, central banks, international organisations, government agencies, academia, and advisory firms. The flagship event of “Hong Kong Green Week” was the “APAC Climate Business Forum” co-organised by the HKMA and the International Finance Corporation. The forum brought together over 400 guests, including top decision-makers from the global commercial and financial sectors, to discuss solutions for unlocking climate financing in APAC. The two-day event covered a wide range of topics, including energy transition, decarbonisation of heavy industries, circular economy, future development of sustainable finance, and emerging climate technologies in emerging and developing markets in APAC. The forum received strong support from both public and private sector entities, co-organising over 10 roundtables, seminars, and other networking events. Topics covered climate financing, carbon markets, electric vehicle supply chains, net-zero transition financing, green finance taxonomy, and financing for green development in Belt and Road regions. In addition, the HKMA and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) co-hosted the “Asia Climate Financing Roundtable” on 29 February 2024 to examine key measures to scale up climate financing and the roles of central banks and regulators in climate risk management. These events form part of the HKMA’s overall efforts to foster and enrich Hong Kong’s green and sustainable finance ecosystem, serving as useful platforms for participants to drive new business developments, share knowledge, and explore new opportunities to address climate financing challenges in APAC. The HKMA has also been actively supporting regional green and sustainable finance development. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the “Alliance for Green Commercial Banks”5 as a collaborative platform bringing together financial institutions, banking industry associations, research institutes, and innovative tech providers in the region to jointly develop green commercial banks. Since March 2021, the Alliance has held 22 training sessions and roundtables, attracting over 7,300 participants from around the world, including APAC, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Americas. In October, the Alliance, together with Crédit Agricole CIB, published its second cutting-edge research report titled “Formulating Ambitious Climate Strategies for Green Banking: Case Studies”. During the year, the HKMA’s Infrastructure Financing Facilitation Office joined the newly established “Coalition for Sustainable Investment Capacity Building” (CASI) and the “Green Investment and Financing Partnership” (GIFP) initiated by the Belt and Road Green Development International Alliance. Collaboration with CASI and GIFP will facilitate capacity building and knowledge sharing, and channel more capital towards green and sustainable projects in Asia and beyond. In August 2023, GFANZ announced the establishment of its Hong Kong chapter, helping to support the net-zero efforts of financial institutions in Hong Kong and the Mainland. The HKMA supports GFANZ’s work in an advisory capacity. To demonstrate the Government’s determination to combat climate change, promote green finance, and strive to make Hong Kong a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the “Government Green Bond Programme” in 2018. The HKMA assists in issuing green bonds under the Programme. To date, the Government has issued approximately US$25 billion equivalent in green institutional and Retail Bonds, with proceeds allocated to over 70 green government projects, such as green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability of the Programme, the Government publishes an annual “Green Bond Report”, detailing the allocation of proceeds raised from green bonds and the expected environmental benefits. The Government continued its regular issuance of green institutional bonds in the 2023-24 fiscal year, issuing approximately US$6 billion equivalent in green bonds in June. This triple-currency offering covered US dollar, Euro, and renminbi bonds of different tenors, attracting a diverse group of investors with enthusiastic subscription, recording nearly US$30 billion equivalent in orders. Notably, the issuance size of renminbi bonds increased from RMB 10 billion in January to RMB 15 billion, and a 10-year renminbi bond was introduced for the first time, helping to extend the Government’s renminbi yield curve and further enrich offshore renminbi product choices. The strong response from global investors to the Government’s green bond issuance reflects their recognition of Hong Kong’s commitment to fostering green and sustainable development. In October, the Government issued a second batch of HKD 20 billion in green Retail Bonds to further foster market developments and promote inclusive finance. This offering provided the public with an investment opportunity with stable returns, enabling them to participate in and benefit from Hong Kong’s green finance development.

As a major global asset owner and manager, the HKMA plays a pivotal role in fostering the development of green and sustainable finance to support the global climate agenda. The HKMA has been a pioneer in responsible investment. Since 2015, the HKMA has led the way in investing in green and sustainable assets, requiring its external investment managers to actively exercise ownership and integrate environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. Adhering to the principle of "Capital Preservation First, Long-term Growth Second"1, the HKMA invests prudently, believing that paying full attention to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors helps mitigate relevant investment risks while unlocking the long-term sustainable worth of investments. As one of the first central banks to sign the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI) and set a "net-zero by 2050" target2 for its portfolio, the HKMA is committed to continuing its responsible investment journey, emphasizing sustainability, especially the pressing issue of climate change, aiming to enhance the resilience of the Exchange Fund and strive for better risk-adjusted long-term yield. As a responsible investor, the HKMA participates in building a sound green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors, regulators and international organizations to jointly develop industry practice standards and foster the adoption of responsible investment by the financial sector and central banks. Through supervisory and co-operation actions, the HKMA strives to promote a future where finance and sustainable development go hand in hand. Figure 1 The Responsible Investment Journey of the Exchange Fund Comprehensive and reliable ESG information is crucial for integrating sustainability and planning a credible climate transition to achieve net-zero targets. To fulfill its promises to support the Glasgow Declaration3 of the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) and the Strategic Plan of the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group, the HKMA leads by example and has compiled this chapter on the responsible investment of the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principles set the tone for the HKMA to balance the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund while practicing responsible investment. The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for monitoring ESG and climate-related risks involved in the Exchange Fund's investment projects. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors the relevant implementation through regular meeting reports from the Sustainable Investment Team of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 2, the ESG Committee under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Strategy Officer, is responsible for coordinating and monitoring various ESG initiatives of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Motions and work progress discussed at quarterly meetings of the ESG Committee are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Moreover, the Green and Sustainable Steering Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA and attended by the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Strategy Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, meets semi-annually to provide guidelines on ESG policies and actions for different functions of the HKMA, including the Exchange Fund Investment Office, to realize the HKMA’s overall ESG targets. Figure 2 Responsible Investment Governance Structure of the Exchange Fund Investment Office As shown in Figure 1, the Exchange Fund Investment Office embarked on its responsible investment journey in 2016, initially focusing on managing ESG risks that may affect the financial performance of the Exchange Fund. With sustainability evolving rapidly and transcending risk considerations to become a strategic priority for major entities worldwide, the Exchange Fund Investment Office reviewed its responsible investment approach. July 2023 marked another milestone when the Exchange Fund Investment Office established a new Business Strategy Department led by the Chief Strategy Officer to coordinate and lead the strategic development of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, incorporating the Responsible Investment Team—now renamed the Sustainable Investment Team—formerly under the Risk Management and Compliance Division. This strategic move reflects the HKMA upgrading the focus of responsible investment from a risk-based approach to a more proactive and forward-looking stance in addressing sustainability-related matters in investment. The Sustainable Investment Team works closely with various teams within the Exchange Fund Investment Office on integrating ESG factors, and assists senior staff of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG, especially climate-related, risks and opportunities across various investment projects: Open Markets Investments — The Credit, Regulation and Compliance Committee, composed of senior staff of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, reviews the integration of ESG factors into credit risk models referencing opinions from the Sustainable Investment Team, and monitors the ESG status of fixed-income portfolios through regular reporting by the Risk Management and Compliance Division. In addition, the Sustainable Investment Team participates in the selection, appointment and monitoring processes of external investment managers for equity portfolios from an ESG perspective (see the section "Fostering Active Ownership" in the "Risk Management" part on page 40 for details). Private Market Investments — The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers ESG-related evaluations made by the private market investment and risk management teams for each proposed investment. The HKMA understands that physical and transition risks4 arising from climate change, as well as related opportunities, will impact the long-term performance and worth of the Exchange Fund's investment projects. The United Nations Environment Programme’s "2023 Emissions Gap Report"5 projects that unless GHG emissions are further reduced globally, the global average temperature will rise by 2.5 to 2.9 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels before 2030. The urgent need for more aggressive policies, technology development or behavioral changes to keep temperature rises manageable may heighten transition risks such as asset devaluation or stranded asset shocks. Meanwhile, extreme weather events are becoming increasingly frequent and severe, posing additional physical risks to investment projects. The HKMA believes that investing in a greener future aligns with the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund, and therefore places particular emphasis on climate-related factors when integrating ESG factors. The HKMA set a target for the Exchange Fund’s portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or sooner in 2022, further demonstrating its commitment to the global climate agenda. The HKMA continues to strengthen its three-pronged approach with a clear focus on decarbonization and transition. The following sections detail the relevant methodology. Figure 3 The HKMA’s Three-Pronged Approach to Responsible Investment In moving towards net-zero targets, the HKMA prefers active engagement over exclusion or divestment from its investable universe. First, maintaining a diverse and sound portfolio is critical to achieving the primary investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Directly excluding certain sectors or industries would narrow the investable universe, potentially impacting investment yield and risk. Through an inclusive approach, the HKMA can seize access to invest in corporates undergoing transition, equipped with advanced technology and sound corporate governance to address changing global climate trends, including those in high-emission sectors. Second, combating climate change requires the transition of core "brown" sectors. Merely excluding relevant investment projects or divesting does not help solve carbon emission issues. Instead, the HKMA supports these sectors by deploying strategic capital and actively exercising ownership, fostering their transition to sustainable and low-carbon practices, thereby bringing positive change for themselves and the world. In response to market developments, the HKMA is refining its net-zero investment strategies to pursue transition outcomes aligned with both the Exchange Fund and global net-zero targets through a full approach, while adhering to its guiding principles of responsible investment. By integrating ESG factors into investment decisions, the HKMA continues to seek sustainable investment and access to foster climate transition and enhance the long-term resilience of the Exchange Fund’s portfolio (Figure 4). The HKMA’s responsible investment maintained good momentum in 2023. In Open Markets, the HKMA launched a new active global equity portfolio themed on sustainability and climate transition, managed by external investment managers, and expanded the application of customized low-carbon equity indices to another portfolio managed by external investment managers. Furthermore, the green, social and sustainability bonds prioritized for investment by the HKMA outperformed the investment baseline, demonstrating the concept of "doing well by doing good". In private markets, the HKMA actively built a resilient long-term growth portfolio, seizing investment opportunities expected to benefit from long-term economic development trends such as climate and energy transitions. For instance, during the year, the HKMA invested in two Asia-focused transition investment funds, reflecting its commitment to addressing Asia's climate transition needs. Figure 4 Continued Actions to Foster ESG Investment The HKMA has invested in a company specializing in producing eco-friendly thermoplastic materials from unsorted household waste (including organic matter such as food waste) and non-recyclable materials. Unlike traditional chemical recycling systems that rely on energy-intensive high-temperature environments to produce plastics, this company pioneered a low-temperature production method powered entirely by solar arrays. This plastic material, produced 100% from waste, serves as a substitute for oil-based resins commonly used in industries such as retail and durable consumer goods, offering a sustainable and versatile option. At the same time, this plastic material is compatible with existing standard manufacturing processes and cutting-edge technologies such as 3D printing. The company firmly supports the circular economy. The figure below illustrates the positive environmental outcomes brought about by its advanced plastic production process: Managed by the International Finance Corporation, MCPP is an innovative arrangement combining funding from institutional investors with the IFC’s own resources to scale up sustainable financing for private firms in emerging markets. The HKMA committed two tranches of US$1 billion each to MCPP in 2017 and 2019 respectively, and further partnered with the IFC to create a new global climate-related investment platform, "MCPP One Planet", in 2021, which is also the world’s first cross-sector emerging market loan portfolio aligned with the Paris Agreement. Through the MCPP Programme, the HKMA has committed loans to 80 sustainable development projects across 19 sectors, including infrastructure, agriculture, property and manufacturing, in 38 developing countries. The IFC collects data on MCPP loans. According to IFC reports, the HKMA’s loan commitments provide support to emerging markets and developing countries in various areas such as economic transition and manpower development. Specifically, projects financed by the HKMA are projected to reduce GHG emissions by approximately 5.6 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent annually, equivalent to the GHG emissions from driving an average gasoline car for 14 billion miles. Figure 5 Projected Average Annual Benefits of HKMA’s MCPP Loan Commitments Since 2020 A green and sustainable finance ecosystem is the cornerstone of future global sustainable development. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to foster responsible investment and upgrade industry capabilities.

The HKMA is committed to becoming a sustainable entity, adopting a multi-pronged approach to reduce its carbon footprint, with the target of achieving net-zero GHG emissions by 2050 or earlier. In addition to fostering environmental sustainability, the HKMA places emphasis on staff physical and mental well-being and social responsibility, and strives to promote financial inclusion and enhance public financial literacy. As a responsible entity, the HKMA has set sustainable development goals under three pillars: environment, staff, and social responsibility. The Green and Sustainability Steering Committee (Steering Committee)1, established in October and chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is the primary decision-making body for various institutional sustainability actions. The predecessor of the Steering Committee was the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which was responsible for leading the HKMA in formulating the vision, strategies, and policy on institutional sustainability and corporate social responsibility matters. At the departmental level, the Assistant Chief Executive (Corporate Development and Operations) oversees the implementation of sustainability activities and regularly submits progress reports to the Steering Committee. The Green Office Task Force and the Volunteer Service Team provide support in co-ordinating institutional sustainability work; the former serves as a platform for brainstorming ideas on creating a green workplace, while the latter aims to foster a culture of participation in volunteer activities. The HKMA has developed a roadmap to guide its transformation. Key areas of focus include implementing decarbonisation strategies in its day-to-day operations, including operating green buildings and data centres, practising green commuting, adopting energy-saving measures, digital tools and greener working modes, waste reduction, and building a sustainability culture. The HKMA also plans to use carbon insetting derivative within its own value chain to mitigate emissions, and adopt carbon offsetting measures for hard-to-abate emissions. Beyond the above-mentioned environmental promises regarding its day-to-day operations, the HKMA continued to introduce greener operational solutions for the wider community, covering channels for banks to submit electronic documents and communications, as well as electronic payments and coin collection programmes for the general public. To strengthen and maintain its operational ability, the HKMA employs a professional workforce, builds a talent pool, and attaches importance to staff physical and mental well-being. On social responsibility, the HKMA encourages staff to participate in volunteer and charitable activities; considers selecting social enterprises in procurement; promotes consumer education on financial services; and works in co-operation with the banking sector to ensure fair access to basic banking services for all sectors of society. The remainder of this chapter sets out details of the above strategies. Under the HKMA’s overall institutional risk management framework, the Risk Committee2, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers potential risks and threats faced by the HKMA in its day-to-day operations, including those arising from climate change. Physical impacts brought about by climate change, such as increased extreme weather causing flooding or other damage, may affect the HKMA’s offices and hinder staff commuting. To manage physical risks, the HKMA regularly updates its business continuity plan to cope with extreme weather conditions. The HKMA also regularly conducts evacuation and backup facility activation drills to ensure staff are always prepared to implement business continuity measures. Office designs also incorporate various measures to mitigate potential risks. Transition risks may affect the HKMA’s energy use, air travel, and waste disposal. The HKMA has been monitoring the transition risks it faces by tracking its own GHG emissions, waste generation, as well as energy consumption and paper usage. The HKMA’s climate target is to achieve net-zero GHG emissions for Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 (air travel) across all aspects of institutional operations by 2050 or earlier. As a near-term emission reduction target, the HKMA plans to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions by converting all existing vehicles in the Authority to electric vehicles; and using 2015 as the baseline year, to reduce Scope 2 emission intensity by 63% by 2030 or earlier through various decarbonisation and offsetting strategies. Despite challenges in identifying Scope 3 emissions, the HKMA will adopt a multi-pronged approach within practicable limits to minimise Scope 3 GHG emissions (e.g., paper usage, waste generation, and air travel). The HKMA’s long-term and near-term emission reduction targets were developed based on the methodology of the Science Based Targets initiative, which has also been validated by the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency. The HKMA has appointed the Hong Kong Quality Assurance Agency to verify its emissions, energy consumption, paper usage, and waste dataset disclosed in this report6. The scope and basis of verification are set out in the “Verification Statement” section of this report. In 2023, in addition to publishing the 2022 Annual Report, the HKMA also published its first standalone 2022 Sustainability Report. The HKMA’s efforts in strengthening ESG reporting were recognised, receiving an ESG Award in the “Public Sector/Not-for-Profit Organisations” category at the “Best Corporate Governance and ESG Awards 2023” organised by the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants. The HKMA is the first financial regulators to receive an award in this category. The judging panel commended the HKMA for meeting good ESG standards, noting that the Sustainability Report is clear and readable, and that the appointment of an independent entity to verify its target-setting methodology and environmental data disclosed in the report reflects its promises to high transparency and accountable reporting. Moreover, the HKMA received the highest Gold Rating in the “Non-profit and Charitable Organisations” category at the “2023 Best Annual Reports Awards” organised by the Hong Kong Management Association. The judging panel praised the HKMA’s annual report for clearly presenting full financial information and making effective use of infographics, suggesting the HKMA’s determination to enhance financial literacy and promote financial inclusion. In recognition of the HKMA’s commitment to caring for the environment, staff, and the community at large, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service has presented the HKMA with the “15 Years+ Caring Organisation” logo for 17 consecutive years since 2006. The HKMA is committed to properly managing the environmental impact caused by its operations. Its internal Green Office Guidelines provided guidelines to staff on resource use and office waste generation. The HKMA has integrated environmental factors into the design, operations, and maintenance of its owned and leased offices. When renovating offices, existing furniture and fitting materials are reused wherever possible to reduce waste, and priority is given to environmentally friendly construction and decoration materials. The HKMA has consistently adhered to this practice, and as a result, was awarded LEED7 Gold certification and BEAM Plus Interiors8 Gold rating in 2021 and 2022 respectively for parts of its offices renovated at Two International Finance Centre. Adopting new technology and leveraging existing technology to improve energy efficiency remains one of the HKMA’s key areas of particular interest. In addition to promoting good habits, such as switching off unnecessary lighting in work areas outside office hours to save electricity, other energy-saving measures include the use of LED lighting, motion sensors, setting air-conditioning room temperatures at appropriate levels, and optimising energy use in IT network infrastructure. The HKMA’s energy consumption continued to decrease, reaching 2.59 MWh per capita9 in 2023, down 29.7% from the 2015 baseline (Chart 1). Given the simplicity of the HKMA’s day-to-day operations, its GHG emissions mainly stem from GHG emissions generated by electricity consumed from fossil fuels. In 2023, the combined intensity of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions from purchased fuel and electricity was 1.48 tCO2e10 per capita, a reduction of 45.2% compared to 2015 (Chart 2). In addition to standardising equipment, office software, and meeting facilities, the HKMA has adopted digital tools and technology, automated and streamlined workflows, built a digitalised working environment, and strengthened online collaboration within the organisation.11 Paperless meetings have become the primary mode of meetings at the HKMA. To further reduce paper usage and increase efficiency, various internal administrative matters are primarily handled through electronic processes. Furthermore, the HKMA encourages staff to embrace green and digitalised working modes, replacing paper-based documents and communications with digital alternatives. Meanwhile, work on implementing an electronic records keeping system is underway. The above green and digitalising measures have yielded positive results. The HKMA’s paper usage intensity in 2023 was 11.55 kg per capita, a notable decrease of 64.8% compared to 2015 (Chart 3). Following the pandemic, a significant share of international activities resumed in physical format. Meanwhile, to foster the development of Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centres, it was inevitable that HKMA staff had to undertake overseas business trips. To mitigate carbon emissions caused by air travel, the HKMA encourages staff participating in overseas activities to take direct flights or combine different business trips where feasible. At the institutional level, the HKMA reduced its Scope 3 emissions by 126 tCO2e in 2023 through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel. In addition, the HKMA participated in a Gold Standard12 certified carbon offset programme to offset the remaining carbon emissions caused by air travel; this programme involves waste-to-energy, solar power generation, and provision of efficient and cleaner cooking facilities in developing countries. The HKMA will continue to make similar arrangements in 2024. The HKMA’s procurement process takes into account sustainability and environmental factors. As part of a full review of the institution’s procurement policy and procedures, the existing practice of procuring green products has been formalised, complying with the environmental specifications of the government’s “Green Procurement List”, especially in the procurement of electrical appliances and office consumables. Moreover, ESG factors and innovative proposals that help enhance productivity and efficiency have been added to tender evaluation criteria. Meanwhile, all suppliers must promise to comply with environmental regulations. Adhering to the “4R” principles—Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle—the HKMA adopts a three-pronged approach to minimise waste generation and manage waste disposal. In addition, the HKMA conducted two waste audits in 2022 and 2023 to assist in formulating targeted waste management strategies. Details of non-hazardous waste generated, including general waste sent to landfills and various types of recyclable waste, are set out in the “Performance Summary” section on page 56. In 2023, the HKMA directly participated for the first time in the Lai See Recycling Programme organised by the property management company of the International Finance Centre offices. Staff handed in a total of about 3,000 used but intact lai see envelopes. These lai see envelopes were subsequently passed to an environmental organisation for distribution to the public for use in the following Lunar New Year.
